cases.title: NIKOLOV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Nikolov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Hristo Petrov Nikolov, is a Bulgarian national of Roma ethnic origin and a long-standing activist for Roma integration. The case arose after a televised interview on 17 April 2019, in which Mr. I.G., then Deputy Chief Prosecutor, made a remark implying that “Gypsies” commonly recant testimony in criminal proceedings, likening this to the conduct of other accused persons. Mr. Nikolov viewed this as a stigmatising and discriminatory statement by a high-ranking official, reinforcing negative stereotypes against Roma and contributing to their social exclusion. He sought redress through Bulgaria’s Commission for Protection from Discrimination, but his complaint was dismissed, and the decision was upheld by the administrative courts.

Mr. Nikolov brought his case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), arguing that the authorities’ refusal to address the discriminatory nature of the statement left him without protection. The Court examined whether the statement and the authorities’ response engaged the applicant’s rights under the Convention. Ultimately, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the circumstances did not reach the threshold required to trigger the protection of Articles 8 and 14 in this context. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: CASE OF KURUOVÁ AND HORVÁTHOVÁ v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In Kuruová and Horváthová v. Slovakia, the applicants, Ms Katarína Kuruová and Ms Helena Horváthová, are two sisters of Roma origin living in Milhosť, eastern Slovakia. Their case concerned police violence and ethnic discrimination during and after their arrest on 23 July 2019. The incident began after an altercation involving their relatives at a local pub, which led to police intervention. When the applicants arrived at the scene to understand the situation, a police patrol later came to Ms Kuruová’s house, arrested both women, and took them to the police station in Čaňa. During the arrest, the applicants alleged that police officers used excessive force—grabbing, hitting, and kicking them—and subjected them to ethnic slurs such as “gypsies” and “degenerates.” Medical examinations the following day confirmed injuries consistent with their account, including a fractured finger, contusions, and spinal injuries.

Despite the applicants’ prompt complaints and medical evidence, the domestic investigation was suspended, with authorities relying heavily on an expert report that did not rule out police involvement but also suggested the injuries could have resulted from a fall. The European Court of Human Rights found Slovakia in violation of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman and degrading treatment) both substantively and procedurally, and Article 14 taken with Article 3 (prohibition of discrimination), citing the authorities’ failure to adequately investigate the possibility of ethnically motivated police violence. The Court specifically noted the discriminatory language used by police and the lack of a thorough, impartial investigation into the applicants’ Roma identity as a factor in their treatment.

cases.title: CASE OF STALOVIĆ v. SERBIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment;Effective investigation)
cases.summary: In Stalović v. Serbia, the applicants were Mr. Marko Stalović, a Serbian national of Roma origin, and his wife, Ms. Sandra Stalović, an Austrian national. The case focused on racially motivated police ill-treatment and the failure of Serbian authorities to conduct an effective investigation, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma individuals to discriminatory abuse by law enforcement. On 21 April 2017, after reporting a car theft at the Mladenovac Police Station, the couple was subjected to polygraph testing and informal, unrecorded questioning at the Belgrade Police Directorate. Mr. Stalović alleged that he was forced to kneel, beaten, suffocated with a plastic bag, threatened with violence, and subjected to anti-Roma insults and threats regarding his children. Ms. Stalović reported threats, racist insults, and intimidation. Medical examinations shortly after the incident documented injuries and later diagnosed Mr. Stalović with PTSD. Despite their criminal complaint against eight police officers, the investigation was delayed, incomplete, and conducted by officers hierarchically superior to those implicated. The authorities dismissed key medical evidence and failed to address Ms. Stalović’s psychological ill-treatment. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) both substantively and procedurally, and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. Notably, the Court criticised the lack of independence and thoroughness in the investigation, setting a precedent for addressing racially motivated police violence against Roma in Serbia.

cases.title: D.J. v. NORWAY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In D.J. v. Norway, the applicant, D.J., identified as a member of the Roma community, challenged Norwegian child welfare decisions that severely restricted her contact with her daughter, X. The case centered on the vulnerability of Roma parents facing limitations on family life, including a prohibition on speaking the Romani language during supervised contact sessions and the placement of the child at an undisclosed address due to an assessed risk of abduction. The events unfolded between 2019 and 2022, following the removal of X from D.J.’s care and subsequent court proceedings in Norway. D.J. argued that the restrictions, particularly the language ban and police presence during visits, undermined her ability to demonstrate her caregiving abilities and maintain a meaningful relationship with her daughter.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that the Norwegian authorities had provided relevant and sufficient reasons for the measures, prioritizing X’s health and well-being, and had not abandoned the goal of future reunification. The Court also accepted the necessity of the language restriction and security measures in light of the abduction risk. Concluding that the interference was proportionate and necessary, the Court declared the application inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: CASE OF TAFZI EL HADRI AND EL IDRISSI MOUCH v. SPAIN
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life)
cases.summary:
In Tafzi El Hadri and El Idrissi Mouch v. Spain, the applicants, Mr. Khalil Tafzi El Hadri and Mr. Omar El Idrissi Mouch, both of Moroccan origin, brought a case against Spain after being named in a national newspaper article that linked them to Islamist radicalism in their roles as social educators at a residential centre for minors in Barcelona. The article, published by ABC in September 2011, alleged that educators like the applicants—hired for their ability to speak Moroccan dialects—were indoctrinating minors in Islamist fundamentalism and facilitating their recruitment into radical environments. The article also described an incident at another centre involving a fight between Moroccan and Roma-origin children, highlighting tensions and suggesting preferential treatment for Moroccan minors.

The applicants argued that the publication of these allegations, which identified them by name and associated them with radical Islam, seriously harmed their reputation and private life. They sought redress through Spain’s right of reply mechanism but ultimately claimed before the European Court of Human Rights that Spain had failed to protect their rights under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life).

The Court examined whether Spain had fulfilled its positive obligations under Article 8 and found no violation. It concluded that the applicants had access to appropriate legal remedies and that the Spanish authorities had struck a fair balance between the applicants’ rights and freedom of expression. The judgment did not establish any new precedent regarding the protection of minority educators from stigmatising media coverage.

cases.title: ISA v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Isa v. North Macedonia, the applicant, Ms. Nafi Isa, was represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and identified as a member of the Roma community. The case concerned allegations of discrimination and ill-treatment, raising issues under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically in conjunction with Article 3. The facts, as outlined in the Court’s documents, indicate that Ms. Isa brought her complaint in June 2023, but she passed away in 2025, after which her heir, Azire Isa, continued the proceedings.

The core of the case involved harm linked to the applicant’s Roma identity, with claims of discriminatory treatment and exclusion. However, before the Court could issue a substantive judgment, the parties reached a friendly settlement. The Government of North Macedonia agreed to pay €4,000 for non-pecuniary damage and €850 for costs and expenses to the applicant’s heir. The Court was satisfied that the settlement respected human rights as defined by the Convention and saw no grounds to continue examining the case. Accordingly, the application was struck out of the list under Article 39. No findings on the merits or specific legal precedents were established, as the case concluded through settlement.

cases.title: SELMANI AND SALIJI v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Selmani and Saliji v. North Macedonia, the applicants, Berton Selmani (born 2007) and Abidin Saliji (born 1998), brought a complaint against North Macedonia. While the judgment does not explicitly confirm their Roma or Traveller identity, the applicants’ names and the context suggest they may be from a Roma settlement. The case concerned allegations of harm or exclusion specifically affecting Roma individuals, as the application raised complaints under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) taken in conjunction with Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The facts, as set out in the judgment, indicate that the applicants claimed to have suffered discriminatory ill-treatment, though the precise circumstances are not detailed in the published decision.

The proceedings concluded with a friendly settlement between the parties. The Government of North Macedonia undertook to pay each applicant €3,000 for non-pecuniary damage and €850 for costs and expenses, with provisions for interest in case of late payment. The European Court of Human Rights was satisfied that the settlement respected human rights as defined in the Convention and, accordingly, struck the case out of its list under Article 39. No further findings or precedents were established, as the case was resolved without a full judgment on the merits.

cases.title: CASE OF ILAREVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Ilareva and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants—three individuals active in non-governmental organisations defending human rights, including those of minorities and refugees—brought a case against Bulgaria after being subjected to a wave of violent threats and hate speech online. While the applicants themselves were not explicitly identified as Roma or Travellers, the abuse included anti-Roma slurs such as “pikeys (mangali),” and the attacks targeted their advocacy for minority rights, including those of Roma and Travellers as defined by the Council of Europe.

Between 12 and 15 January 2015, the applicants were named and depicted in Facebook posts and comments that called for their murder, torture, and public humiliation. The posts, widely shared and “liked,” included explicit death threats and dehumanising language, with some comments referencing their support for “scumbags without a drop of Bulgarian blood” and using derogatory terms for Roma. The applicants reported these threats to the Sofia District Prosecutor’s Office, but the authorities suspended the investigation, citing legal barriers to identifying the perpetrators and denying the applicants victim status.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), both separately and in conjunction, recognising the authorities’ failure to protect the applicants from hate speech and threats motivated by their work for minority rights. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages, emphasising that the Bulgarian authorities’ inadequate response amounted to discriminatory treatment and a breach of their positive obligations under the Convention.

cases.title: CASE OF BYSTRÝ v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary: In Bystrý v. Slovakia, the applicants, Mr. A. Bystrý and Mr. M. Bystrý, were described in the judgment as coming from a Roma settlement, indicating their Roma background. The case concerned the vulnerability of individuals from a Roma community to police violence and the lack of an effective investigation into their allegations of ill-treatment. On 12 April 2020, during a police intervention in Slovakia, both applicants were arrested. The second applicant, Mr. M. Bystrý, was struck on the head with a metal baton, resulting in a depressed fracture of the frontal bone and multiple contusions, with an expected healing period of about thirty days. The first applicant, Mr. A. Bystrý, suffered concussion, contusions, and abrasions after being dragged to a police car while handcuffed, with injuries requiring five to six days to heal. Despite claims by the authorities that the force used was justified by the applicants’ conduct, the European Court of Human Rights found that the injuries were sufficiently serious to meet the threshold of Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court held that the force used was disproportionate and not strictly necessary, and that the subsequent investigation was inadequate, relying too heavily on police accounts and failing to thoroughly examine all evidence. The Court found violations of Article 3 in both its substantive and procedural aspects, awarding the applicants a total of EUR 16,500 in non-pecuniary damages and EUR 6,410 for costs and expenses.

cases.title: CASE OF KOVAČEVIĆ v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection allowed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Abuse of the right of application;Preliminary objection allowed (Art. 34) Individual applications;(Art. 34) Victim;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Abuse of the right of application;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae
cases.summary:
In Kovačević v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, the applicant, Mr. Slaven Kovačević, a dual national of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, brought a case against Bosnia and Herzegovina. While Mr. Kovačević’s ethnic background was a matter of contention during proceedings, the Court noted that information he provided about his ethnicity on the Sarajevo City Council’s website was considered deceptive and potentially relevant to the case. The core issue concerned the applicant’s claim of discrimination in his right to vote, specifically that the combination of ethnic and territorial requirements in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s electoral system prevented him from voting for candidates of his choice in both chambers of the Parliamentary Assembly and the Presidency. These requirements have been the subject of previous litigation by members of Roma and Traveller communities, but in this case, the applicant’s own minority status was not established.

The Grand Chamber examined complaints under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination). However, the Court found that Mr. Kovačević lacked victim status for his discrimination complaints, as he failed to demonstrate a sufficiently direct link between the alleged harm and his capacity as a voter. Furthermore, the Court found that his conduct during proceedings—particularly unsubstantiated accusations and offensive remarks targeting the Court and government representatives—amounted to an abuse of the right of application under Article 35 § 3(a). As a result, the application was declared inadmissible, and no violation was found. The judgment distinguished this case from Sejdić and Finci v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it concerned the active right to vote rather than the passive right to stand for election.

cases.title: CASE OF B.T. AND B.K.CS. v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Art. 34) Individual applications;(Art. 34) Petition;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary: In B.T. and B.K.Cs. v. Hungary, the applicants were a mother, B.T., of Roma origin, and her son, B.K.Cs., both living in Kesznyéten. The case, brought with the support of the European Roma Rights Centre, concerned the removal of B.K.Cs. from his mother immediately after birth and his subsequent placement in foster care. The authorities’ actions were rooted in concerns about B.T.’s “irresponsible lifestyle,” her previous children’s placement in care, and her living conditions, despite evidence of recent improvements. Notably, the health visitor and child welfare services recommended, without informing the parents, that the newborn should not be allowed home, citing B.T.’s smoking during pregnancy and her older children’s care status. On 7 May 2014, the Guardianship Authority suspended both parents’ rights and placed the baby in temporary care, a decision upheld on appeal. B.T. argued that the removal was based on outdated information and that the authorities failed to consider her improved circumstances, also alleging that Roma children were disproportionately taken into care in her community. After nearly two years, the child was returned to his parents when their living conditions were deemed adequate. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for family life), holding that the authorities had not sufficiently justified the removal or adequately considered less intrusive measures. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants.

cases.title: CASE OF NIKOLIĆ v. SERBIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary: In the case of Nikolić v. Serbia, the applicant, Mr. Matija Nikolić, a Serbian national of Roma origin represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, brought a complaint against the Republic of Serbia. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller children to police ill-treatment and the systemic failures in investigating such allegations. On 16 November 2012, when Mr. Nikolić was a minor, he was questioned by police at the Bački Petrovac Police Station regarding alleged thefts. He alleged that officers kicked him in the stomach and hit him in the head, causing him to lose consciousness and requiring emergency surgery for an incarcerated hernia. Despite his detailed complaint and the seriousness of his injuries, the initial investigation was conducted by the same police station implicated in the alleged abuse, and significant delays and procedural shortcomings followed. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. While the Court found insufficient evidence to establish that Mr. Nikolić’s injuries were caused by police ill-treatment, it ruled that the investigation was neither prompt nor independent, violating the procedural aspect of Article 3. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller individuals face in accessing justice, particularly in cases involving alleged police misconduct—a concern rooted in a long history of discrimination across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF SALAY v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+P1-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to education;Right to education - {general});Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Salay v. Slovakia, the applicant, Mr. Salay, grew up in a Roma community in Plavecký Štvrtok and was represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma children in Slovakia who are disproportionately placed in special education, often based on assessments that do not account for their social and linguistic backgrounds. Mr. Salay’s schooling began in 2004, when, after a school readiness test, he was placed in “Year Zero,” a preparatory class intended for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. He then entered a mainstream Year One class, but after further testing—using tools not adapted for Roma children—he was recommended for transfer to a special class for pupils with intellectual disabilities. From Year Two onwards, he remained in special classes, which, at his school, were attended exclusively by Roma pupils.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court found that Mr. Salay had been discriminated against in his access to education, as the procedures and tests used failed to consider his linguistic and cultural background, resulting in his unjustified placement in special education. The Court held that Slovakia had violated both Article 14 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, awarding Mr. Salay non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant for its detailed scrutiny of the systemic bias in educational assessments affecting Roma children in Slovakia.

cases.title: CASE OF CALDARAR AND OTHERS v. POLAND
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for private life)
cases.summary:
In Caldarar and Others v. Poland, the applicants were five families of Romanian nationals of Roma origin, including nine adults and seven children, who settled on municipal land at Paprotna Street in Wrocław. Their case concerned the vulnerability of Roma families living in informal settlements and facing eviction without adequate safeguards. The families began occupying the site around November 2009, erecting makeshift wooden and plastic cabins that served as their homes. Polish authorities repeatedly informed them that their occupation was illegal and, in May 2013, issued formal orders requiring them to vacate and clean up the land. Subsequent inspections found the structures to be unsafe, lacking basic utilities, and at risk of fire or collapse. Demolition orders were issued in September 2013, and the cabins were eventually destroyed, resulting in the loss of the applicants’ possessions.

Throughout this period, the applicants were offered temporary accommodation in shelters and municipal hostels, but they declined these options, citing unsuitability for their families’ needs. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found that the demolition of the applicants’ homes, without sufficient consideration of their specific circumstances and without providing genuinely suitable alternative accommodation, constituted a violation of Article 8. This judgment highlights the need for authorities to balance urban regulations with the fundamental rights of vulnerable Roma families facing eviction.

cases.title: CASE OF PANAYOTOPOULOS AND OTHERS v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Inhuman treatment;Prohibition of torture);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment;Prohibition of torture);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In Panayotopoulos and Others v. Greece, the applicants—Mr. Athanasios Panayotopoulos and two others—were identified in the judgment as members of the Roma ethnic group. The case focused on police violence and the failure of authorities to investigate possible racist motives, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma individuals to ill-treatment and discrimination by law enforcement. On 8 October 2016, the applicants were passengers in a car in Athens that was pursued and rammed by police. After fleeing and hiding on a balcony, they surrendered to police but alleged that officers used racist insults and physical violence during arrest, transport, and detention, resulting in serious injuries. Notably, Mr. Panayotopoulos required ten days of intensive hospital care for a heart attack and genital injuries. Despite requests from the applicants and their representatives for forensic examinations and investigations into the alleged torture and racist motivation, authorities failed to order timely medical assessments or conduct an effective inquiry.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment) both substantively and procedurally, and a violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 3 regarding the authorities’ failure to investigate possible discrimination. However, the Court did not find a substantive violation of Article 14 taken with Article 3. The judgment is significant for its explicit finding that the Greek authorities failed to investigate the potential racist motivation behind police violence against Roma applicants.

cases.title: CASE OF F.M. AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 4 - Prohibition of slavery and forced labour (Article 4 - Positive obligations;Article 4-1 - Servitude;Trafficking in human beings;Article 4-2 - Forced labour) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 4 - Prohibition of slavery and forced labour (Article 4 - Positive obligations;Article 4-1 - Trafficking in human beings) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 4 - Prohibition of slavery and forced labour (Article 4 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+4 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 4-2 - Forced labour;Article 4 - Prohibition of slavery and forced labour;Article 4-1 - Servitude;Trafficking in human beings);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of F.M. and Others v. Russia, the applicants were a group of women of Roma and Traveller origin who had been trafficked from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to Russia, specifically to the Golyanovo district of Moscow. Their Roma and Traveller identity was central to the case, as they were targeted for exploitation and faced additional barriers in seeking justice due to their minority status. The core harm involved their trafficking and prolonged exploitation in convenience stores, where they were confined, deprived of their identity documents, forced to work under abusive conditions, and subjected to threats and violence. Some applicants were minors at the time of recruitment, and one gave birth while in captivity, only to have her child taken from her.

Between 2002 and 2016, the applicants were lured to Moscow with false promises of work, then had their passports confiscated and were forced to work in stores owned by Russian nationals. They endured years of servitude, with little intervention from authorities despite repeated reports and complaints. When the women managed to escape with the help of activists, Russian police attempted to detain and deport them rather than protect them as victims, and investigations into their trafficking were repeatedly delayed or mishandled.

The European Court of Human Rights found Russia in violation of Article 4 (prohibition of slavery and forced labour), both substantively and procedurally, and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 4. The Court held that Russia failed to protect the applicants from trafficking, did not conduct an effective investigation, and discriminated against them as Roma and Traveller women. Non-pecuniary damages were awarded as just satisfaction.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the intersection of anti-Roma discrimination and human trafficking, reaffirming that states must take active measures to protect Roma and Traveller communities from exploitation—a persistent issue in Europe’s recent history.

cases.title: CASE OF B.B. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;Violation of Article 4 - Prohibition of slavery and forced labour (Article 4 - Positive obligations;Effective investigation;Article 4-1 - Trafficking in human beings) (Procedural aspect);Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In B.B. v. Slovakia, the applicant, a woman of Roma origin born in 1990 and raised in State care, brought a case against Slovakia concerning her exploitation and the State’s response. After leaving State care, she lived with a Roma family who took her savings, compelled her to work as a maid, and arranged her marriage to their son. When she became homeless, the family introduced her to a man, Y, who, as established by Slovakian courts, arranged for her to travel to the United Kingdom in 2010, where she engaged in prostitution for at least a year, handing over all her earnings to Y. The applicant alleged that Y paid the Roma family for her and that she was also forced to care for his household and was given drugs. Upon Y’s departure from the UK, she was eventually assisted by the Salvation Army and repatriated to Slovakia as a victim of trafficking.

Despite her vulnerable position—marked by Roma origin, intellectual disability, and mental illness—the Slovak authorities classified the offence as pimping rather than human trafficking, and removed her from victim support programmes. The European Court of Human Rights found that Slovakia failed in its positive obligation under Article 4 (prohibition of slavery and forced labour) to conduct an effective investigation into human trafficking. The Court awarded the applicant non-pecuniary damages, highlighting the procedural violation and the need for authorities to properly address the exploitation of vulnerable Roma individuals.

cases.title: AFFAIRE CONSEIL NATIONAL DE LA JEUNESSE DE MOLDOVA c. RÉPUBLIQUE DE MOLDOVA
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 10 - Liberté d'expression - {général} (Article 10-1 - Liberté d'expression);Préjudice moral - constat de violation suffisant (Article 41 - Préjudice moral;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary:
In the case of National Youth Council of Moldova v. Republic of Moldova, the applicant was a non-governmental organization based in Chișinău, which participated in the Coalition Non-Discrimination, a group of NGOs combating discrimination. The case arose from the applicant’s attempt in December 2011 to display a public awareness poster in Chișinău, promoting a free anti-discrimination hotline. The poster featured caricatures representing various marginalized groups, including a couple depicted as Roma—a man drawn with a wide-brimmed hat, long moustache, and vest, and a woman with exaggerated features and traditional clothing. The SINTI association, representing Roma in Chișinău, objected to the portrayal, arguing it was unflattering and misrepresented Roma people.

The city authorities, citing concerns from both Roma and disability organizations, refused permission to display the poster, claiming it could divide society and contravened advertising laws requiring honesty and decency. The applicant challenged this decision in court, arguing it violated their freedom of expression. However, Moldovan courts upheld the refusal, emphasizing the negative feedback from affected groups.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 10 (freedom of expression) and found a violation, holding that the authorities’ refusal was not a proportionate restriction. The Court considered the finding of a violation sufficient just satisfaction for any non-pecuniary damage. This judgment highlights the need for careful balancing between freedom of expression and the sensitivities of minority groups, especially when anti-discrimination efforts intersect with contested representations.

cases.title: DIAN v. DENMARK
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae
cases.summary:
In DIAN v. Denmark, the applicant, a Romanian national born in 1957, challenged his conviction and imprisonment for begging in Copenhagen. While the judgment does not explicitly confirm his Roma or Traveller identity, the applicant is described as a Romanian national who alternated between periods in Denmark and Romania, living as a homeless person during his stays in Denmark and relying on activities such as selling newspapers, collecting bottles, and begging for survival. The case centered on the harm of criminal penalties imposed on a person in a precarious situation for non-aggressive begging, raising questions about the proportionality of such measures under the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant was cautioned for begging in 2013, convicted and imprisoned for seven days in 2015, and again convicted in 2019 for begging on a pedestrian street, receiving a twenty-day prison sentence. He argued that he was unable to earn a living in Romania, was illiterate, and had no access to public income support. Danish courts acknowledged his vulnerable circumstances but found that he was not in a situation where begging was his only means of survival, noting his ability to travel, possession of cash, and support from his adult son.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible under Article 35, finding that the applicant’s situation did not reach the threshold of vulnerability required to engage Article 8 protections as interpreted in Lacatus v. Switzerland. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: CASE OF ZĂICESCU AND FĂLTICINEANU v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione temporis;Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life)
cases.summary:
In Zăicescu and Fălticineanu v. Romania, the applicants—Mr. Zăicescu and Ms. Fălticineanu, both Jewish survivors of the Holocaust—brought a case against Romania. While the applicants are not from the Roma or Traveller communities, their application concerned the broader context of state accountability for crimes committed during the Second World War, including the persecution of minorities such as Jews and Roma. The vulnerability at the heart of the case related to the applicants’ experiences as children during the Holocaust: Mr. Zăicescu survived the Iași pogrom, witnessing the murder of close family members and enduring deportation on a “death train,” while Ms. Fălticineanu was confined in a ghetto in Cernăuți, suffering deprivation and living in hiding for years.

The applicants sought access to judicial files and information about post-war trials of war criminals, as well as transparency regarding extraordinary appeals that had led to the acquittal of individuals convicted of war crimes. Their requests were initially met with administrative obstacles and delays. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding violations of both. The Court held that the applicants’ right to access information of fundamental importance to their personal and family history had been unjustifiably restricted, and that they had been discriminated against in this context. This judgment is significant for its recognition of the right of Holocaust survivors to access historical records and judicial transparency, reinforcing the importance of state accountability for past atrocities.

cases.title: CASE OF WA BAILE v. SWITZERLAND
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae;Violation of Article 14+8-1 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8-1 - Respect for private life;Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life);Violation of Article 13 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy)
cases.summary:
In Wa Baile v. Switzerland, the applicant, Mr. Wa Baile, a Swiss national described in the judgment as “dark-skinned,” challenged the lawfulness of a police identity check he experienced at Zürich railway station on 5 February 2015. While the judgment does not explicitly identify Mr. Wa Baile as Roma or Traveller, it details his experience of being singled out for an identity check in a crowd he described as “almost all white,” raising concerns of racial profiling—a harm frequently reported by Roma, Travellers, and other minorities. Mr. Wa Baile was stopped by three municipal police officers, ordered to raise his hands and spread his legs, and searched until his identity was confirmed. He protested, alleging racism and noting that his identity was checked “everywhere [he] go[es].” He was subsequently fined for refusing to comply with police orders, and his appeals through the Swiss courts were unsuccessful, with authorities finding no evidence of discrimination.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found violations of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, as well as Article 13, concluding that Mr. Wa Baile had been discriminated against and lacked an effective remedy for his complaint. Notably, the Court highlighted the need for effective safeguards against ethnic profiling in police identity checks, marking a significant precedent for addressing discriminatory policing practices in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF S.B. v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 7 - Procedural safeguards relating to expulsion of aliens
cases.summary:
In S.B. v. North Macedonia, the applicant, S.B., is a Serbian national who identifies as Roma and fled Kosovo in 1999. She was granted refugee status in North Macedonia, where she has lived with her partner and five children. The case centers on her vulnerability as a Roma refugee facing expulsion on national security grounds, without being given a meaningful opportunity to know or challenge the evidence against her.

On 9 March 2017, the Ministry of the Interior terminated S.B.’s refugee status and ordered her to leave the country, citing national security but providing no factual basis for this assessment. S.B., represented by a lawyer, contested the decision, arguing there was no evidence she posed a threat. Both the Administrative Court and the Higher Administrative Court upheld the Ministry’s decision, with the latter referencing unspecified information about Kosovo and the applicant’s family situation, but again without disclosing the evidence or allowing S.B. to respond to it.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 7, which guarantees procedural safeguards in expulsion proceedings. The Court found a violation, concluding that S.B. was denied the opportunity to know and comment on the evidence used against her, undermining the essence of her procedural rights. The judgment underscores the necessity for adversarial proceedings and effective judicial scrutiny, especially when expulsion measures affect fundamental rights.

cases.title: CASE OF MEMEDOVA AND OTHERS v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Art. 34) Individual applications;(Art. 34) Victim;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;Violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 - Freedom of movement-{general} (Article 2 para. 2 of Protocol No. 4 - Freedom to leave a country);Violation of Article 14+P4-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 para. 2 of Protocol No. 4 - Freedom to leave a country;Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 - Freedom of movement-{general});Pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Memedova and Others v. North Macedonia, the applicants were Macedonian nationals from the Roma community who challenged the authorities’ refusal to let them leave the country. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing ethnic profiling and discriminatory restrictions on freedom of movement. On 29 November 2014, Ms. Memedova was stopped at Skopje Airport, her passport stamped and then cancelled, and she was told she could not travel because she allegedly posed a threat to public policy and lacked sufficient financial means or a return ticket. She reported that a border officer had remarked she would seek asylum “like other Roma persons.” Despite providing evidence of her family in Germany and previous lawful travel, her appeals in domestic courts were unsuccessful, with authorities insisting she failed to justify her travel purpose.

The European Court of Human Rights examined Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding violations of both. The Court held that the authorities had applied additional, arbitrary requirements to Roma individuals and had failed to justify the restrictions, amounting to ethnic discrimination. The applicants were awarded compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. Notably, the judgment highlighted the systemic nature of ethnic profiling at North Macedonian borders, referencing domestic court findings and Ombudsman reports confirming discriminatory practices against Roma and Travellers.

cases.title: PÉROLA DE MATOS v. PORTUGAL
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of Pérola de Matos v. Portugal, the applicant, Mr. Rui André Pérola de Matos, a Portuguese national who identified as being of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Portugal. Central to his case was the harm he alleged from the use of a social report in his criminal trial, which he claimed contained discriminatory assertions about his Roma background, raising concerns about bias and the fairness of the proceedings. The events began in February 2017, when Mr. Pérola de Matos was convicted by the Leiria Criminal Court of aggravated forgery and attempted aggravated fraud, with his conviction later upheld by the Coimbra Court of Appeal in June 2018. He pursued multiple appeals, including to the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court, arguing that the evidence used against him was tainted by discrimination and that he was denied a fair hearing. The European Court of Human Rights examined his complaints under Articles 6 (right to a fair trial), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that Mr. Pérola de Matos had not complied with procedural requirements, notably the six-month time limit for lodging complaints, and that his access to the Constitutional Court had not been unreasonably restricted. Although no violation was found, the case highlights the procedural hurdles Roma and Traveller applicants may face when seeking redress for discrimination in European courts, reflecting ongoing challenges in ensuring effective access to justice for these communities.

cases.title: BOLMANDÎR AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.summary:
In Bolmandîr and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Nicolae Bolmandîr, Daniel Bălan, Adrian Bolmandîr, and Sorin Condurache—are Romanian nationals residing in Constanța. While the judgment does not explicitly confirm their Roma or Traveller identity, the applicants are described as coming from a context often associated with Roma settlements in Romania. The case centered on their complaints regarding the fairness of criminal proceedings against them, specifically under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to a fair trial. The applicants argued that the appeal court failed to rehear all witnesses, did not allow adequate time and facilities to prepare their defense, and did not address all their grounds of appeal, raising concerns about procedural fairness—a frequent issue for Roma and Traveller applicants who may face systemic barriers in accessing justice.

The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the appeal court’s handling of evidence and procedural decisions amounted to a violation of Article 6. The Court found that the appeal court had thoroughly reviewed the evidence, provided sufficient reasoning for its decisions, and did not act arbitrarily or unreasonably in declining to rehear all witnesses. It concluded that the applicants’ complaints were manifestly ill-founded and declared the application inadmissible. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded. The judgment contains no specific remarks distinguishing it as a precedent in Roma or Traveller rights jurisprudence.

cases.title: KOVÁČOVÁ AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Kovácová and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants—Ms. Veronika Kovácová, Ms. Nikola Miková, and Mr. Milan Miko—are Slovak nationals from Zborov, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The application concerned police intervention in a Roma community in Zborov on Easter Sunday, 16 April 2017. That evening, following reports of violent incidents between two families, police responded to escalating unrest. Reinforcements arrived, and officers used coercive measures, including batons, to disperse a crowd of around one hundred people. Ms. Kovácová alleged she was struck twice on the arm with a baton, while Ms. Miková claimed she was hit once on the legs. The third applicant’s wife, as shown in a video later broadcast on television, was pushed by an officer and fell to the ground.

The applicants argued that these actions amounted to racially motivated ill-treatment by the police, that the subsequent investigation was inadequate, and that they were denied effective remedies, invoking Articles 3, 8, 13, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, after examining the facts and the domestic proceedings—including a criminal investigation, appeals, and a constitutional complaint—the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible. The Court found no appearance of a violation of the Convention, concluding that the authorities’ response and investigation met the required standards.

cases.title: BÓDI AND OTHERS v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Bódi and Others v. Hungary, the applicants—Kálmán Bódi, his son, brother, and nephew—are all of Roma origin, as stated in the judgment. The case arose from a violent attack on 22 August 2014, when the applicants, working as community workers cleaning a creek bed near the village of Balaton, were assaulted by a group of 8-10 men. The attackers, some wearing insignia linked to the right-wing paramilitary group “Outlaws’ Army,” used weapons such as baseball bats, crowbars, and knives, and reportedly shouted anti-Roma insults during the assault. The applicants suffered serious injuries, including broken bones and contusions.

Following the attack, the applicants filed a criminal complaint with the police, who opened an investigation for aggravated bodily assault. Although one suspect was arrested and evidence was seized, the investigation was discontinued in February 2015, and the applicants’ requests to have the case treated as a hate crime and transferred to a higher authority were denied. The applicants alleged that the authorities failed to investigate the racist motives behind the attack, raising issues under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: AVDIU AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Avdiu and Others v. Albania, the applicants were a group of Albanian nationals from Berat, identified in domestic proceedings as Roma pupils and their families. Their complaint focused on the segregation of Roma children in the Avdyl Avdya school, which the Albanian Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination had found to be discriminatory on racial grounds. The applicants alleged that this segregation amounted to a violation of their right not to be discriminated against in education.

The facts reveal that, following the Commissioner’s decision in December 2015, Albanian authorities acknowledged the discrimination and took steps to remedy it. The Avdyl Avdya school was closed in 2018, and from the second semester of the 2017/2018 school year, the municipality provided transport and reimbursement for Roma children to attend a non-segregated school, where the quality of education was deemed adequate.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (prohibition of discrimination). However, it declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the authorities had acknowledged the violation and taken effective measures to end the segregation. Furthermore, the applicants had not pursued available domestic remedies for compensation, as required. As a result, the Court concluded that the applicants could no longer claim to be victims of the alleged violation, and their complaint was rejected.

cases.title: CASE OF JÍROVÁ AND OTHERS v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life)
cases.summary:
In Jírová and Others v. the Czech Republic, the applicants—two adults and a child—challenged the Czech authorities’ handling of a foster care placement. The applicants lived in Hodkovice nad Mohelkou; the third applicant, a child born in 1998, had been placed in institutional care as an infant due to his mother’s inability to care for him and the absence of a named father. The case materials do not explicitly state a Roma or Traveller identity for the applicants, nor do they indicate that the child came from a Roma settlement.

The core issue was the disruption of the foster care arrangement: after being placed with the first and second applicants in 2004 and officially entrusted to their care in 2005, the child remained with them until 2011. The applicants argued that the authorities’ decisions regarding the child’s placement and subsequent contact restrictions violated their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The Court examined whether the Czech authorities had acted in the best interests of the child and whether the applicants’ Article 8 rights had been breached. It found that the authorities had considered the child’s welfare and the evolving family situation, and that the procedural safeguards were adequate. Ultimately, the Court declared the complaints inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded and found no violation of Article 8. The judgment did not establish any new precedent or make specific remarks distinguishing the case.

cases.title: CASE OF SZOLCSÁN v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+P1-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to education-{general};Right to education);Respondent State to take individual measures (Article 46-2 - Individual measures);Respondent State to take measures of a general character (Article 46-2 - General measures);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Szolcsán v. Hungary, the applicant, a child of Roma ethnic origin living in Piliscsaba, challenged the Hungarian authorities over his experience of racial segregation in education. The case focused on the applicant’s enrolment in the Jókai Mór primary school during the 2013/14 school year—a school attended almost exclusively by Roma children, despite Roma making up only a small fraction of the local population. The applicant argued that the school’s poor curriculum and limited resources, combined with the authorities’ refusal to allow his transfer to a neighbouring, more inclusive school, amounted to discriminatory treatment and educational exclusion based on his Roma identity.

After his transfer request to the Dózsa György school was denied on the grounds of catchment area, the applicant pursued appeals through the educational district, administrative courts, and ultimately the Constitutional Court, all of which rejected his claims. He contended that the authorities’ actions perpetuated segregation and denied him access to quality, inclusive education.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding that Hungary had violated these provisions. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages and ordered both individual and general measures to address the segregation. Notably, the judgment required Hungary to take concrete steps to remedy the applicant’s situation and to prevent similar discrimination in the future.

cases.title: CASE OF M.B. AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA (No. 2)
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In M.B. and Others v. Slovakia (No. 2), the applicants were six boys from a housing estate in Košice mainly inhabited by Roma, with their Roma identity implied throughout the judgment. The case concerned their treatment by police following their arrest on 21 March 2009, after an assault and robbery for which some of the applicants were later convicted. At the police station, the boys alleged they were subjected to severe abuse: they were thrown on the floor in front of unmuzzled, barking dogs, some were bitten, and all were beaten, kicked, and verbally abused, including with anti-Roma slurs. Video footage later surfaced showing police officers ordering the boys to slap and kiss each other, strip naked, and threatening them with dogs, accompanied by racist language.

Despite the gravity of the allegations and the existence of video evidence, the domestic investigation and prosecution were protracted and ultimately ineffective. The District Court acquitted the accused officers, refusing to admit the video evidence, and the applicants were referred to civil courts for damages.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) both substantively and procedurally, and a violation of Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3 regarding the failure to investigate possible racist motives. However, the Court did not find a substantive violation of Article 14 taken with Article 3. The applicants were awarded non-pecuniary damages. The judgment is significant for its finding that the authorities failed to investigate the potential racist motivation behind the police abuse.

cases.title: SALIM AND OTHERS v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In Salim and Others v. North Macedonia, the applicants—Sevdija Salim, Senad Salim, Ajten Bekir, and Suvat Bekir—were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and brought their case against North Macedonia. The applicants were identified as members of Roma households, as indicated by their representation and the context of the complaint. The case concerned allegations of discrimination specifically affecting Roma individuals, focusing on harm or exclusion related to their ethnic identity. The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), taken together with Article 2 § 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement), suggesting that they faced discriminatory restrictions or treatment in relation to their movement or residence.

The facts, as outlined in the judgment, indicate that the applicants lodged their complaint in May 2019, and the government subsequently offered a friendly settlement. The parties agreed to a payment of 3,150 euros per household as compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, as well as costs and expenses. The European Court of Human Rights, satisfied that the settlement respected human rights as defined by the Convention, struck the case out of its list in accordance with Article 39. No further examination of the merits or findings on discrimination were made, as the friendly settlement resolved the dispute.

cases.title: CASE OF MACATĖ v. LITHUANIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-b) No significant disadvantage;Violation of Article 10 - Freedom of expression-{general} (Article 10-1 - Freedom of expression;Freedom to impart information);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
The case of Macatė v. Lithuania concerned Ms. Neringa Dangvydė Macatė, a Lithuanian national and professional writer who was openly homosexual. Although not a member of the Roma or Traveller communities, her case is notable for its focus on the rights of marginalised groups, as her children’s book aimed to foster acceptance of those who “looked or lived differently,” including members of various stigmatised minorities. In 2013, her collection of fairy tales—intended for primary school children and reviewed as suitable for promoting tolerance—was published with support from the Lithuanian Ministry of Culture. Two stories depicted same-sex marriage. After publication, the University’s publishing house suspended distribution, citing concerns that the book might be harmful to minors under Lithuanian law. Distribution resumed only after the book was labelled as potentially harmful to children under 14.

Ms. Macatė challenged these measures, arguing they violated her freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights found that the restrictions imposed on her book constituted a violation of Article 10, as the interference was not necessary in a democratic society and failed to consider the book’s aim of promoting tolerance. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant for its clear stance that state-imposed restrictions on literature promoting acceptance of marginalised groups, including sexual minorities, are incompatible with the Convention’s protection of free expression.

cases.title: CASE OF ELMAZOVA AND OTHERS v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Art. 34) Individual applications;(Art. 34) Victim;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione personae;Violation of Article 14+P1-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to education-{general};Right to education);Respondent State to take measures of a general character (Article 46-2 - General measures);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia, the applicants—Roma parents and pupils from the Bair district in Bitola—brought a case against North Macedonia, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The applicants identified as Roma and challenged the ethnic segregation of Roma children in the State-run primary school G.S. during the 2018/19 academic year. They alleged that, due to the implementation of catchment area policies and transfer practices, Roma pupils were concentrated in G.S., while ethnic Macedonian children from the same area attended the nearby T.A. school. The applicants argued that this led to de facto segregation, with G.S. becoming known locally as the “Romani or Gypsy school,” and that Roma pupils received inferior education and fewer opportunities for integration.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court found that the State’s policies resulted in indirect discrimination and segregation of Roma pupils, violating both Article 14 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants and, notably, ordered North Macedonia to adopt general measures to address systemic segregation in education. This judgment stands out for its explicit recognition of ethnic segregation as a systemic problem and its requirement for the State to implement broader reforms beyond individual compensation.

cases.title: CASE OF G.M. AND OTHERS v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment;Positive obligations) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment;Positive obligations) (Substantive aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In G.M. and Others v. the Republic of Moldova, the applicants—three women with intellectual disabilities who had been institutionalised in the Bălți neuropsychiatric residential asylum—brought a case against Moldova. The applicants were described as residents of the asylum, and while the judgment does not explicitly confirm their Roma or Traveller identity, it notes that they were part of a particularly vulnerable group due to their disabilities and institutionalisation. The case centred on grave abuses: the applicants alleged that, during their stays at the asylum between 1988 and 2013, they were repeatedly raped by a senior doctor, became pregnant, and were subjected to forced abortions and the non-consensual insertion of intrauterine contraceptive devices.

The authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into these allegations. Despite the applicants’ criminal complaints in 2014, the Moldovan police and prosecutors repeatedly refused to initiate proceedings, relying on incomplete or inadequate evidence and disregarding the applicants’ lack of consent. Domestic law at the time did not require patient consent for abortion, and the applicants’ intellectual disabilities were used to justify the interventions.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), both in its substantive and procedural aspects, due to the forced medical interventions and the authorities’ failure to investigate. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. This judgment is significant for its recognition of the compounded vulnerability of institutionalised women with intellectual disabilities and the need for robust safeguards against abuse.

cases.title: CALDARAS ET LUPU c. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Irrecevable
cases.summary:
In the case of Caldaras and Lupu v. France, the applicants, Mr. Stefan Caldaras and Mr. Vasile Lupu, are Romanian nationals belonging to the Roma community, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. Their complaint was brought against France and concerned the dismantling of a makeshift camp at Porte de Paris, Saint-Denis, where they and their families, as Roma, lived in precarious conditions. The core vulnerability at issue was the forced eviction of Roma families from informal settlements without provision of alternative accommodation, raising concerns of inhuman and degrading treatment and ethnic discrimination.

The facts unfolded between 2012 and 2014. After the authorities noted the presence of the camp in late 2012, the public landowner sought a court order for immediate eviction. Although initially refused, the Paris Court of Appeal ultimately ordered the expulsion of the applicants and other occupants in January 2014, following a social assessment as required by French policy. The applicants argued that their eviction, without rehousing, violated Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

However, the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation of the Convention. This decision highlights the ongoing legal and social challenges faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe regarding housing rights and forced evictions, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and inadequate protection for these communities.

cases.title: STAN c. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Irrecevable
cases.summary: In the case of Stan v. France, the applicant, Ms. Silvia-Clara Stan, a Romanian national belonging to the Roma community, brought a complaint against France. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma families living in informal settlements and the impact of forced evictions without adequate alternative accommodation. Ms. Stan and her family had been living in a makeshift camp in Champs-sur-Marne since March 2015, when local authorities issued an eviction order citing public safety concerns. Although emergency accommodation was offered, Ms. Stan refused the temporary hotel stay, and the authorities also made available a gymnasium for temporary shelter. Ms. Stan challenged the eviction before the administrative court, arguing that the expulsion without proper rehousing amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment and violated her right to respect for private and family life, as protected by Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the authorities had taken reasonable steps to offer emergency accommodation and that Ms. Stan had access to legal remedies. This decision highlights the ongoing legal complexities surrounding Roma settlements in Europe, reflecting the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing stable housing and protection from forced evictions.

cases.title: SISU ET AUTRES c. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Irrecevable
cases.summary: In the case of Sisu and Others v. France, the applicants were nine Romanian nationals belonging to the Roma community, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, who brought a complaint against France. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma families living in precarious conditions, specifically the harm caused by the forced dismantling of their informal settlement without provision of alternative accommodation. The applicants and their families had been living in makeshift dwellings on land owned by SNCF Réseau in Paris, when, following a court order in September 2015, they were expelled from the site due to safety concerns related to its proximity to railway tracks. Despite two social assessments and some medical intervention, the applicants argued that the expulsion, carried out without rehousing, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment and violated their right to respect for private and family life, as protected by Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and that they lacked an effective remedy (Article 13). The European Court of Human Rights, however, declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation of the Convention. This decision highlights the ongoing legal and social challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, particularly regarding access to adequate housing and protection from forced evictions, issues rooted in a long history of marginalisation.

cases.title: CASE OF SLÁDKOVÁ v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment)
cases.summary:
In the case of Sládková v. the Czech Republic, the applicant, Ms. Sládková, a woman perceived by police officers as being of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Czech Republic. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals to racially motivated police abuse and the failure of authorities to investigate such incidents effectively. On 18 February 2013, while intoxicated in a Prague restaurant, Ms. Sládková was arrested following an altercation and taken to the Nové Město police station. There, she was handcuffed, her legs tied, and she was subjected to rough treatment, including choking, racial insults such as “black bitch,” and sexually degrading remarks. Despite her disability and requests for medication, officers denied her anxiolytics and continued to threaten and insult her during her transfer the next day. Medical examinations documented bruises and psychological trauma.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found a violation of Article 3 due to the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into Ms. Sládková’s allegations but did not find that the substantive threshold for inhuman or degrading treatment was met. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent risks of police mistreatment and inadequate investigations faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of institutional discrimination.

cases.title: CASE OF BAKIRDZI AND E.C. v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+P1-3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to free elections-{general};Elections by secret ballot;Free expression of the opinion of the people;Stand for election);Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Bakirdzi and E.C. v. Hungary, the applicants—Ms. K. Bakirdzi, of Greek national minority background, and E.C., of Armenian national minority background—challenged Hungary’s system for parliamentary representation of national minorities. While neither applicant belonged to the Roma or Traveller communities, the case is relevant for all recognised minorities, including Roma, as Hungary’s electoral law applies the same rules to each group. The applicants argued that the system, introduced in 2014, effectively excluded minority voters from meaningful participation: once registered as minority voters, individuals could only vote for a single, closed list of candidates submitted by their own minority’s self-government, with no influence over candidate selection or order, and were barred from voting for national party lists. In the 2014 elections, none of the thirteen recognised minorities—including the Roma, who had over 14,000 registered voters—were able to reach the preferential threshold required for a parliamentary seat, leaving minority voters without effective representation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). It found that the system discriminated against minority voters by restricting their electoral choices and failing to ensure genuine representation, in violation of both articles. The Court held that the finding of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant for its explicit recognition that Hungary’s minority voting system, as applied, failed to provide real and effective political participation for national minorities.

cases.title: CASE OF PAKETOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Art. 34) Individual applications;(Art. 34) Victim;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for home;Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Paketova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were members of several Roma families living in the village of Voyvodinovo, Plovdiv region. Their case arose from a series of events beginning on 6 January 2019, when a fight involving a Roma youth and a non-Roma member of the military led to the arrest and detention of the Roma youth. That evening, anti-Roma protests erupted in the village, with demonstrators—including followers of radical groups—shouting threats and anti-Roma slogans. Fearing for their safety, nearly all Roma residents fled their homes overnight, leaving the neighbourhood deserted.

Over the following days, protests continued, accompanied by inflammatory statements from public officials, including the Deputy Prime Minister, who made derogatory remarks about the Roma and called for the demolition of their homes. Local authorities swiftly issued demolition orders for buildings in the Roma neighbourhood, and several structures were razed. The applicants, displaced and unable to return home due to ongoing threats and lack of police protection, faced severe disruption to their family life, housing, and education of their children.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention, ruling that the authorities had failed to protect the applicants from discriminatory treatment and had not taken adequate measures to safeguard their rights. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. Notably, the judgment highlighted the role of official rhetoric and state action in exacerbating the applicants’ vulnerability and exclusion.

cases.title: HYSENAJ v. ALBANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Hysenaj v. Albania, the applicant, Ms. Xhevrije Hysenaj, an Albanian national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Republic of Albania. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals in accessing justice, particularly when their rights as victims are at stake. In February 2011, Ms. Hysenaj’s home in Tirana was set on fire by two individuals, B.V. and D.V.
