Although the authorities opened a criminal investigation and Ms. Hysenaj requested to be kept informed and to lodge a civil claim, she was not notified about the progress of the case or the trial. The accused were convicted and sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, but Ms. Hysenaj only learned of the judgment after the trial had concluded, effectively preventing her from participating or seeking compensation within those proceedings.

Ms. Hysenaj argued that this failure violated her right of access to a court under Article 6, as well as her rights under Articles 13 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alleging discrimination based on her Roma origin. However, the European Court of Human Rights found the application inadmissible, noting that Ms. Hysenaj could have pursued a separate civil claim for compensation regardless of the criminal proceedings. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller individuals may face in seeking justice, but also clarifies the Court’s approach to access to court claims. It reflects ongoing challenges for Roma communities in Europe, who have historically encountered obstacles in securing equal treatment before the law.

cases.title: CASE OF Y.P. v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae;Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary: In Y.P. v. Russia, the applicant, a woman from Krasnoyarsk described in the judgment as living in a Roma settlement, brought a case against Russia after being sterilised without her informed consent. The case highlights the vulnerability of women from Roma settlements to medical interventions that disregard their autonomy and reproductive rights. In August 2008, while in her thirtieth week of pregnancy, the applicant was admitted to a municipal maternity hospital due to complications. She signed a consent form for a Caesarean section explicitly excluding sterilisation. During surgery, doctors discovered a uterine rupture and, after a panel discussion, decided to suture the uterus but also sealed her only remaining fallopian tube, effectively sterilising her. The applicant was not properly informed about the sterilisation or its consequences, and was even advised not to tell her husband. She only learned the full implications two years later when she was unable to conceive. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), emphasising the lack of informed consent and the disregard for the applicant’s autonomy. The Court awarded her compensation for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment underscores the necessity of respecting patient autonomy, particularly for women from vulnerable communities, in medical decision-making.

cases.title: CASE OF J.I. v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of J.I. v. Croatia, the applicant, a woman of Roma origin living in Zagreb, brought a complaint against Croatia concerning the authorities’ response to threats and intimidation by her father, who had previously been convicted of raping her. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller women who are survivors of sexual violence, especially when facing ongoing threats and seeking protection from state authorities. After her father was imprisoned for multiple acts of rape and incest, he was later granted prison leave in 2015. During these periods, the applicant learned from relatives that he was searching for her and had threatened to kill her, prompting her to contact the police on several occasions out of fear for her safety. Despite her repeated pleas and clear distress, the police response was dismissive and failed to initiate an effective investigation or provide adequate protection, with officers at times displaying insensitivity and a lack of support.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, focusing on the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation. The Court found a violation of Article 3, concluding that Croatian authorities had not taken the applicant’s situation seriously enough or acted with the necessary diligence. The applicant was awarded compensation for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the duty of states to protect Roma and Traveller women from repeat victimisation and to ensure that their complaints are treated with the seriousness and sensitivity required, particularly in light of the historical marginalisation and discrimination faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF P.H. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2 - Positive obligations;Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of P.H. v. Slovakia, the applicant, a sixteen-year-old girl of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Slovakia concerning her treatment by police and the state’s failure to protect her life. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller children in police custody, especially regarding the risk of ill-treatment and the lack of safeguards for their well-being. On 17 January 2017, P.H. was apprehended for petty theft in a shopping mall and transported to a police station in Spišská Nová Ves. During the journey, she alleged that police officers used racial slurs and slapped her, and at the station, she was left unsupervised near a window, from which she fell seven metres to the ground, sustaining serious injuries and memory loss. The authorities’ investigation into her allegations was superficial and failed to address the possible connection between her Roma identity, the alleged abuse, and her fall.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 (right to life), both its substantive and procedural aspects. The Court found that Slovakia had violated Article 2 by failing to protect P.H.’s life while in custody and by not conducting an effective investigation into the incident. The Court awarded her compensation for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the obligation of states to ensure the safety and dignity of Roma and Traveller children in detention, against a backdrop of persistent discrimination and inadequate protection in Europe.

cases.title: SUCHÝ v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Suchý v. the Czech Republic, the applicant, Mr. Jaroslav Suchý, brought a complaint against the Czech Republic concerning discrimination in education. The application, as described in the Court’s appendix, raised issues under Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, specifically alleging discrimination against Roma pupils. While the judgment does not explicitly confirm Mr. Suchý’s Roma identity, the context and nature of the complaint—discrimination of Roma pupils—imply that he is from a Roma background or acting in relation to Roma educational exclusion.

The case centered on the vulnerability of Roma children facing unequal treatment in the Czech education system, a longstanding issue in the country. Mr. Suchý alleged that Roma pupils were subjected to discriminatory practices, particularly in access to and quality of education. The application was lodged in February 2016.

Before the Court could rule on the merits, the parties reached a friendly settlement. The Czech Government agreed to pay Mr. Suchý 4,000 euros in compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, resolving the dispute. The Court, satisfied that the settlement respected human rights, struck the case out of its list in September 2022. No formal finding of a violation was made, as the matter was resolved amicably.

cases.title: CASE OF MATA v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect)
cases.summary:
In Mata v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. Péter Mata, a Hungarian national described in the judgment as being of Roma origin, brought a case against Hungary concerning his alleged ill-treatment by police and the possible racist motives behind it. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police brutality and racially motivated abuse. On the night of 8–9 September 2014, police were called to a party in the village of Fulókércs. After an altercation, Mr. Mata was handcuffed and taken to the Encs Police Department. He alleged that during the 15-kilometre journey and at the police station, he was repeatedly hit, subjected to anti-Roma insults, and sprayed with tear gas. Medical reports the following day confirmed chest contusions and an open wrist wound, which was aggravated by handcuffing over a recent surgical site. Despite Mr. Mata’s prompt complaint and consistent account, the domestic investigation was discontinued for lack of evidence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and found that Mr. Mata had sustained injuries while in police custody, and the authorities failed to provide a convincing alternative explanation. The Court unanimously found a violation of Article 3 and awarded Mr. Mata €19,500 in non-pecuniary damages and €5,000 for costs and expenses. The judgment did not separately address the alleged racist motivation or the adequacy of the investigation, considering the main legal issue resolved.

cases.title: CASE OF BALKASI AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect)
cases.summary:
In Balkasi and Others v. Albania, the applicants were members of a Roma family living in Tirana, who alleged police ill-treatment and a lack of effective investigation following a violent incident in their former home village of Fier. On 13 December 2013, police officers entered the applicants’ garden while searching for a fugitive. According to the applicants, the officers—masked and armed—forced entry, assaulted several family members, and threatened reprisals if they complained. The applicants sought medical attention the next day but were told to file a criminal complaint first. When they attempted to do so at the local police station, officers refused to record their complaint and discouraged further action, with one officer apologizing and suggesting a friendly settlement. The family also reported the incident to the People’s Advocate, Albania’s ombudsman institution.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found no substantive violation of Article 3, as the evidence did not conclusively establish that the applicants suffered treatment reaching the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment. However, the Court found a procedural violation of Article 3, holding that Albanian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the applicants’ credible allegations of police violence. This judgment highlights the obligation of states to investigate claims of ill-treatment, especially when raised by vulnerable groups such as Roma families.

cases.title: CASE OF X AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list (Art. 37) Striking out applications-{general};(Art. 37-1-a) Absence of intention to pursue application;Violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 - General prohibition of discrimination (Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 - General prohibition of discrimination);Respondent State to take individual measures (Article 46-2 - Individual measures);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In X and Others v. Albania, the applicants were children from Roma and Egyptian communities attending the “Naim Frashëri” elementary school in Korça, Albania. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Egyptian pupils who, over several academic years, made up between 89% and 100% of the school’s population. This concentration resulted from a food assistance programme intended to boost attendance among Roma and Egyptian children, but which inadvertently led to their segregation from other pupils. Despite recommendations from Albania’s Commissioner for the Protection from Discrimination and the People’s Advocate to address this imbalance, the authorities’ measures—such as expanding food support and proposing school mergers—failed to significantly alter the school’s ethnic composition. By the 2019/20 academic year, Roma and Egyptian pupils still accounted for 60–90% of the school’s enrolment, with applicants alleging that non-Roma/Egyptian pupils were only nominally registered.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination) and found a violation, recognising that the applicants had suffered indirect discrimination in access to education. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages and required Albania to take individual measures. Notably, the judgment underscores that even well-intentioned policies can perpetuate segregation if not carefully implemented and monitored.

cases.title: CASE OF L.F. v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
cases.summary:
In L.F. v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. L.F., was a resident of Gyöngyöspata and identified in the judgment as a member of the Roma community. The case arose from a period of heightened anti-Roma sentiment in the town, following paramilitary marches and the election of a new mayor associated with the Jobbik party in July 2011. Amidst these tensions, on 13 October 2011, the mayor, accompanied by municipal officials and police officers, entered and inspected every room of Mr. L.F.’s home without prior notice or explanation. The applicant’s wife and children were present during the inspection, which was allegedly recorded on video. The stated justification was to check compliance with housing regulations and to verify eligibility for social benefits, but subsequent investigations revealed there was no legal basis or ongoing procedure that would have permitted such an intrusion.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right to respect for private and family life, including the home. The Court found that the authorities’ actions constituted an unjustified interference with Mr. L.F.’s home, violating Article 8. The judgment noted that similar inspections had targeted other Roma families in Gyöngyöspata, as reported by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Rights of National and Ethnic Minorities. This case is significant for its recognition of the discriminatory context in which the violation occurred, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma families to arbitrary and unlawful state action.

cases.title: AFFAIRE Y.P. c. BULGARIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Enquête effective) (Volet procédural);Violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8-1 - Respect de la vie privée)
cases.summary: In the case of Y.P. v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Y.P., was a minor living in a Roma settlement in Bulgaria, as indicated by the judgment’s references to her community context. The case concerned the vulnerability of a young Roma girl who alleged she had been the victim of sexual assault, and the subsequent failure of the authorities to conduct an effective investigation. In April or May 2015, Y.P. reported to the authorities that she had been raped. The investigation involved multiple witness interviews, medical and psychiatric examinations, and DNA analysis. One suspect admitted to consensual relations, but the evidence was contradictory, and the authorities could not conclusively establish non-consensual intercourse. Despite indications of sexual activity with a minor under fourteen, the investigation stalled: after September 2017, there were significant delays, and ultimately, the case was suspended without identifying or prosecuting any perpetrator. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), finding violations of both due to the lack of an effective investigation. The Court awarded Y.P. 20,000 euros in non-pecuniary damages. Notably, the Court observed that while there was no evidence the investigation was tainted by ethnic bias, the authorities’ procedural failures left the applicant without justice or remedy.

cases.title: CASE OF A.Ö. AND H.Ö. v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary: In A.Ö. and H.Ö. v. Romania, the applicants were two sisters, with the first applicant, A.Ö., described in the judgment as a woman of Roma ethnic origin. The case focused on the vulnerability of a Roma minor in state care who alleged sexual abuse and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. In 2018, while living in a care home in Romania, A.Ö. reported being sexually abused by an older man. Despite her age and vulnerable status, the investigation by Romanian authorities was marred by significant shortcomings: officials mistakenly recorded her age, relied solely on the suspect’s statements, failed to assess her capacity to consent, and allowed harmful stereotypes—such as blaming the minor for provoking the abuse—to influence their approach. Additionally, A.Ö. was represented by an employee of the care home (against which complaints had been made) and an ex officio lawyer, neither of whom took meaningful action on her behalf. The European Court of Human Rights found that these failures amounted to a violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation into inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court awarded A.Ö. €12,500 in non-pecuniary damages. The judgment highlighted the persistent problem of inadequate responses to gender-based violence against Roma women and girls in Europe.

cases.title: FAULKNER AND MCDONAGH v. IRELAND
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded
cases.summary:
In Faulkner and McDonagh v. Ireland, the applicants, Ms. Christina Faulkner and Ms. Bridget McDonagh, are sisters and members of the Traveller community, which has been officially recognised as a distinct ethnic group in Ireland since 2017. Their case concerned the vulnerability of Travellers facing eviction from unauthorised roadside encampments and the adequacy of alternative accommodation provided by local authorities. After leaving a halting site in 2013 due to family tragedy, both applicants and their families settled with their caravans on the roadside at Coonagh near Limerick City, seeking proximity to schools for their children. Despite being placed on the housing list, the applicants either rejected or found unsuitable the accommodation offered by the Council, citing personal and cultural reasons, and continued to live at the Coonagh site until December 2017. The Council initiated legal proceedings to remove them, arguing their occupation was unauthorised under planning laws.

The applicants claimed before the European Court of Human Rights that the eviction orders interfered with their right to respect for their home under Article 8 of the Convention, and that the domestic courts had not properly considered the proportionality of this interference. However, the Court declared the applications inadmissible, finding them manifestly ill-founded under Article 35. The Court noted that the applicants had withdrawn their domestic appeals and that the Irish authorities had provided opportunities for alternative accommodation, with the decision-making process meeting the procedural requirements of Article 8.

cases.title: MIHALACHE v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Mihalache v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Mihalache, described in the proceedings as a member of the Roma community, brought a case against Romania after being denied the right to claim compensation following the accidental death of a child he considered his own. The case centered on the applicant’s inability to assert paternity after the child’s death, a situation with particular resonance for Roma and Traveller families, where formal recognition of parenthood may not always align with community or familial realities. The events took place in Romania, where, after the child’s fatal accident, the applicant was not permitted to participate as a civil party in the compensation proceedings because he had not been legally recognised as the child’s father during the child’s lifetime. Romanian law at the time did not allow posthumous recognition of paternity in such circumstances. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), both alone and in combination. The Court found no evidence that the applicant’s exclusion was linked to his Roma origin or that Roma were disproportionately affected by the legal provisions. As a result, the application was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, with no violation found.

cases.title: DJAFER v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Djafer v. North Macedonia, the applicant, Ms. Sofija Djafer, was represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and is identified in the case materials as being associated with the Roma community. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma individuals in the context of alleged failures by state authorities to effectively investigate a death, raising issues of potential exclusion from justice. The facts, as presented in the judgment, indicate that Ms. Djafer lodged an application under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to life, specifically complaining about the ineffective investigation into a death. The application was introduced on 15 January 2020, and the Government of North Macedonia subsequently offered a friendly settlement. Under the terms of this settlement, the Government agreed to pay Ms. Djafer 12,000 euros for non-pecuniary damage and costs, with the payment to be made within three months. The European Court of Human Rights, satisfied that the settlement respected human rights as defined by the Convention, struck the case out of its list in accordance with Article 39. The judgment does not contain any specific remarks or findings that distinguish this case beyond the friendly settlement procedure.

cases.title: SALAY AND ZEMANOVÁ v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Salay and Zemanová v. Slovakia, the applicants, Mr. Andrej Salay (later represented by his son, Mr. Adrián Salay) and Ms. Lucia Zemanová, Slovak nationals residing in Plavecký Štvrtok, challenged the removal order of their home. The applicants lived in a settlement home to several hundred Roma, and were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, suggesting a Roma community context, though their identity is not explicitly confirmed in the judgment. The case centered on the vulnerability of individuals living in informal housing, often affecting Roma and Traveller communities, who face legal and practical barriers to regularising their homes.

In the 1990s, the applicants built a dwelling without legal title to the land or the necessary permits. In 2012, Slovak authorities initiated proceedings, offering the applicants a chance to regularise the construction. The applicants did not respond to this opportunity, leading to an order for the removal of their home. They argued that the proceedings were discriminatory, as other constructions in the area were not targeted, and that the process was prohibitively complex.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life). However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not engaging with the regularisation process. The Court found no evidence of discrimination or arbitrariness in the authorities’ actions, and no violation was established.

cases.title: RIEDLINGER v. GERMANY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Riedlinger v. Germany, the applicant, Mr. Karl-Reiner Riedlinger, a German national, brought a case against Germany after assisting a Roma family with seven children in Hamburg in legal and administrative matters. The case arose following the death of the children’s mother in 2014, after which their father, who had sole custody, was advised by the youth office to seek a contact ban against Mr. Riedlinger. Allegations of sexual abuse against Mr. Riedlinger were investigated but ultimately dismissed for lack of evidence. Nevertheless, in February 2016, the Hamburg-Bergedorf District Court issued an interim order prohibiting any contact between Mr. Riedlinger and the children, citing concerns for the children’s well-being and the father’s right to determine third-party contact.

Throughout the proceedings, conflicting accounts emerged: the father claimed he was pressured by the youth office to apply for the ban, while one of the children expressed a wish to maintain contact with Mr. Riedlinger. The domestic courts ultimately upheld the contact ban, finding that Mr. Riedlinger’s involvement interfered with support measures for the children.

Mr. Riedlinger complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 (right to a fair trial), alleging excessive length and unfairness in the proceedings. The Court found Article 6 applicable but declared the application inadmissible, concluding that the proceedings were not unreasonably lengthy or unfair, and that Mr. Riedlinger’s complaints were manifestly ill-founded.

cases.title: CASE OF MEMEDOV v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In Memedov v. North Macedonia, the applicant, Mr. Memedov, was represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and described himself as of Roma origin. The case arose from an incident on 5 May 2013 in the Topaana Roma neighbourhood of Skopje, where police intervened to arrest a fugitive. After the arrest, tensions escalated and police reinforcements arrived. Mr. Memedov was among several people arrested inside a local shop. He alleged that police officers insulted him with anti-Roma slurs and physically assaulted him, including being punched and struck with batons, despite his lack of resistance. Medical records documented significant bruising and later post-traumatic stress disorder. The applicant claimed that the ill-treatment was racially motivated and that authorities failed to investigate this aspect, amounting to institutional anti-Gypsyism.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Mr. Memedov had suffered ill-treatment of sufficient severity to engage Article 3 and that the authorities failed to investigate the possible racist motives behind the police conduct. It held that there had been a violation of Article 3, both substantively and procedurally, and a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 3. The judgment specifically recognised the failure to address potential institutional racism in the investigation of police violence against a Roma individual.

cases.title: BEKIR AND OTHERS v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Bekir and Others v. North Macedonia, the applicants—comprising several Roma families, including children, pregnant women, and individuals with disabilities—were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. They had been living for years in an informal settlement known as “Polygon” on the banks of the River Vardar in Skopje, alongside other Roma families. The settlement, consisting of makeshift shelters and lacking basic amenities, was marked by extreme poverty and social exclusion.

The case arose after, on 1 August 2016, local authorities carried out a clean-up operation at the site, demolishing the applicants’ homes and destroying belongings, including a water pump. The authorities justified the action as necessary for public health and environmental reasons, offering the residents accommodation in a homeless shelter, which the applicants refused, seeking instead social flats. The applicants alleged that they were not given prior notice or an opportunity to challenge the demolition, and that no adequate alternative housing was provided.

The applicants complained under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), and 13 (right to an effective remedy), arguing that their forced eviction and the lack of procedural safeguards violated their rights. However, the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not exhausted available domestic remedies. The Court did not examine the merits of the alleged violations, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: ASANOVSKI AND OTHERS v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In Asanovski and Others v. North Macedonia, the applicants—Vites Asanovski, Djeljana Asanovska, Stojan Asanovski, Bedati Sulimanov, and Fazli Demirovski—were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and identified as members of the Roma community. The case concerned allegations of discrimination and restrictions on freedom of movement, issues that often disproportionately affect Roma and Traveller groups. The applicants complained that they had been prevented from leaving North Macedonia, raising claims under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The facts, as set out in the judgment, indicate that the applicants were stopped at the border and denied exit from the country, a measure they argued was discriminatory and unjustified. The government and the applicants reached a friendly settlement, with the authorities agreeing to pay each applicant or household €2,500 for non-pecuniary damage and costs. The European Court of Human Rights, satisfied that the settlement respected human rights standards, struck the case out of its list without examining the merits. This resolution closed the proceedings without a formal finding of a violation but acknowledged the applicants’ grievances through compensation.

cases.title: MADĚROVÁ v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Maděrová v. the Czech Republic, the applicant, Ms Anna Maděrová, a Czech national, brought a case against the Czech Republic concerning her sterilisation in 1982 at Znojmo hospital. While the judgment does not explicitly state Ms Maděrová’s Roma or Traveller identity, it notes that she approached the Ombudsperson in 2005 during an inquiry into the forced sterilisation of Roma women, suggesting her experience was linked to this broader context of harm affecting Roma and Traveller women in the Czech Republic.

The case centred on the applicant’s sterilisation without her informed consent during her second caesarean delivery. Ms Maděrová only signed a consent form two days after the procedure and later discovered, through the Ombudsperson’s investigation, that her sterilisation had been irregular and unnecessary. Despite attempts at reversal and fertility treatments, she was unable to have more children. She sought criminal and civil remedies, but her claims for compensation were dismissed as time-barred, with courts finding she had been aware of the sterilisation since 1982 or, at the latest, 2005.

The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaints under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), but declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the domestic courts had properly applied limitation periods and that Ms Maděrová’s access to justice had not been unduly restricted, given the established legal framework and her personal circumstances.

cases.title: CASE OF MILOSAVLJEVIĆ v. SERBIA
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 10 - Freedom of expression-{general} (Article 10-1 - Freedom of expression)
cases.summary:
In Milosavljević v. Serbia, the applicant, Mr. Milosavljević, a journalist and editor-in-chief of the weekly magazine Svetlost in Kragujevac, brought a case against Serbia after being found liable for defamation. The case arose from two articles he published in June 2010, reporting on the attempted sexual assault of an underage girl described as being of Romani origin and a street vendor. The articles criticized the silence of local authorities, police, and NGOs regarding the incident, and questioned whether the lack of action was due to the victim’s Romani background. The reporting also speculated about a possible cover-up and referred to the possibility of the victim’s family being paid off to withdraw their complaint.

Following publication, the alleged perpetrator, a municipal official, sued for defamation and was awarded compensation. Mr. Milosavljević argued before the European Court of Human Rights that his freedom of expression under Article 10 had been violated, emphasizing the public interest in exposing the vulnerability and exclusion faced by Roma, particularly in cases of violence against Romani girls.

The Court examined whether the interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression was justified. It found no violation of Article 10, concluding that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance between the applicant’s right to report on matters of public interest and the protection of the reputation of others. The judgment did not set a new precedent regarding reporting on Roma-related issues but highlighted the need for careful factual reporting, especially in sensitive cases involving vulnerable individuals.

cases.title: CASE OF M.B. AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In M.B. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants—three young men from Košice, described in the judgment as living near a housing project mainly inhabited by Roma—brought a case against Slovakia concerning their treatment by police. The case focused on the applicants’ vulnerability as individuals from a Roma-populated area, alleging they were subjected to police violence and that their ethnicity was a factor in their ill-treatment.

On 21 March 2009, following an assault and robbery near their neighborhood, the applicants were apprehended by police. While being transported in a police car, they claimed that Officer J.C. struck each of them in the face with a gloved hand, causing injuries, in an attempt to extract information about the other assailants. The applicants later alleged that their Roma background contributed to their treatment. Although a separate, widely publicized incident of police abuse at the station occurred later that day, the Court’s examination was limited to the events in the police car.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found no substantive violation of Article 3 regarding the alleged ill-treatment itself, but it did find a procedural violation of Article 3 due to the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into the applicants’ complaints. The applicants were awarded compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The judgment specifically noted concerns about the independence of police investigations into police misconduct, highlighting systemic shortcomings in Slovakia’s investigative procedures.

cases.title: CASE OF PASTRAMA v. UKRAINE
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life)
cases.summary:
In Pastrama v. Ukraine, the applicant, Ms. Pastrama, lived in an unauthorised tent encampment in Kyiv inhabited by Roma, as described in the judgment. On 30 May 2012, plain-clothed police officers arrived at the encampment, led the Roma residents out, and set fire to their tents and belongings, firing shots in the air and killing a dog. Male residents were forced to strip to the waist and were photographed. The officers reportedly stated they were acting under orders to clear the area ahead of the 2012 UEFA European Football Championship. These events, witnessed by children, left the Roma residents homeless and dispossessed.

Following the incident, Ms. Pastrama and other former residents sought assistance from human rights organisations, which prompted calls for a criminal investigation. However, the authorities repeatedly refused to open or pursue a thorough investigation, citing lack of evidence or inability to locate the victims, despite having their contact information. Appeals by Ms. Pastrama and her lawyer were dismissed on procedural grounds, and the investigation was discontinued multiple times without meaningful steps to clarify the facts or hold anyone accountable.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), holding that Ukraine failed in its positive obligation to protect the applicant’s home and private life and to conduct an effective investigation into the destruction of the Roma encampment.

cases.title: CASE OF GHAILAN AND OTHERS v. SPAIN
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
cases.summary:
In Ghailan and Others v. Spain, the applicants—a married couple of Moroccan origin and their two children—challenged the demolition of their home in the Cañada Real Galiana settlement in Madrid. The applicants were part of a community that included a significant proportion of Roma and other marginalized groups, as reflected in a 2011 census cited in the judgment, though the applicants themselves were Moroccan nationals. The case centered on the vulnerability of families living in informal settlements, facing repeated evictions and demolitions due to the unlawful status of their dwellings on public land reserved for livestock routes.

The applicants built their home without planning permission in 2004–2005 and registered it as their residence. Despite warnings and demolition orders from the Madrid authorities, they remained in the house until it was demolished in October 2007. After attempting to rebuild, they faced further eviction proceedings. Throughout, the authorities followed administrative procedures, including notifications and opportunities for appeal, though the applicants did not always respond or exhaust available remedies.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life, including home). It found no violation, concluding that the authorities’ actions were lawful, proportionate, and accompanied by procedural safeguards. The Court noted the authorities’ efforts to balance enforcement with social support, given the applicants’ vulnerable situation within a diverse and disadvantaged settlement.

cases.title: CASE OF BUDINOVA AND CHAPRAZOV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Budinova and Chaprazov v. Bulgaria, the applicants, Ms. Budinova and Mr. Chaprazov, both of Roma origin and working as journalists in Sofia, brought a case against Bulgaria concerning anti-Roma hate speech by a prominent politician. The case focused on the harm caused by repeated public statements targeting Roma, which the applicants argued amounted to harassment and incitement to discrimination. Between May and June 2005, Volen Siderov, leader of the Ataka political party, made a series of televised and published remarks describing “Gypsy terror,” accusing Roma of widespread criminality, and portraying them as a threat to Bulgarian society. The applicants, personally affected as Roma and as public figures reporting on Roma issues, initiated proceedings under Bulgaria’s Protection from Discrimination Act, seeking an end to such statements and a public apology. Bulgarian courts, however, dismissed their claims, finding the statements were protected political speech.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private life) in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found that Bulgaria had failed in its positive obligation to protect the applicants from discriminatory hate speech, resulting in a violation of both articles. The Court considered the finding of a violation sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage. Notably, the judgment emphasized that states must take effective measures against hate speech targeting vulnerable minorities, especially when it comes from influential public figures.

cases.title: CASE OF BEHAR AND GUTMAN v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Behar and Gutman v. Bulgaria, the applicants, Mr. Behar and Mr. Gutman, both of Jewish ethnic origin, brought a case against Bulgaria after being personally affected by a series of public statements made by a prominent politician, Mr. Siderov, leader of the Ataka party. While the applicants themselves are not Roma or Travellers, the case is notable for its discussion of hate speech targeting multiple minorities, including Roma, and for referencing Bulgarian case-law on anti-Roma harassment. The applicants alleged that Mr. Siderov’s books and public remarks, which included deeply offensive stereotypes and conspiracy theories about Jews, amounted to harassment and incitement to discrimination, infringing their dignity and creating a hostile environment.

The events unfolded in Bulgaria from 2004 onwards, with the applicants initiating proceedings in 2006 under the Protection from Discrimination Act. They sought a court order to stop Mr. Siderov’s statements and a public apology. Bulgarian courts, however, did not provide effective protection.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 8 (right to respect for private life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding that Bulgaria had failed in its positive obligations to protect the applicants from discriminatory harassment. The Court found violations of Article 8 and Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, but considered the finding of a violation sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage. The judgment is significant for its explicit reference to domestic case-law on anti-Roma hate speech, highlighting the broader context of minority protection under the Convention.

cases.title: REDJEPOVI v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In Redjepovi v. North Macedonia, the applicants, Nehru Redjepov and Djemile Redjepova, were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and are identified in the case materials as applicants from a Roma background. The case concerned a complaint under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to life. While the judgment does not detail the underlying events, the involvement of the European Roma Rights Centre and the nature of the complaint suggest the applicants raised concerns about a serious incident affecting their right to life, a vulnerability often experienced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

The application was lodged in June 2018 and related to events in North Macedonia. Before the Court could issue a substantive judgment, the parties reached a friendly settlement. The Government of North Macedonia agreed to pay the applicants €6,000 in compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, as well as costs and expenses. The Court was satisfied that the settlement respected human rights as defined by the Convention and, accordingly, struck the case out of its list under Article 39.

This resolution means the Court did not rule on the merits of the applicants’ Article 2 complaint, and no legal precedent was set regarding the specific circumstances of the case.

cases.title: JUSINOVA v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Jusinova v. North Macedonia, the applicant, Ms. Mizafer Jusinova, was represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and is identified in the case materials as a member of the Roma community. The application concerned a serious incident involving the right to life, protected under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. While the judgment does not detail the underlying events, the involvement of the European Roma Rights Centre and the reference to Article 2 suggest the case related to a life-threatening situation or loss of life affecting a Roma individual. The application was lodged in December 2018, and both parties subsequently reached a friendly settlement. Under this agreement, the Government of North Macedonia undertook to pay Ms. Jusinova €12,000 in compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, as well as costs and expenses. The European Court of Human Rights was satisfied that the settlement respected the principles of the Convention and, accordingly, struck the case out of its list under Article 39. No findings of a violation were made, as the case was resolved amicably before a full judgment on the merits.

cases.title: AFFAIRE LACATUS c. SUISSE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8-1 - Respect de la vie privée);Préjudice moral - réparation (Article 41 - Préjudice moral;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary:
In Lacatus v. Switzerland, the applicant, Ms. Violeta-Sibianca Lacatus, is a Romanian national belonging to the Roma community, who brought a case against Switzerland. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face poverty and social exclusion, and for whom begging may be a necessary means of survival. Between 2011 and 2013, Ms. Lacatus, unable to find work during her stays in Geneva, resorted to begging on the streets. She was repeatedly fined under Geneva’s blanket ban on begging, had small amounts of money confiscated, and was detained for short periods. Ultimately, she was sentenced to a 500 CHF fine, with a five-day prison term in case of non-payment, and was later imprisoned for failing to pay.

The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found that the blanket prohibition and the penalties imposed on Ms. Lacatus were disproportionate, failing to consider her individual circumstances and the necessity of begging for her survival. It ruled that Switzerland had violated Article 8 and awarded her compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant as it affirms the rights and dignity of Roma and Travellers, challenging the criminalisation of poverty and recognising the historical marginalisation these communities have faced across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF LACATUS v. SWITZERLAND
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Lacatus v. Switzerland, the applicant, Ms. Violeta-Sibianca Lacatus, is a Romanian national who belongs to the Roma community. Her case against Switzerland focused on the criminalisation of begging, a practice she resorted to while living intermittently in Geneva from 2011, due to her inability to find work. The harm at the centre of the case was the imposition of a 500 Swiss franc fine on Ms. Lacatus for unintrusive begging on public streets, followed by five days’ imprisonment when she could not pay. The authorities also confiscated a small sum of money from her, which she had collected while begging.

Ms. Lacatus challenged these measures, arguing that they violated her rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 10 (freedom of expression), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Swiss courts upheld the ban, finding no violation. However, the European Court of Human Rights found that the blanket ban on begging, as applied to Ms. Lacatus—a highly vulnerable Roma woman—was disproportionate and failed to consider her specific circumstances. The Court held that Article 8 had been violated and awarded her compensation for non-pecuniary damage. Notably, the judgment emphasised that such automatic and severe sanctions diminish the human dignity of those reduced to begging for survival, and that less restrictive measures should have been considered.

cases.title: CASE OF X AND Y v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect)
cases.summary:
In X and Y v. North Macedonia, the applicants—two minors from Skopje, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre—brought a case against North Macedonia concerning police ill-treatment and the authorities’ response. The applicants, identified as ethnic Roma in the proceedings, alleged that on 19 May 2014, following a robbery near a Roma neighbourhood, police officers intercepted and detained X (aged sixteen) and Y (aged thirteen). Witnesses, including family members, described how both boys were punched, kicked, and subjected to ethnic slurs by police officers demanding confessions. Medical records from the following day documented bruising and bodily injury to X, while Y was described as visibly distressed, bleeding, and having urinated in his clothes.

Despite these accounts and supporting medical evidence, the internal police investigation dismissed the complaint, finding no excessive force had been used. The applicants also pursued civil claims alleging discrimination on the basis of their Roma origin, but the domestic courts found no evidence of discriminatory conduct or excessive delay in the investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). While it found no substantive violation—meaning it did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the applicants were ill-treated by police—it held that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the allegations, constituting a procedural violation of Article 3. No damages were awarded, but the judgment highlights the obligation of states to thoroughly investigate credible claims of police abuse, especially where vulnerable Roma minors are concerned.

cases.title: CASE OF R.R. AND R.D. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In R.R. and R.D. v. Slovakia, the applicants, R.R. and R.D., are members of the Roma community living in Moldava nad Bodvou, a town in eastern Slovakia with a significant Roma population. The case centers on a police operation conducted on 19 June 2013 in their neighborhood, which the applicants argued was a form of collective punishment and retaliation following an earlier altercation between local Roma residents and police. During the operation, both applicants alleged that police officers forcibly entered their homes, subjected them to physical violence—including beatings with batons and, in R.R.’s case, the use of an electroshock weapon—and humiliated them, causing injuries and severe distress. Medical reports confirmed injuries consistent with their accounts.

Despite the seriousness of these allegations, the authorities’ investigation into the incident was found to be inadequate and ineffective. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that both applicants had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment at the hands of the police, and that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation. Importantly, the Court also found a violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 3, recognizing that the applicants’ Roma ethnicity was a factor in their ill-treatment and the lack of proper investigation. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to both applicants. This judgment is significant for its explicit acknowledgment of ethnic discrimination as a central element in police violence and investigative failures against Roma individuals in Slovakia.

cases.title: RAYNOVI v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Raynovi v. Bulgaria, the applicants, Mr. Dragomir Lyubomirov Raynov and Ms. Galina Borisova Raynova, Bulgarian nationals, brought a case against Bulgaria following the violent death of their son, B.R., during a neighbourhood conflict in Sofia on 4 July 2010. The events unfolded in a predominantly Roma neighbourhood, with the applicants’ son becoming involved in a brawl that escalated into mob violence. The initial quarrel began between two neighbours—one allegedly of Bulgarian ethnic origin and the other allegedly of Roma origin—over property occupation. After the dispute intensified, a large group, apparently from the Roma community, gathered, and B.R. was fatally beaten by several individuals after a series of confrontations.

The applicants argued that the police failed to protect their son’s life, invoking Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to life). They claimed the authorities should have anticipated the risk of escalation, given the location and the dynamics of the conflict, and criticised the delayed and insufficient police response. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the police had a positive obligation to prevent the killing. The Court found no evidence that the authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to B.R.’s life before the violence erupted, nor that the situation was so volatile as to require a different operational response. The application was declared inadmissible, with the Court concluding that the police response did not breach Article 2.

cases.title: CASE OF NAGY v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of Nagy v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. Nagy, a Hungarian national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Hungary concerning his treatment by police officers. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma individuals to police ill-treatment and the failure of authorities to provide effective protection and redress. On 2 May 2012, Mr. Nagy was taken to the Gyömrő Police Station for questioning about a theft committed by another person. During his time in custody, an altercation occurred between him and two police officers, resulting in Mr. Nagy sustaining multiple injuries, including contusions on his chest, wrists, arms, and other areas. Medical examinations confirmed these injuries shortly after his release. Despite his consistent account and the medical evidence, the domestic investigation was repeatedly discontinued, with authorities citing inconclusive evidence and failing to question a key officer identified by Mr. Nagy.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found both a substantive and procedural violation of Article 3: Mr. Nagy had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment while in police custody, and the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into his allegations. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller communities, as it reaffirms the heightened duty of states to protect vulnerable minorities from police abuse and to ensure accountability, against a backdrop of longstanding discrimination faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE HIRTU ET AUTRES c. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Traitement dégradant;Traitement inhumain);Violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8-1 - Respect de la vie familiale;Respect de la vie privée);Violation de l'article 13+8-1 - Droit à un recours effectif (Article 13 - Recours effectif) (Article 8-1 - Respect de la vie familiale;Respect de la vie privée;Article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale);Préjudice moral - réparation (Article 41 - Préjudice moral;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary: In Hirtu and Others v. France, the applicants were Romanian nationals belonging to the Roma community, represented by the European Roma Rights Center, who had lived in France for many years—some for over a decade. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing forced evictions from informal settlements, a recurring issue that disproportionately affects these communities and disrupts their family life, education, and access to housing. In 2013, after a previous eviction, the applicants and their families, including many children, settled with 43 caravans on municipal land in La Courneuve, near Paris. Following a mayoral request, the prefect issued an order on 29 March 2013 demanding that the “gens du voyage” vacate the site within 48 hours, citing public health and safety concerns. Only one applicant, Mr. Hirtu, managed to challenge the order in court due to the short deadline, but his claim was initially dismissed on procedural grounds and later rejected on appeal. The European Court of Human Rights examined Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found no violation of Article 3 but held that France had violated Article 8 and Article 13 in conjunction with Article 8, awarding moral damages. This judgment is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in Europe regarding forced evictions and the need for effective legal remedies, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation and inadequate protection of their rights.

cases.title: CASE OF DZAUROVA v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
cases.summary:
In Dzaurova v. Russia, the applicant, Ms. Isiyat Israilovna Dzaurova, a Russian national born in 1979, brought a case against the Russian Federation. While the judgment does not explicitly state her Roma or Traveller identity, Ms. Dzaurova was among a group of internally displaced persons (IDPs) who settled in the town of Karabulak, Ingushetia, after leaving Chechnya in 1994. The case centers on the vulnerability of displaced families—many from marginalized backgrounds—facing eviction from emergency accommodation without adequate alternative housing.

After being granted IDP status in 1996, Ms. Dzaurova and her children lived in a municipal facility known as “Promzhilbaza” from 2003 until their eviction in 2014. The authorities initiated eviction proceedings, citing fire safety violations and the lack of formal tenancy agreements. In September 2013, the local court ordered the eviction of Ms. Dzaurova and others, despite her absence from the hearing and her claim that she had not been properly notified. Her appeals, arguing that she remained in need of housing and had lawfully resided as an IDP, were dismissed.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), specifically regarding respect for home. The Court held that the authorities failed to balance the applicant’s need for housing against public interests and did not provide sufficient procedural safeguards before eviction. This judgment highlights the requirement for careful scrutiny and procedural fairness in eviction cases involving vulnerable displaced persons.

cases.title: CASE OF HUDOROVIČ AND OTHERS v. SLOVENIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Abuse of the right of application;Preliminary objection joined to merits (Art. 34) Individual applications;(Art. 34) Victim;Preliminary objection joined to merits (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae;No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for home;Respect for private life);No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for home;Respect for private life);No violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8-1 - Respect for home;Respect for private life;Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Positive obligations);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Positive obligations);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Positive obligations)
cases.summary: In Hudorovič and Others v. Slovenia, the applicants, Mr. Branko Hudorovič and his son Aleks Kastelic, are members of the Roma community living in the informal settlement of Goriča vas in Ribnica Municipality, Slovenia. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers who, due to irregular settlement status, face exclusion from essential public utilities such as safe drinking water and sanitation. The applicants lived in makeshift wooden huts without access to water, sewage, or sanitation, relying on polluted streams or distant sources for water and using open areas for defecation. Despite repeated requests to local authorities and attempts to regularise their situation, the settlement’s informal status and legal restrictions on building permits prevented connection to public infrastructure. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but found no violation, concluding that Slovenia had not failed in its positive obligations given the complex legal and factual context. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing basic services, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation across Europe despite evolving legal protections.

cases.title: AFFAIRE HUDOROVIČ ET AUTRES c. SLOVÉNIE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire jointe au fond (Art. 35) Conditions de recevabilité;(Art. 35-3-a) Requête abusive;Exception préliminaire jointe au fond (Art. 34) Requêtes individuelles;(Art. 34) Victime;Exception préliminaire jointe au fond (Art. 35) Conditions de recevabilité;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae;Non-violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8 - Obligations positives;Article 8-1 - Respect du domicile;Respect de la vie privée);Non-violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8 - Obligations positives;Article 8-1 - Respect du domicile;Respect de la vie privée);Non-violation de l'article 14+8 - Interdiction de la discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8-1 - Respect du domicile;Respect de la vie privée;Article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale;Obligations positives);Non-violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Obligations positives);Non-violation de l'article 14+3 - Interdiction de la discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Interdiction de la torture;Obligations positives)
cases.summary:
In the case of Hudorovič and Others v. Slovenia, the applicants, Mr. Branko Hudorovič and his son Aleks Kastelic, are members of the Roma community living in the informal settlement of Goriča vas in the municipality of Ribnica, Slovenia. The case focused on the applicants’ vulnerability as Roma, specifically their lack of access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation—an issue affecting many Roma and Traveller communities across Europe due to historic exclusion and marginalisation.

For over thirty years, the Roma community in Goriča vas has lived on land not designated for residential use, in makeshift wooden huts without legal access to water, sewage, or electricity. Despite repeated requests to local authorities for connection to public utilities, the residents were denied due to the settlement’s irregular status and planning restrictions. Efforts to relocate the community failed amid local opposition and internal disagreements. The applicants and other residents were left to collect water from a cemetery or polluted stream and to defecate outdoors, highlighting the severe deprivation faced by many Roma in accessing basic services.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found no violation of these articles, concluding that Slovenia had not failed in its positive obligations, given the settlement’s illegal status and the state’s efforts to address the situation.

This judgment is significant as it clarifies the limits of state obligations regarding access to water and sanitation for Roma and Traveller communities, while also reflecting the persistent challenges these groups face in securing equal treatment and basic living conditions in Europe. The case highlights the ongoing impact of historical discrimination and the need for targeted measures to address the exclusion of Roma and Travellers from essential services.

cases.title: CASE OF A.P. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary: In the case of A.P. v. Slovakia, the applicant, A.P., is a young man of Roma origin living in Rudňany, Slovakia. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face police violence and inadequate protection from state authorities. On 11 February 2015, when A.P. was 16 years old, he was identified by another Roma boy as a possible attacker in a minor incident. Municipal police officers confronted A.P. in front of his school, where he alleged that he was grabbed, punched in the face, and then further assaulted at the police station, all while being pressured to confess. Medical records from the same day confirmed injuries consistent with his account. Despite his complaints, the initial police investigation was superficial, relying mainly on the officers’ testimonies and failing to consider independent witnesses or the possibility of racial motivation. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found both a substantive violation, due to the ill-treatment by police, and a procedural violation, due to the ineffective investigation. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the obligation of states to protect Roma and Travellers from police abuse and to ensure thorough investigations, reflecting ongoing concerns about anti-Roma violence and discrimination in Europe.

cases.title: MEMET AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Memet and Others v. Romania, thirty-seven Romanian nationals of Roma ethnic origin brought a case against the Romanian state, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The applicants, all members of the Roma community, alleged that they had suffered discrimination and violations of their rights following the demolition of their homes in Eforie Sud. The core harm at issue was the forced eviction of Roma families, the destruction of their homes without adequate notice or alternative accommodation, and their subsequent relocation to substandard modular containers, raising concerns about discrimination and the right to adequate housing.

The events began in September 2013, when the mayor of Eforie ordered the demolition of the applicants’ homes, which were built without authorisation on public land. On 27 September 2013, their homes were demolished, leaving them homeless. The applicants were initially offered shelter in an abandoned school, but were later evicted again in July 2014 and moved to small modular containers, which they claimed lacked basic utilities at first. The applicants pursued domestic remedies, and in 2017 the Romanian courts ordered the authorities to provide social housing and awarded compensation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 14 of the Convention, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the applicants had obtained adequate redress at the national level, including compensation and orders for social housing. This case highlights the importance of effective domestic remedies for Roma and Traveller communities facing eviction, reflecting ongoing challenges in securing housing rights and combating discrimination in Europe.

cases.title: DŽELADIN v. NORTH MACEDONIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Dželadin v. North Macedonia, the applicant, Ms. Dženifer Dželadin, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the State of North Macedonia. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing restrictions on their freedom of movement and discrimination based on ethnic origin. Ms. Dželadin alleged that she had been subjected to unjustified limitations on her right to leave the country, a measure that disproportionately affected her as a Roma woman, and amounted to discriminatory treatment. The events giving rise to the case occurred when Ms. Dželadin was prevented from crossing the border, a practice that has been reported as affecting many Roma individuals in the region, though the specific date and location were not detailed in the Court’s summary.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Government of North Macedonia acknowledged, through a unilateral declaration, that Ms. Dželadin’s rights under these provisions had not been respected and offered her €2,250 in compensation. The Court accepted this declaration and struck the case out of its list, noting that the compensation was consistent with similar cases.

This case is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face regarding discriminatory border practices in Europe. The Court’s approach reflects a broader recognition of systemic issues affecting Roma rights, particularly in the context of freedom of movement and equal treatment.

cases.title: YUSEINOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Partly struck out of the list;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary: In Yuseinova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were six families—21 individuals in total—of Roma ethnicity, all Bulgarian nationals, living in the Hadzhi Dimitar neighbourhood of Plovdiv. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities facing forced eviction and demolition of their only homes, often without adequate procedural safeguards or alternative accommodation. Between 1991 and 2005, the applicants had built brick houses on municipal land without permits, but the authorities had tolerated their presence for years. In January 2015, the mayor ordered the demolition of their homes, citing unlawful construction, and gave them thirty days to comply. Some applicants challenged the orders in court, arguing that eviction would render their families homeless and that the authorities had failed to consider the proportionality of such a drastic measure or provide alternative housing. While the lower courts upheld the demolition orders, the Supreme Administrative Court eventually quashed the order against one applicant, referencing the need for a proportionality assessment under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, most applicants withdrew their complaints to the European Court, some reportedly under pressure from local authorities, and the Court ultimately struck out or found inadmissible the remaining applications. This case underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller families face in securing housing rights and procedural fairness, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation in Bulgaria and across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF ZAYKINA v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
cases.summary:
In Zaykina v. Russia, the applicant, Ms. Dinara Vyacheslavovna Zaykina, a Russian national, brought a case against Russia concerning her right to remain in her long-term home. While the judgment does not explicitly state her Roma or Traveller identity, Ms. Zaykina’s circumstances reflect the precarious housing situations often faced by vulnerable minorities, including those from Roma settlements. The case centered on the risk of eviction from a flat in St Petersburg, which Ms. Zaykina had shared with her grandmother since childhood and where she was officially registered as a resident.

The dispute began after the death of Ms. Zaykina’s uncle in 1998, when questions arose over the right to occupy the flat. Ms. Zaykina and her grandmother initiated court proceedings to clarify that a minor, registered at the address but never having lived there, had no right to the premises. In response, the minor’s mother sought Ms. Zaykina’s eviction. Despite her longstanding residence and contributions to the household, a district court ordered her eviction in 2007, a decision later quashed on appeal for failing to consider key evidence of her family ties and residence.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for home), holding that the Russian authorities had not adequately balanced Ms. Zaykina’s right to her home against competing interests. The Court awarded her compensation, emphasizing the need for careful scrutiny in eviction cases where long-term residence and family life are at stake.

cases.title: PANAYOTOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Partly struck out of the list;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Panayotova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants—Ms Donka Kamenova Panayotova, Ms Lilia Savkova Makaveeva, and Mr Rumyan Sergeev Rusinov—are Bulgarian nationals who identify as Roma, bringing their case against the Bulgarian state. The heart of their complaint was the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to hate speech and public incitement to discrimination, particularly when such rhetoric is propagated by influential political actors. The case arose after the nationalist political party Ataka published a brochure in 2011 titled “Gypsy Criminality – A Danger for the State,” which featured inflammatory language and imagery targeting Roma, including headlines such as “A Chronology of Gypsy Banditry” and derogatory references to “Roma scum.” The applicants, supported by NGOs, sought criminal proceedings and the dissolution of Ataka, arguing that the authorities’ failure to act amounted to a breach of their rights.
