The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the Court ultimately found the application partly inadmissible and partly struck it out of the list, without finding a violation or awarding remedies.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in Europe regarding hate speech and the adequacy of state responses. Against a backdrop of rising nationalist rhetoric in the 2010s, the case underscores the ongoing struggle for effective protection against group-based vilification.

cases.title: CASE OF LINGURAR v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In Lingurar v. Romania, the applicants—members of a Roma family living in Vâlcele—brought a case against Romania following a violent police raid on their home. The applicants, all identifying as Roma, alleged that they were targeted and mistreated by law enforcement because of their ethnicity. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma communities to discriminatory policing and the use of ethnic stereotypes, which often result in excessive force and a lack of effective investigation into abuses.

On 15 December 2011, at around 5 a.m., a large group of police officers and gendarmes, many wearing balaclavas, forcibly entered the Lingurar family’s home. The applicants described being dragged from their beds, beaten, and humiliated in front of their family, including a young child. Two male applicants were taken outside without being allowed to dress, further assaulted, and then transported to the police station. Despite medical evidence of injuries, the authorities justified the raid by referencing alleged criminality within the Roma community and dismissed the applicants’ complaints, relying on stereotypes and failing to conduct an impartial investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3, both in the substantive ill-treatment and in the authorities’ failure to investigate effectively. The Court awarded damages to the applicants. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent problem of ethnic profiling and police violence against Roma and Travellers in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination and impunity.

cases.title: CASE OF KOVÁCS v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of Kovács v. Hungary, the applicants—four individuals from the same family, all members of the Roma minority—brought a complaint against Hungary concerning police violence. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face institutional racism and disproportionate use of force by law enforcement. On the night of 3 September 2013, the applicants were stopped by police at a petrol station in Sátoraljaújhely. Despite offering no resistance, they were subjected to derogatory remarks about their Roma origin, physically assaulted, handcuffed, and transported to the police station, where the abuse continued. The first applicant was beaten and denied medical care, the second was assaulted and humiliated, the third was repeatedly hit, and the fourth suffered a broken wrist after being kicked while handcuffed.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found that the injuries sustained by the applicants reached the threshold of severity required by Article 3 and that the force used by the police was unjustified and contrary to human dignity. Consequently, the Court held that Hungary had violated Article 3 and awarded damages to the applicants.

This judgment is significant as it reaffirms the Court’s commitment to protecting Roma and Travellers from police brutality and institutional discrimination, a persistent issue in Europe with deep historical roots.

cases.title: CASE OF LAKATOŠOVÁ AND LAKATOŠ v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 - Right to life;Article 2-1 - Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In the case of Lakatošová and Lakatoš v. Slovakia, the applicants, a married couple of Roma origin living in Hurbanovo, Slovakia, brought a complaint against the Slovak state following a violent attack on their family. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of authorities to properly investigate and address such hate crimes. On 16 June 2012, an off-duty municipal police officer, Mr J., armed with an illegally acquired gun, drove to the applicants’ home in a predominantly Roma neighbourhood. Without warning, he entered their yard and opened fire on the family, killing three relatives and seriously injuring both applicants. Mr J. later confessed, making statements that revealed his actions were motivated by longstanding negative attitudes and frustrations towards Roma people.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 (right to life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Slovakia had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the possible racist motives behind the attack, constituting a violation of both articles taken together. The applicants were awarded just satisfaction for the harm suffered.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent threat of anti-Roma violence in Europe and the obligation of states to investigate and address hate crimes thoroughly. The case reflects a broader historical context of discrimination and inadequate protection for Roma and Traveller communities across the continent.

cases.title: CASE OF DIMOVIĆ AND OTHERS v. SERBIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 6+6-3-d - Right to a fair trial (Article 6 - Criminal proceedings;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing) (Article 6 - Right to a fair trial;Article 6-3-d - Examination of witnesses);No violation of Article 6+6-3-d - Right to a fair trial (Article 6 - Criminal proceedings;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing) (Article 6 - Right to a fair trial;Article 6-3-d - Examination of witnesses)
cases.summary:
In the case of Dimović and Others v. Serbia, the applicants—three Serbian nationals of Roma origin—brought a complaint against the Serbian state. Their Roma identity was central to the case, as it raised concerns about the fairness of criminal proceedings involving members of the Roma and Traveller communities, who have historically faced prejudice and stereotyping in the justice system. The applicants were accused and later convicted of robbery and burglary following incidents in March 2008 near Subotica, where property was stolen from a local resident and the victim was violently assaulted. The prosecution relied heavily on a statement made by a co-accused, R.K., who later retracted his testimony, and on witness accounts that described the suspects as “Roma men.” The applicants argued that they were unable to question R.K. in court, undermining their right to a fair trial.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, focusing on the right to a fair trial and the right to examine witnesses. The Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d), concluding that the applicants’ convictions were based on untested evidence and that the safeguards for a fair hearing had not been met. This judgment is significant as it highlights the need for robust procedural protections for Roma and Traveller defendants, especially in contexts where anti-Roma bias may influence criminal proceedings. The case reflects ongoing concerns about institutional discrimination against Roma and Travellers in Europe’s justice systems.

cases.title: CASE OF MAGYAR JETI ZRT v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 10 - Freedom of expression-{general} (Article 10-1 - Freedom of expression);Pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Magyar Jeti Zrt v. Hungary, the applicant was Magyar Jeti Zrt, a company operating the Hungarian online news portal 444.hu. The case arose from an incident at a primary school in Konyár, Hungary, where the majority of students were Roma. On 5 September 2013, a group of intoxicated football supporters stopped at the school, shouted racist insults, threatened the Roma children, and behaved aggressively, prompting teachers to hide the children and call the police. The leader of the local Roma minority government, J.Gy., gave an interview about the incident, which was uploaded to YouTube and later linked in an article by 444.hu.

The harm at the centre of the case was the racist intimidation suffered by Roma children, which was widely reported in the media. However, the legal proceedings focused on the applicant company’s liability for defamation after it published a hyperlink to the interview, in which J.Gy. had linked the attackers to the political party Jobbik, known for its anti-Roma rhetoric.

Hungarian courts found Magyar Jeti Zrt liable for disseminating defamatory statements by merely linking to the video, ordering the removal of the hyperlink and publication of the judgment. The European Court of Human Rights examined Article 10 (freedom of expression) and found a violation, ruling that holding a news portal strictly liable for hyperlinking to third-party content unduly restricted press freedom. The Court awarded pecuniary damages to the applicant.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it highlights the importance of robust media reporting on anti-Roma incidents, especially in a context where Roma communities have long faced discrimination and violence in Hungary and across Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE MAGYAR JETI ZRT c. HONGRIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 10 - Liberté d'expression-{général} (Article 10-1 - Liberté d'expression);Dommage matériel - réparation (Article 41 - Dommage matériel;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary:
In Magyar Jeti Zrt v. Hungary, the applicant was Magyar Jeti Zrt, a media company operating the Hungarian news website 444.hu. The case arose from an incident on 5 September 2013 in Konyár, Hungary, where a group of football supporters stopped near a primary school attended mainly by Roma children. The supporters, reportedly intoxicated, shouted racist abuse and threats at the children, prompting teachers to hide the pupils and call the police. The head of the local Roma minority self-government, J.Gy., gave an interview to a Roma-focused media outlet, attributing the incident to members of the Jobbik political party. This interview was posted on YouTube.

The next day, 444.hu published an article about the incident, including a hyperlink to the YouTube video. The article described the targeted threats against the Roma pupils and referenced the statements made by J.Gy. Jobbik sued for defamation, arguing that the hyperlink disseminated false and damaging claims about the party. Hungarian courts found Magyar Jeti Zrt liable, ordering the removal of the hyperlink and publication of the judgment.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 10 (freedom of expression) and found a violation, holding that imposing objective liability for merely linking to third-party content unduly restricted press freedom. The Court awarded just satisfaction for pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant for clarifying that holding media strictly liable for hyperlinks, without considering intent or context, is incompatible with Article 10.

cases.title: BARAHONA GUACHAMIN ET AUTRES c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Irrecevable
cases.summary:
In Barahona Guachamin and Others v. Italy, the applicants—foreign nationals and one Italian citizen—lived in the “Borghetto,” an informal settlement in Rome’s fourth district, near the Ponte Mammolo metro station. The Borghetto, established in the late 1990s, was home to a diverse group of migrants, asylum seekers, and homeless people, including individuals from Roma settlements, though the judgment does not explicitly confirm Roma or Traveller identity for the applicants. The case centered on the vulnerability of these residents, who faced sudden eviction and demolition of their makeshift homes without formal notification or provision of alternative accommodation.

On 11 May 2015, following concerns about public safety and hygiene, municipal and national police, along with social services and civil protection, carried out the eviction and demolition. Many residents, including some applicants, were given little time to collect belongings before being removed. The applicants complained that they had not been properly notified of the eviction and were thus unable to challenge it in court, raising issues under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 6 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not exhausted available domestic remedies, as they could have challenged the administrative act or sought compensation in Italian courts. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: CASE OF POPOV AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction);Non-pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Popov and Others v. Russia, the applicants were members of four families residing in a Moscow dormitory building originally provided by the Ministry of Finance’s security service as employment-related accommodation. While the applicants’ Roma or Traveller identity is not explicitly stated in the judgment, the case was brought by families from a Roma settlement. The core issue was the vulnerability of these families to eviction without alternative housing, raising concerns about exclusion and the right to respect for their home.

The facts reveal that, beginning in the 1990s, the adult male applicants were granted accommodation in the dormitory due to their employment, and their wives and children joined them over the following years. Despite long-term residence—some for over five years—their legal status in the building was challenged. In 2007 and again in 2009, the Federal Treasury initiated eviction proceedings against the adult female applicants, arguing they had moved in without permission. Russian courts ordered their eviction without providing alternative accommodation, despite the presence of minor children and the families’ arguments that they had a lawful right to reside together.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life, and home) and found a violation, holding that the eviction orders constituted a disproportionate interference with the applicants’ right to respect for their home. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages, recognizing the significant impact of the threat of eviction on the families’ lives. Notably, the judgment referenced Connors v. the United Kingdom, affirming that the protection of “home” under Article 8 applies broadly, not only to cases involving Roma or Travellers.

cases.title: CASE OF BURLYA AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list (Art. 37) Striking out applications-{general};(Art. 37-1) Striking out applications;Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae;Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation);Violation of Article 14+8-1 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for home;Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Burlya and Others v. Ukraine, the applicants were Ukrainian nationals of Roma ethnicity who had lived in the village of Petrivka, Odessa Region. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to collective violence and the failure of state authorities to protect them from discrimination and forced displacement. On 7 September 2002, following the murder of a local youth allegedly by a Romany man, tensions escalated in the village. Over the next days, local officials and police attended meetings where the expulsion of Roma residents was discussed and ultimately supported. On 9 September, the applicants were warned by police to leave the village as a violent mob was expected. That night, a crowd ransacked and destroyed Roma homes, while police present failed to intervene, resulting in the applicants losing their homes and being forced to sell their properties at a loss.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), including their intersections. The Court found that Ukraine had failed to protect the applicants from discriminatory violence and had not conducted an effective investigation, awarding non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent vulnerability of Roma and Travellers in Europe to mob violence and state inaction, reflecting a long history of discrimination and forced displacement across the continent.

cases.title: CASE OF LEVAKOVIC v. DENMARK
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Expulsion)
cases.summary:
In Levakovic v. Denmark, the applicant, Mr. Gimi Levakovic, was born in the Netherlands in 1987 and moved to Denmark as an infant, where he lived with his parents and extended family. The case does not explicitly confirm Mr. Levakovic’s Roma or Traveller identity, but the European Roma Rights Centre intervened as a third party, and the facts refer to his large family network in Denmark, suggesting a background from a Roma settlement. The central issue was the expulsion order imposed on Mr. Levakovic following a series of criminal convictions, including multiple robberies, theft, and related offences, despite his lifelong residence and family ties in Denmark.

Mr. Levakovic argued that expulsion would sever his only meaningful social and familial connections, as he had never lived in Croatia or the former Yugoslavia, did not speak the language, and had no family there. He also suffered from ADHD and mental health issues. The Danish courts, however, ordered his permanent expulsion after a conviction for two robberies, weighing the seriousness and repeated nature of his offences against his integration in Denmark.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) but found no violation. The Court held that the Danish authorities had properly balanced Mr. Levakovic’s private life and integration against the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and that the expulsion was proportionate in the circumstances. The judgment does not contain a specific precedent or remark distinguishing it beyond the proportionality assessment.

cases.title: AYDAROV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Aydarov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were two extended families of Bulgarian nationals of Roma ethnic origin—the Aydarovi and Ilievi families—living in the Kremikovtsi settlement near the village of Marchevo. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma families facing the demolition of their homes, which were built without official permits on municipal land, in a settlement inhabited exclusively by Roma and established in the late 1960s. The applicants, including children with serious health conditions, lived in basic brick houses that were subject to demolition orders issued by the Bulgarian authorities between 2010 and 2011, after inspections found the buildings to be unlawful. While one family sought judicial review of the demolition order, the other did not, and neither succeeded in preventing the orders from becoming final.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), arguing that the demolition orders and their enforcement were disproportionate and failed to consider their individual circumstances. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies, as required by Article 35 of the Convention.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families often face when seeking protection against forced evictions, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and legal exclusion across Europe.

cases.title: ABEDINOV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Abedinov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Abedinov, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Macedonian authorities. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, focusing on alleged discrimination and restrictions on freedom of movement, issues that have historically affected these communities across Europe. Mr. Abedinov claimed that he had suffered discriminatory treatment and limitations on his right to liberty of movement, invoking several articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination). Before the Court could issue a judgment on the merits, the parties reached a friendly settlement: the government agreed to pay Mr. Abedinov 2,500 euros to cover non-pecuniary damages and costs, with the payment to be made within three months. Satisfied that the settlement respected human rights, the Court struck the case from its list. This resolution is significant as it demonstrates the potential for amicable settlements in cases involving Roma rights, reflecting ongoing efforts to address longstanding patterns of discrimination and exclusion faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: ZEKIROV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Zekirov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Zekirov, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Macedonian authorities. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma individuals facing discrimination and restrictions on their freedom of movement, a recurring issue for Roma and Travellers across Europe. Mr. Zekirov alleged that he had suffered discriminatory treatment and violations of his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically concerning freedom of movement and protection from discrimination. The events giving rise to the case occurred in Macedonia, where Mr. Zekirov claimed that state actions had unjustly limited his ability to travel and had treated him differently due to his Roma identity. Before the European Court of Human Rights could issue a substantive judgment, the parties reached a friendly settlement: the government agreed to pay Mr. Zekirov 2,500 euros to cover non-pecuniary damages and costs, resolving the matter. The Court, satisfied that the settlement respected human rights, struck the case from its list. This outcome is significant as it demonstrates the potential for redress through the Convention system for Roma and Travellers, who have historically faced systemic barriers to equal treatment and freedom of movement in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF JANSEN v. NORWAY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary: In Jansen v. Norway, the applicant, Ms. Jansen, is a Norwegian national of Roma origin who brought a case against Norway concerning the removal of her daughter, A, from her care and the severe restrictions placed on their contact. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families to child welfare interventions, especially where cultural misunderstandings and stereotypes may influence decisions about parental capacity and family life. After A’s birth in 2011, Ms. Jansen, then 19, faced instability and violence within her family home, leading to repeated stays at a parent-child centre. Following incidents involving her father, including violence and threats, the Norwegian Child Welfare Service placed A in emergency foster care in June 2012, citing concerns about Ms. Jansen’s ability to protect her child and the risk of abduction by her family. Contact between mother and child was limited to supervised sessions, sometimes as little as one hour per month, with police presence. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life, and found that Norway had violated this right by failing to sufficiently consider less intrusive alternatives and the evolving circumstances of the applicant. The Court awarded Ms. Jansen non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it underscores the need for child welfare authorities to avoid disproportionate interference in Roma and Traveller family life, reflecting a broader European context of historical overrepresentation of Roma children in care systems.

cases.title: HASANI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Hasani v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Ms Emrana Hasani, is a stateless person born in Kosovo in 1986 who settled in Macedonia as a minor after fleeing Kosovo in 1999. While the judgment does not explicitly confirm her Roma identity, Ms Hasani referred to reports highlighting the difficulties Roma face in obtaining personal identification documents in Kosovo, suggesting her connection to the Roma and Traveller communities. The case centered on her vulnerability as a stateless person at risk of expulsion to Kosovo, where she claimed she would face discrimination and practical obstacles, particularly due to her lack of identification documents and her fear of persecution.

After years of asylum in Macedonia, Ms Hasani’s status was revoked in 2007, and she was ordered to leave the country. Despite having four children with a Macedonian national, she was repeatedly instructed to regularize her status through marriage or by obtaining documents from Kosovo, which she argued was impossible due to her statelessness and fear of return. Domestic courts upheld the termination of her asylum, finding no evidence of a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment if she returned to Kosovo.

The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaints under Articles 3, 8, and 13 of the Convention but declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that Ms Hasani had not substantiated a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 and had not exhausted available remedies to regularize her status. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: CASE OF LOPES DE SOUSA FERNANDES v. PORTUGAL
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-3-a) Manifestly ill-founded;No violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2 - Positive obligations;Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
The case of Lopes de Sousa Fernandes v. Portugal was brought by Ms. Lopes de Sousa Fernandes, who is not identified in the judgment as belonging to the Roma or Traveller communities. The case concerned the death of her husband, António Rui Calisto Fernandes, following a series of medical complications after minor nasal surgery at Vila Nova de Gaia Hospital in late 1997. After the operation, Mr. Fernandes suffered from severe headaches and was repeatedly admitted to hospital with worsening symptoms, including bacterial meningitis, ulcers, and ultimately peritonitis. Despite multiple hospitalizations and treatments at two different hospitals, his condition deteriorated, and he died on 8 March 1998 from septicaemia caused by peritonitis and a perforated viscus.

The applicant alleged that her husband’s death resulted from negligent medical care and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to life. While the Court found no violation of the substantive aspect of Article 2—meaning the medical care itself did not reach the threshold of a breach—it did find a violation of the procedural aspect. Specifically, the authorities failed to carry out an effective investigation into the death. The Court awarded the applicant compensation for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment clarified the scope of the State’s procedural obligations under Article 2 in the context of alleged medical negligence.

cases.title: CASE OF ALKOVIĆ v. MONTENEGRO
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Alkovic v. Montenegro, the applicant, Mr. Alkovic, is a Roma and Muslim man who, at the relevant time, lived with his family in Podgorica, Montenegro. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to ethnically and religiously motivated hostility, particularly when state authorities fail to provide effective protection or investigation. Between May and September 2009, Mr. Alkovic and his family endured a series of threatening and degrading incidents from neighbours, including gunshots fired in the direction of his home, repeated use of anti-Roma and anti-Muslim slurs, and a menacing message and cross drawn on his apartment door during a religious holiday. Despite Mr. Alkovic’s repeated complaints and the evidence he provided, the Montenegrin authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into these incidents or to address the discriminatory motives behind them.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Montenegro had violated both articles by failing to protect Mr. Alkovic from discriminatory attacks and by not investigating the incidents adequately. The Court awarded Mr. Alkovic non-pecuniary damages for the harm suffered. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent risks faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe and reinforces the obligation of states to actively protect minorities from hate-motivated violence and discrimination, a concern rooted in the long history of marginalisation of Roma and Travellers across the continent.

cases.title: KÓSA v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies
cases.summary: In Kósa v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms. Amanda Kósa, is a Hungarian national who identifies as Roma, living in the Huszár township of Nyíregyháza—a neighbourhood predominantly inhabited by Roma and marked by poverty and social exclusion. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma children to educational segregation, particularly following the closure of the local school and the subsequent opening of a new school by the Greek Catholic Church, which was attended almost exclusively by Roma pupils. After the original township school was closed in 2007 as part of a desegregation effort, Roma children, including Ms. Kósa, were distributed among other schools, but faced exclusion and hostility. In 2011, a new church-run school opened in the township, and Ms. Kósa’s parents enrolled her there, citing her asthma and the lack of a school bus as reasons for not sending her to a more distant school. Ms. Kósa later transferred to a mainstream school in the town centre. She alleged that her placement in the church-run school amounted to segregation and discrimination on the basis of her Roma identity. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), but ultimately declared the application inadmissible, finding that Ms. Kósa had not exhausted all available domestic remedies. This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller applicants may face in challenging educational segregation, a persistent issue in Europe given the long history of Roma exclusion from mainstream education.

cases.title: NATIONALDEMOKRATISCHE PARTEI DEUTSCHLANDS (NPD) v. GERMANY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Nationaldemokratische Partei Deutschlands (NPD) v. Germany, the applicant was the National Democratic Party of Germany, a political party, which is not a member of the Roma or Traveller communities as defined by the Council of Europe. The case did, however, centre on harm directed at Roma and Sinti, as the NPD’s press release promoted negative stereotypes about the immigration of Sinti and Roma from Bulgaria and Romania, alleging welfare abuse and high crime rates—claims that perpetuate stigma and discrimination against these groups. 

The events unfolded in May 2014, during the campaign for the European Parliament elections. The NPD published a press release on its website announcing a panel discussion on “immigration of Sinti and Roma,” naming several public figures as participants without their consent. The venue was falsely advertised, and the individuals named, including the chairperson of the Central Council of German Sinti and Roma, had not agreed to participate. After requests to cease using their names were ignored, legal action was taken, resulting in a court injunction against the NPD.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 10 (freedom of expression) but found the application inadmissible. The Court held that the German courts had struck a fair balance between the NPD’s freedom of expression and the protection of the reputation and rights of others, particularly those targeted by the press release.

This case is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Sinti face regarding harmful public discourse and the importance of legal protections against the spread of discriminatory narratives, especially in the context of political campaigning in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF M.F. v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In the case of M.F. v. Hungary, the applicant, M.F., is a Hungarian national of Roma origin living in Gyöngyöspata. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the failure of authorities to address racially motivated abuse. On 12 August 2010, M.F. was apprehended by police in connection with a theft and taken to the Gyöngyös Police Department. He alleged that, over several hours, he was repeatedly beaten, kicked, and insulted by police officers and security guards, who made explicit references to his Roma identity, including threats that invoked anti-Roma stereotypes. Medical examinations later that day documented multiple bruises, contusions, and swelling consistent with his account of ill-treatment.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that M.F. had suffered degrading treatment at the hands of the police and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, violating both the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 3. Furthermore, the Court found a violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 3 regarding the authorities’ failure to investigate the possible discriminatory motive, though not for the substantive ill-treatment itself. The judgment underscores the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, particularly in police custody, and reinforces the obligation of states to protect minority groups from racially motivated violence and to ensure accountability—an issue of ongoing concern given the historical marginalisation of Roma and Travellers across the continent.

cases.title: KOKKONIS AND CHALILOPOULOU v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Kokkonis and Chalilopoulou v. Greece, the applicants, Mr. Zois Kokkonis and Ms. Nikolitsa Chalilopoulou, a married couple from Patra, Greece, described themselves as being of Roma origin. Their case centered on alleged discrimination and procedural unfairness following their conviction for theft. On 7 January 2009, they were convicted in absentia by the Patras Court of First Instance and sentenced to twelve months’ imprisonment. After appealing, their hearing was adjourned once due to their lawyer’s absence, but on the rescheduled date—3 May 2011—neither the applicants nor their lawyer attended. The court proceeded to try them “as if present” and reduced their sentence to ten months. The applicants sought annulment of the proceedings, citing force majeure: Mr. Kokkonis had been hospitalized with acute illness, and Ms. Chalilopoulou was caring for him and their children. Their applications were dismissed as inadmissible, as Greek law only allowed annulment for those tried strictly in absentia, not “as if present.” Before the European Court of Human Rights, they argued violations of Articles 6 (fair trial), 13 (effective remedy), and 14 (non-discrimination), specifically referencing their Roma identity. The Court found the application inadmissible, holding that Article 6 did not apply to the annulment proceedings, and thus Articles 13 and 14 were also inapplicable. No remedies were awarded.

cases.title: CASE OF ACHIM v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life)
cases.summary:
In the case of Achim v. Romania, the applicants, a Roma couple living in Mănăstirea, Călărași, brought a complaint against the Romanian state concerning the removal of their seven children from their care. As members of the Roma community, the applicants faced heightened vulnerability, particularly regarding state intervention in family life and the risk of discriminatory practices in child protection proceedings. The case arose after social services, responding to concerns about the children’s welfare and living conditions in 2010, placed the children in care, citing neglect, poor hygiene, lack of school and medical enrolment, and the parents’ limited cooperation with authorities. Despite subsequent improvements to their home and efforts to maintain contact with their children, the authorities maintained the placement, and the parents’ attempts to have their children returned were unsuccessful in domestic courts.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found no violation, concluding that the authorities’ actions were justified by the need to protect the children’s welfare and that the applicants had not exhausted all domestic remedies. This judgment highlights the complex balance between child protection and family rights, especially for Roma and Traveller families who have historically faced disproportionate state intervention and systemic discrimination in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF RANĐELOVIĆ AND OTHERS v. MONTENEGRO
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2 - Positive obligations;Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of Ranđelović and Others v. Montenegro, the applicants were the next-of-kin of several Roma who died or disappeared in a tragic incident at sea, bringing their complaint against the State of Montenegro. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face life-threatening risks when seeking safety or better opportunities, and whose families are left without answers or justice when tragedies occur. On the night of 15 August 1999, around seventy Roma boarded the boat “Miss Pat” on the Montenegrin coast, aiming to reach Italy. The boat, dangerously overcrowded, sank a few hours later. By the end of August, only one survivor was found, and thirty-five bodies were recovered, with many more missing. Despite the gravity of the incident, the ensuing investigation and criminal proceedings were marked by significant delays, repeated adjournments, and a lack of effective action, with the process dragging on for over a decade and ultimately resulting in the acquittal of all accused for lack of evidence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to life, focusing on the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation. The Court found a violation of Article 2, concluding that the Montenegrin authorities had failed to carry out a prompt and thorough investigation into the deaths and disappearances. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the persistent barriers to justice faced by these communities, particularly in the context of migration and systemic neglect, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation across Europe.

cases.title: DIMITROVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Dimitrova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were members of three Roma families from the Varna municipality, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of “Roma and Travellers.” They brought a case against Bulgaria, alleging that their forced eviction and the demolition of their homes exposed them to particular vulnerability as Roma, including degrading treatment and discrimination. The families had lived for up to twenty years in municipally owned dwellings in Varna, which were declared unfit for habitation and ordered demolished in late 2008. On 5 December 2008, without alternative accommodation arranged, police and private security evicted the families, including infants and children, in winter conditions. Some applicants reported being left in the street for hours or even overnight, with one family sheltering under a block of flats with a newborn baby. The applicants also alleged that officials made insulting remarks referencing their Roma identity.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not exhausted available domestic remedies, particularly those under Bulgarian anti-discrimination and administrative law.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families often face when seeking justice for forced evictions and discriminatory treatment. It underscores the importance of accessible remedies in national law, especially given the historical context of housing insecurity and marginalisation experienced by Roma communities across Europe.

cases.title: EMINOV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Eminov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Eminov, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Macedonian state. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma individuals in seeking justice for alleged violations of their fundamental rights, a context where Roma and Travellers have historically faced barriers to effective remedies. Mr. Eminov’s application concerned serious allegations, including potential violations of Article 2 (right to life) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, though the specific facts of the incident were not detailed in the Court’s final decision. During the proceedings, the Government offered a friendly settlement, agreeing to pay Mr. Eminov 9,000 euros in compensation for non-pecuniary damage, with clear terms for payment and interest in case of delay. The European Court of Human Rights accepted this settlement, finding it consistent with respect for human rights, and struck the case out of its list under Article 39. This outcome is significant as it demonstrates the potential for friendly settlements to provide redress for Roma applicants, reflecting ongoing efforts to address historical injustices and improve access to justice for Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: PALFREEMAN v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Palfreeman v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Jock Anthony Palfreeman, an Australian national, brought a complaint against Bulgaria after being refused transfer to serve his prison sentence in Australia. The case arose from an incident in Sofia on 27 December 2007, when Mr. Palfreeman intervened in a street altercation involving a group of young people and two Roma men. According to the facts as stated in the judgment, Mr. Palfreeman claimed he acted to protect the Roma men, who were being attacked, but during the ensuing confrontation he fatally stabbed one member of the group and seriously injured another. He was convicted of murder in 2009 and sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Mr. Palfreeman argued that the refusal to transfer him to Australia, where his family resides, interfered with his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He highlighted the hardship of maintaining family contact due to the distance and the limited ability of his relatives to visit him in Bulgaria.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that Article 8 did not guarantee a right to serve a sentence in one’s home country, nor did Bulgarian law or international agreements create such a right in this case. The Court concluded that the refusal to transfer Mr. Palfreeman fell outside the scope of Article 8 and thus was incompatible ratione materiae with the Convention.

cases.title: CIOBAN v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Cioban v. Romania, the applicants, all Romanian nationals of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police abuse and the alleged failure of authorities to investigate such incidents effectively, particularly when discrimination is involved. On 18 May 2009, outside a shopping centre in Oradea, the applicants were accused by local police of parking violations and littering, with officers explicitly referencing their Roma identity as the basis for suspicion. When the applicants denied the accusations and refused to sign the offence report, they alleged that police officers threatened, physically assaulted, and verbally abused them. One applicant, who attempted to film the incident, was forcibly removed from his car, beaten, handcuffed, and taken to the police station, where he was compelled to sign the report without being allowed to read it. Medical evidence later confirmed his injuries.

The applicants lodged a criminal complaint, but the investigation was closed without prosecution. They argued that the authorities’ actions and the subsequent investigation were discriminatory and ineffective, invoking Articles 5, 6, 13, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had failed to comply with domestic procedural requirements, particularly the time limits for challenging prosecutorial decisions.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller communities often face when seeking justice for alleged police misconduct. It underscores the importance of accessible remedies and timely legal action, especially given the historical context of systemic discrimination against Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: CAZACLIU AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Cazacliu and Others v. Romania, the applicants were seventy-six Romanian nationals of Roma ethnic origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, who lived or had lived in Tulcea. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing forced eviction, homelessness, and substandard living conditions, compounded by discriminatory attitudes from local authorities. In July 1999, a fire destroyed the applicants’ informal Roma settlement in central Tulcea, leaving them homeless. After living outdoors, they moved into an abandoned state-owned building with the authorities’ permission, but were later evicted following its sale to a private investor. In October 2006, the applicants, including children, elderly, and persons with disabilities, were forcibly evicted and offered only inadequate shelter: a derelict former army barracks (“Pichet”) or mobile homes on a former rubbish dump, both lacking basic amenities and exposing residents to health and safety risks.

The applicants alleged violations of several Convention rights, including Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). However, the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. Despite the inadmissibility, the case is significant as it documents the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in accessing adequate housing and equal treatment in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation and forced evictions.

cases.title: CASE OF ŠKORJANEC v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation;Positive obligations);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Škorjanec v. Croatia, the applicant, Ms. Maja Škorjanec, brought a complaint against Croatia after she was violently attacked alongside her partner, who is of Roma origin. The case focused on the vulnerability of individuals associated with Roma and Traveller communities, particularly the risk of racially motivated violence and the failure of authorities to recognise and investigate such hate crimes. On 9 June 2013, in Zagreb, Ms. Škorjanec and her partner were assaulted by two men at a flea market. The attackers shouted anti-Roma slurs, threatened to kill them, and physically assaulted both, with Ms. Škorjanec suffering a head injury. Despite clear evidence that the attack was motivated by hatred towards Roma, Croatian authorities treated Ms. Škorjanec’s injuries as unrelated to her association with her Roma partner and failed to investigate her case as a hate crime.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding violations of both, including their combined application. The Court held that Croatia failed to fulfil its positive obligation to investigate whether Ms. Škorjanec was targeted due to her association with a Roma individual and awarded her non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it clarifies that protection against hate crimes under the European Convention extends not only to Roma and Travellers themselves but also to those closely associated with them, reinforcing the need for effective investigations into racially motivated violence in Europe’s historical context of anti-Roma discrimination.

cases.title: AFFAIRE FOGARASI ET AUTRES c. ROUMANIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Traitement dégradant;Traitement inhumain) (Volet matériel);Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Enquête effective) (Volet procédural)
cases.summary: In Fogarasi and Others v. Romania, the applicants—a family of four, all members of the Roma community—brought a case against Romania concerning police violence and the lack of an effective investigation. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police abuse and the failure of authorities to protect them from inhuman and degrading treatment. On 4 July 2008, following a neighbourhood dispute in Acîş, police were called to the applicants’ home. After an initial visit, officers returned with reinforcements, leading to a confrontation in which the first applicant was struck on the head by a neighbour while police looked on. Later, special police forces arrived at the local dispensary, where the family had sought medical help, and forcibly detained the applicants—including their 13-year-old daughter—subjecting them to physical violence both en route to and inside the police station. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found that the first three applicants had suffered such treatment at the hands of the police and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, thus violating both the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent risks of police brutality and impunity faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination and neglect.

cases.title: AFFAIRE TALPIS c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Exceptions préliminaires jointes au fond et rejetées (Article 35-1 - Épuisement des voies de recours internes);Violation de l'article 2 - Droit à la vie (Article 2 - Obligations positives;Article 2-1 - Vie) (Volet matériel);Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Enquête effective;Obligations positives) (Volet procédural);Violation de l'article 14+2 - Interdiction de la discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 - Droit à la vie;Article 2-1 - Vie);Dommage matériel - demande rejetée (Article 41 - Dommage matériel;Satisfaction équitable);Préjudice moral - réparation (Article 41 - Préjudice moral;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary: In the case of Talpis v. Italy, the applicant, Ms. Mihaela Talpis, a Romanian national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Italy concerning the authorities’ failure to protect her and her family from domestic violence. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller women, who often face intersecting discrimination and barriers in accessing effective protection from abuse. After enduring years of physical abuse from her husband, Ms. Talpis moved with her family to Italy in 2011, hoping for a safer future. Despite repeated incidents of violence—including a brutal assault in June 2012 and a knife attack in August 2012—Ms. Talpis’s pleas for help were met with inadequate police response and insufficient support services. She was not properly informed of her rights or available protection measures, and her requests for urgent intervention were delayed. Tragically, in November 2013, her husband killed their son and attempted to murder Ms. Talpis. The European Court of Human Rights found that Italy had violated Article 2 (right to life), Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2, due to its failure to protect Ms. Talpis and her family. The Court awarded her compensation for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant as it underscores the duty of states to protect Roma and Traveller women from gender-based and intersectional violence, reflecting a broader European context of persistent discrimination and institutional neglect.

cases.title: CASE OF TALPIS v. ITALY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objections joined to merits and dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2 - Positive obligations;Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation;Positive obligations) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 - Right to life;Article 2-1 - Life);Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In Talpis v. Italy, the applicant, Ms. Talpis, a Moldovan national, brought a case against Italy following years of severe domestic violence at the hands of her husband. While the judgment does not explicitly state that Ms. Talpis is a member of the Roma or Traveller communities, it describes her as a Moldovan national who migrated to Italy with her family. The case centers on the vulnerability of a woman facing repeated physical abuse, threats, and harassment, culminating in the tragic killing of her son by her husband.

After enduring ongoing violence, Ms. Talpis sought police intervention in June 2012 following an assault on herself and her daughter. Despite clear evidence of abuse and repeated requests for protection, the authorities failed to provide adequate support or take timely preventive measures. In August 2012, after another violent attack, Ms. Talpis was forced to seek refuge in a women’s shelter, but local social services refused to fund her accommodation. She lodged a formal complaint in September 2012, yet for months, no effective investigative or protective steps were taken.

The European Court of Human Rights found that Italy had violated Article 2 (right to life) in its substantive aspect, Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) in its procedural aspect, and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) taken together with Article 2. The Court awarded Ms. Talpis non-pecuniary damages, highlighting the authorities’ failure to protect victims of domestic violence and to respond without discrimination.

cases.title: CASE OF BOACĂ AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of Boacă and Others v. Romania, the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin, heirs of I.B., who had initiated proceedings before his death. The case was brought against the Romanian state and concerned the Boacă family, a Roma household, who alleged police brutality during a raid on their home. The vulnerability at the heart of the case lay in the disproportionate and violent police intervention against a Roma family, including children, reflecting broader patterns of discriminatory treatment faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe.

On 27 August 2008, police officers, including a rapid intervention squad, forcibly entered the Boacă family home in Clejani, following allegations that a non-Roma girl was being held there against her will. Despite the girl’s repeated statements that she was staying voluntarily, police broke windows, fired rubber bullets, and used tear gas. The sixth applicant, a 15-year-old boy, was injured by a rubber bullet, and two young children lost consciousness due to tear gas exposure. The family’s subsequent complaints of police brutality were dismissed by domestic authorities, and the investigation was found to be ineffective.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found both a substantive violation (due to the excessive force used) and a procedural violation (due to the lack of an effective investigation). This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent issue of police violence and inadequate state response towards Roma and Traveller communities in Romania, echoing a long history of marginalisation and abuse across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF KIRÁLY AND DÖMÖTÖR v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Király and Dömötör v. Hungary, the applicants, Mr. János Király and Mr. Tamás Dömötör, both of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Hungary concerning their treatment during and after an anti-Roma demonstration in Devecser. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to racist intimidation and the failure of state authorities to protect them from hate-motivated threats and violence. On 5 August 2012, following tensions between Roma and non-Roma residents, a demonstration was organised by far-right groups and attended by hundreds, including members of Jobbik and other extremist organisations. The event featured inflammatory speeches inciting hatred against Roma, followed by a march through the Roma neighbourhood where demonstrators shouted death threats, racist insults, and threw stones and concrete at Roma homes. Despite a significant police presence, the authorities failed to intervene effectively or investigate the threats and violence adequately.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found that Hungary had violated Article 8 by failing to provide adequate protection and to investigate the applicants’ complaints, awarding them non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it highlights the ongoing risks faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe and reinforces the obligation of states to actively protect minorities from hate-driven intimidation and violence, a persistent issue in the region’s recent history.

cases.title: CASE OF V.M. AND OTHERS v. BELGIUM
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list (Article 37-1 - Striking out applications;Article 37-1-c - Continued examination not justified)
cases.summary:
In V.M. and Others v. Belgium, the applicants were a family from Serbia, including several children, who had spent most of their lives in Serbia before seeking asylum in France and later in Belgium. The family, described in the judgment as having stayed at Place Gaucheret in Brussels “where other Roma families were staying,” were thus implied to be from a Roma settlement. Their case centered on the vulnerability of Roma families facing exclusion from asylum reception facilities and the risk of destitution during asylum proceedings.

After unsuccessful asylum applications in France, the family arrived in Belgium in March 2011 and were placed in a reception centre. Belgian authorities, applying the Dublin II Regulation, sought to transfer them back to France, which eventually agreed to accept them. The applicants challenged this decision, citing poor reception conditions previously experienced in France and the health needs of their disabled daughter. Following the expiry of their leave to remain, the family was excluded from their Belgian reception centre and spent several days in precarious conditions in Brussels.

The European Court of Human Rights ultimately struck the case out of its list under Article 37(1)(a) of the Convention, as the applicants had lost contact with their lawyer and were deemed no longer interested in pursuing the application. The Court found no evidence that the loss of contact was due to actions by the Belgian authorities or to the applicants’ precarious living conditions. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

cases.title: AFFAIRE BAGDONAVICIUS ET AUTRES c. RUSSIE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire rejetée (Article 35-1 - Epuisement des voies de recours internes);Exception préliminaire rejetée (Article 35-3 - Requête abusive);Exception préliminaire jointe au fond et rejetée (Article 34 - Victime);Radiation du rôle (Article 37-1 - Radiation du rôle);Partiellement irrecevable (Article 35-1 - Epuisement des voies de recours internes);Violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8-1 - Respect du domicile);Non-violation de l'article 34 - Requêtes individuelles (Article 34 - Entraver l'exercice du droit de recours);Dommage matériel et préjudice moral - réparation (Article 41 - Préjudice moral;Dommage matériel;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary:
In the case of Bagdonavicius and Others v. Russia, the applicants were members of six Roma families who had lived for decades in the village of Dorojnoe, in the Kaliningrad region. As Roma, they belonged to a group historically subjected to forced settlement policies and ongoing discrimination in Russia. The heart of the case was the vulnerability of these Roma families, who faced eviction and demolition of their homes, threatening their right to respect for private and family life and their established community ties.

The facts revealed that, following a 1956 Soviet decree forcing Roma to settle, the applicants’ families built homes in Dorojnoe, some registering their addresses and obtaining official documents. However, after the dissolution of the USSR, many did not formalise property rights. In the early 2000s, local authorities initially planned to develop the village but later reversed course, instead targeting the Roma community with negative public statements and associating the village with drug trafficking. Between 2005 and 2006, authorities initiated proceedings that led to the demolition of the applicants’ homes, despite their attempts to regularise their situation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found a violation of Article 8, holding that the evictions and demolitions were disproportionate and failed to adequately consider the applicants’ long-standing ties to their homes. The Court awarded both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face regarding housing rights and state-led evictions, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and forced displacement across Europe.

cases.title: PETRACHE ET TRANCA c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Irrecevable
cases.summary: In Petrache and Tranca v. Italy, the applicants, Ms. Elena Petrache and Ms. Liliana Tranca, Romanian nationals of Roma origin, brought a case against Italy concerning their threatened eviction from a temporary accommodation centre in Rome. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing eviction from emergency housing, particularly when one member, Ms. Petrache, was recognised as severely disabled and dependent on daily assistance. The applicants had lived in the “Ex-Cartiera” emergency centre since 2011. In March 2016, the Rome municipality ordered them to leave as part of a broader policy to close such centres, offering alternative accommodation in the “Villaggio della Solidarietà”—a segregated site for Roma families, which the applicants refused, citing its unsuitable and discriminatory conditions. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 14 of the Convention, but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies, as their legal challenge to the eviction was still pending before Italian courts. This case is significant as it underscores the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families often face when seeking protection from forced evictions, reflecting ongoing challenges in accessing justice and adequate housing in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF ADAM v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Remainder inadmissible;No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Adam v. Slovakia, the applicant, Mr. Adam, is a Slovak national of Romani origin who brought a complaint against Slovakia. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, focusing on the risk of ill-treatment and inadequate protection during police custody—a situation where Roma individuals have historically faced disproportionate harm and lack of effective remedies. On 18 December 2010, when Adam was sixteen, he and two other Romani minors were arrested by police in south-eastern Slovakia after being identified as suspects in a mugging. Adam alleged that, during his detention, police officers subjected him to psychological pressure and physical violence, including slaps and punches to the head, and denied him food, water, and rest. Although a medical report noted a bruised and swollen cheek, the authorities dismissed his complaint, and the investigation into his allegations was cursory and inconclusive.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. While the Court found no substantive violation of Article 3 regarding the alleged ill-treatment itself, it held that Slovakia had violated the procedural aspect of Article 3 by failing to conduct an effective investigation into Adam’s claims. The Court awarded Adam compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it reinforces the obligation of states to thoroughly investigate credible allegations of police abuse, especially given the historical context of systemic discrimination and mistrust between Roma communities and law enforcement in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF PILAV v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 - General prohibition of discrimination;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction);Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
The case of Pilav v. Bosnia and Herzegovina concerned Dr. Ilijaz Pilav, a Bosniac (Bosniak) politician from Srebrenica, in the Republika Srpska entity. Although not a member of the Roma or Traveller communities, Dr. Pilav’s situation is relevant for understanding discrimination based on ethnic origin in the context of political participation. In 2006, Dr. Pilav sought to stand as a candidate for the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the Central Election Commission rejected his candidacy, explaining that under the Constitution and Election Act, only Serbs residing in Republika Srpska could stand for election from that entity, while Bosniacs and Croats could only stand from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Dr. Pilav’s appeals to the domestic courts were unsuccessful, with the Constitutional Court justifying the restriction as necessary for maintaining peace and the constitutional order established by the Dayton Agreement.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, which prohibits discrimination. The Court found that Dr. Pilav had been excluded from standing for election solely because of his ethnic origin and place of residence, amounting to unjustified discrimination. The Court held that Bosnia and Herzegovina had violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. No pecuniary damages were awarded, and the finding of a violation was deemed sufficient satisfaction. This judgment reinforces the principle that constitutional arrangements, even those rooted in peace agreements, must not perpetuate ethnic discrimination in political rights.

cases.title: AFFAIRE WINTERSTEIN ET AUTRES c. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Dommage matériel et préjudice moral - réparation (Article 41 - Préjudice moral;Dommage matériel;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary:
In Winterstein and Others v. France, the applicants were a group of French nationals belonging to the Roma and Traveller communities, including families such as the Wintersteins, Mouches, Lefèvres, and others. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing eviction from long-standing settlements without adequate consideration of their needs or alternative accommodation, a situation that has historically exposed these groups to instability and discrimination.

The events took place in Herblay, France, where, for many years, the applicants and their families had lived in caravans and makeshift homes on land known as the Bois du Trou-Poulet. In 2005, French authorities initiated eviction proceedings, and the applicants were ordered to leave, with some forced to abandon their homes and possessions. Despite their requests for rehousing on family land or in social housing, many remained without stable accommodation, moving between temporary sites or living with relatives.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found that France had violated Article 8 by failing to assess the proportionality of the evictions and by not sufficiently considering the applicants’ specific needs for alternative accommodation. The Court awarded compensation for both material and moral damages.

This judgment is significant as it reinforced the obligation of states to consider the unique circumstances and vulnerabilities of Roma and Traveller communities in eviction cases, marking a step forward in the protection of their housing rights in Europe, against a backdrop of longstanding marginalisation.

cases.title: KONGRESNA NARODNA STRANKA AND OTHERS v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Kongresna Narodna Stranka and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, the applicants included the National Congress Party for the Protection of the Human Rights of War Veterans and Citizens, along with 45 individuals, three of whom identified as belonging to the Roma and Albanian ethnic minorities. The case was brought against Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the applicants challenging their exclusion from standing in national elections due to their non-affiliation with any of the country’s “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats, or Serbs), a system that has historically disadvantaged Roma and other minorities.

The core vulnerability at issue was the structural discrimination faced by Roma and other minorities, who, under Bosnia and Herzegovina’s constitutional framework, are excluded from certain political rights unless they declare affiliation with a constituent people. This exclusion perpetuates the marginalisation of Roma and Travellers, denying them equal participation in public life.

The facts unfolded as follows: the Party was refused registration for the 2010 elections because their application was late, and again in 2014 for failing to meet procedural requirements. The applicants argued that, as individuals not identifying with a constituent people—including three Roma applicants—they were barred from standing for election, invoking Article 14 (non-discrimination), Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination).

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and had not been prevented from participating in elections due to their ethnicity, but rather due to procedural shortcomings.
