This case highlights the ongoing barriers Roma and other minorities face in accessing political rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion despite previous landmark rulings such as Sejdić and Finci v. Bosnia and Herzegovina.

cases.title: CASE OF R.B. v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible (Article 35-3 - Manifestly ill-founded);Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of R.B. v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms. R.B., is a member of the Roma community living in the village of Gyöngyöspata. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma residents who faced intimidation and threats from right-wing paramilitary groups, highlighting the persistent risk of ethnically motivated harassment. In March 2011, following a demonstration by a right-wing political party, several paramilitary groups marched through the Roma neighbourhood, shouting racist insults and making violent threats. On 10 March 2011, four men passed by Ms. R.B.’s house, yelling anti-Roma slurs and threatening her and her family, with one man swinging an axe towards her. Despite her complaints and the clear evidence of intimidation, the authorities discontinued criminal proceedings, reasoning that the threats were not directed at a specific person and thus did not meet the threshold for prosecution.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and found a violation, concluding that the Hungarian authorities failed in their positive obligation to protect Ms. R.B. from intimidation and to adequately investigate the racist motives behind the threats. The Court awarded Ms. R.B. non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the duty of states to protect Roma and Traveller communities from ethnically motivated intimidation, especially in a historical context where such groups have faced systemic discrimination and insufficient state protection across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF BOACĂ AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Boacă and Others v. Romania, the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin, including the heirs of I.B., who had initiated proceedings before his death. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police brutality and ethnic discrimination, particularly in the context of law enforcement interventions. On 30 March 2006, following an altercation in Clejani, members of the Boacă family, including I.B. and his sons, were apprehended by police. The applicants alleged that police officers, accompanied by a rapid intervention squad, forcibly detained them, subjected them to physical violence, and used ethnic slurs such as “wretched disgraceful gypsies.” I.B. was severely beaten, lost consciousness, and required hospital treatment, while other family members, including minors, were also mistreated and coerced into signing confessions.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of degrading treatment), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and their combination. The Court found violations of Article 3 both substantively (due to police brutality) and procedurally (due to the lack of an effective investigation), as well as a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 3 regarding the authorities’ failure to investigate possible racist motives. The applicants were awarded compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Travellers’ rights, as it highlights the persistent problem of police violence and the necessity for authorities to investigate potential ethnic discrimination, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation faced by Roma communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF BALÁZS v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Article 35-3 - Ratione materiae);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Effective investigation);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Balázs v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. Balázs, a young man of Roma origin living in Szeged, brought a complaint against Hungary concerning the authorities’ response to a racially motivated assault. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to racially charged violence and the failure of state authorities to adequately investigate such incidents, particularly when the victim is a member of the Roma community. On 21 January 2011, Mr. Balázs and his girlfriend were leaving a club when they were subjected to degrading, anti-Roma insults and objects thrown at them by three men. A fourth man, Mr. E.D., who falsely presented himself as a police officer, joined in the abuse and later physically assaulted Mr. Balázs. Despite visible injuries to both men, only Mr. E.D. received immediate medical attention, and the subsequent investigation by Hungarian authorities failed to properly examine the racist motive behind the attack or to take sufficient investigative steps.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Hungary had violated both articles, specifically noting the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into the racist nature of the assault. Mr. Balázs was awarded non-pecuniary damages as just satisfaction. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the obligation of states to actively investigate and address hate crimes against Roma and Travellers, a group historically subjected to discrimination and violence across Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE V.M. ET AUTRES c. BELGIQUE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire jointe au fond (Article 35-1 - Epuisement des voies de recours internes);Exception préliminaire rejetée (Article 35-1 - Epuisement des voies de recours internes);Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Traitement dégradant) (Volet matériel);Non-violation de l'article 2 - Droit à la vie (Article 2-1 - Vie) (Volet matériel);Violation de l'article 13+3 - Droit à un recours effectif (Article 13 - Recours effectif) (Article 3 - Interdiction de la torture;Traitement dégradant);Dommage matériel - réparation (Article 41 - Dommage matériel;Satisfaction équitable)
cases.summary:
In the case of V.M. and Others v. Belgium, the applicants were a Serbian Roma family—Mr. V.M., Ms. G.S.M., and their children—who sought asylum in Belgium after fleeing discrimination and hardship in Serbia and Kosovo. Their vulnerability was heightened by their Roma identity and the severe health needs of their eldest daughter, who was disabled and suffered from epilepsy. After unsuccessful asylum attempts in France and a return to Serbia, the family arrived in Belgium in March 2011 and applied for asylum. Belgian authorities, applying the EU “Dublin II” Regulation, ordered the family to return to France and, crucially, withdrew their access to reception facilities and material support before their asylum procedure was fully resolved. As a result, from late September 2011, the family, including young children and a pregnant mother, were left homeless in Brussels for several weeks, relying on public spaces and charity for survival.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found that Belgium had violated Article 3 by exposing the family to degrading living conditions and Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3 for failing to provide an effective remedy. The applicants were awarded compensation for material damage. This judgment is significant as it highlights the particular risks faced by Roma and Traveller families in the asylum process, especially when state procedures fail to account for their heightened vulnerability—a recurring issue in Europe’s recent migration history.

cases.title: CASE OF V.M. AND OTHERS v. BELGIUM
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 13+3 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Degrading treatment);Pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of V.M. and Others v. Belgium, the applicants were a Serbian Roma family—Mr. V.M., Mrs. G.S.M., and their children—who sought asylum in Belgium after experiencing severe discrimination and hardship in Serbia and Kosovo due to their Roma identity. The family’s vulnerability was heightened by their eldest daughter’s significant disabilities and the mother’s pregnancy, making their need for stability and medical care especially urgent. After unsuccessful asylum attempts in France and a return to Serbia, the family arrived in Belgium in March 2011, where they applied for asylum. Belgian authorities, applying the Dublin II Regulation, ordered their return to France, despite the family’s explanations of their precarious situation and health needs. The applicants were given only seven days to leave, and their attempts to provide evidence of their circumstances were not adequately considered.

The European Court of Human Rights examined Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 13 (right to an effective remedy), finding that Belgium had violated both. The Court held that the authorities failed to assess the family’s vulnerability and health needs before ordering their removal, and that the available remedies were not sufficiently effective. Pecuniary damages were awarded to the applicants. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the obligation of states to consider the specific vulnerabilities of Roma and Traveller families, particularly in asylum and removal proceedings, against a backdrop of persistent discrimination and exclusion across Europe.

cases.title: LUPU v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Lupu v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Lupu, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma individuals to ill-treatment and discrimination, issues that have historically affected Roma and Travellers across Europe. Mr. Lupu alleged that he had suffered treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment, and that this was compounded by discrimination on the grounds of his Roma identity, invoking Article 14. The events giving rise to the complaint occurred in Romania, where Mr. Lupu claimed to have experienced both ill-treatment and a lack of effective protection from the authorities. However, before the European Court of Human Rights could examine the merits of his case, Mr. Lupu indicated that he no longer wished to pursue his application. As a result, on 30 June 2015, the Court struck the case out of its list, finding no special circumstances requiring further examination under Article 37. While no violation was found or remedies awarded, the case highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in seeking justice for alleged discrimination and ill-treatment, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: G.H. v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of G.H. v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms G.H., a Hungarian national represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, brought a complaint against Hungary. While the applicant’s own ethnic identity is not explicitly stated, her husband is identified as Roma, and the case was supported by an organisation specialising in Roma and Traveller rights, situating the matter within the broader context of Roma and Traveller vulnerability. The harm at the centre of the case concerned the risk of forced or non-consensual sterilisation, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma and Traveller women in Europe, raising serious concerns about reproductive rights and discrimination.

On 8 February 2008, Ms G.H., then 34 and pregnant with twins, was admitted to Miskolc Hospital for an emergency Caesarean section. During her admission, she discussed sterilisation with her doctors and verbally consented to the procedure, but her written consent was not obtained as required by law. After the operation, Ms G.H. sued the hospital, arguing that the lack of written consent violated her rights to self-determination, privacy, and equal treatment. Hungarian courts acknowledged the procedural breach and awarded her compensation and an apology, but found no evidence of racial discrimination or that the sterilisation was performed against her will.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 8 (right to respect for private life), but declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that Ms G.H. had given informed oral consent, that domestic courts had thoroughly examined her claims, and that she had received adequate redress, including compensation and an apology.

This case is significant as it highlights the importance of procedural safeguards in protecting the reproductive rights of Roma and Traveller women, while also demonstrating the Court’s approach when domestic remedies have been provided. Historically, Roma and Traveller communities have faced systemic violations of reproductive rights, making judicial scrutiny of such cases essential for upholding human dignity and equality.

cases.title: CASE OF MIHAYLOVA AND MALINOVA v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In Mihaylova and Malinova v. Bulgaria, the applicants—a mother and daughter of Roma origin from Samokov—brought a case against Bulgaria following the fatal shooting of Mr. Boris Mihaylov, their partner and father, by police. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face disproportionate police violence and inadequate investigations into such incidents. On the night of 3 August 2004, police responded to a report of three “gypsies” allegedly attempting to break into a lorry. When officers arrived, the men fled; Chief Sergeant S pursued and caught Mr. Mihaylov, leading to a struggle in which the officer fired two shots, one of which struck Mr. Mihaylov in the head at close range, resulting in his death. The subsequent investigation was marred by significant procedural shortcomings, including poor evidence preservation, contradictory police statements, and a lack of clarity regarding the use of force.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to life and requires an effective investigation into deaths caused by state agents. The Court found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2, concluding that the investigation into Mr. Mihaylov’s death was ineffective. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the persistent problem of inadequate state responses to police violence against Roma individuals—a pattern rooted in a long history of discrimination and marginalisation across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF CIORCAN AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 - Right to life;Article 2-1 - Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In the case of Ciorcan and Others v. Romania, thirty-seven Romanian nationals of Roma origin from the Apalina neighbourhood in Reghin brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The applicants, all identifying as Roma, alleged that they were subjected to excessive police violence and discriminatory treatment during a police operation. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma communities to disproportionate use of force by law enforcement and the lack of effective investigations into such incidents, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation.

On 7 September 2006, following a quarrel between a Roma resident and a police officer, a large contingent of police, including special forces, entered the Apalina neighbourhood to summon suspects. As residents, including women and children, gathered in the street, police used tear gas and fired shots—some into the crowd—resulting in over twenty-five Roma being injured, several seriously. Medical evidence confirmed gunshot wounds and life-threatening injuries among the applicants. Despite the gravity of the incident, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the use of force and the possible discriminatory motives behind the operation.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 (right to life), both substantively and procedurally, Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment, procedural aspect), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2. The Court emphasised the need for effective remedies and investigations in cases involving vulnerable minorities. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent risks faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, particularly regarding police violence and the failure of states to protect their rights and dignity, against a backdrop of historical discrimination.

cases.title: CASE OF M.A. v. SLOVENIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Positive obligations) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of M.A. v. Slovenia, the applicant, a woman of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Slovenia concerning the authorities’ handling of her case after she was subjected to a violent rape in 1983. The vulnerability at the heart of this case lies in the applicant’s experience as a Roma woman, a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of “Roma and Travellers,” who often face heightened risks of violence and barriers to justice due to discrimination and marginalisation.

On the evening of 3 November 1983, while eight months pregnant and returning home from work in Maribor, the applicant was abducted and raped by three men, all of whom were also of Roma origin. She immediately reported the crime, and the suspects were arrested. However, the ensuing criminal proceedings were plagued by repeated delays, adjournments, and absences of the accused or their counsel. Despite the gravity of the crime, it took over twenty-five years for the case to reach a final judgment, with significant portions of the proceedings occurring after Slovenia ratified the European Convention on Human Rights in 1994.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), focusing on the State’s procedural obligations. The Court found a violation of Article 3, concluding that the Slovenian authorities failed to conduct an effective and prompt investigation and trial. This judgment highlights the critical importance of timely justice for victims of serious crimes, especially for Roma and Traveller women, who have historically faced systemic obstacles in accessing protection and redress in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF MARIAN CHIRIȚĂ v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect)
cases.summary: In the case of Marian Chiriță v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Marian Chiriță, is a Romanian national of Roma ethnic origin who was serving a prison sentence in Romania. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma detainees, who often face systemic barriers to adequate healthcare in detention, compounding their marginalisation. Mr. Chiriță, suffering from severe heart disease and other chronic conditions, was repeatedly denied timely and appropriate medical treatment while in prison. Despite a final court order in November 2009 requiring his admission to a public hospital for urgent bypass surgery, the authorities failed to ensure he received the necessary care, instead keeping him within the prison health system, which was not equipped for such complex procedures. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found that Romania had violated Article 3, concluding that the authorities’ failure to provide adequate medical care and to enforce the court order caused Mr. Chiriță prolonged physical and mental suffering. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the obligation of states to protect the dignity and health of Roma detainees, a group historically subjected to discrimination and neglect within European prison systems.

cases.title: CASE OF CENTRE FOR LEGAL RESOURCES ON BEHALF OF VALENTIN CÂMPEANU v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 34 - Locus standi);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2 - Positive obligations;Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 13+2 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 2 - Right to life);Respondent State to take measures of a general character (Article 46-2 - Measures of a general character)
cases.summary:
In the case of Centre for Legal Resources on behalf of Valentin Câmpeanu v. Romania, the applicant was the Centre for Legal Resources (CLR), acting on behalf of Valentin Câmpeanu, a young man of Roma ethnicity. Mr. Câmpeanu, abandoned at birth and living with severe intellectual disabilities and HIV, was among the most vulnerable members of the Roma and Traveller communities, facing compounded discrimination due to his ethnicity, disability, and orphan status. The case concerned the failure of Romanian authorities to provide adequate care and protection to Mr. Câmpeanu, who, after being moved between institutions, was ultimately placed in a medical and social care centre ill-equipped to meet his complex needs. In February 2004, at the age of 18, he was admitted to the Cetate-Dolj Centre in a severely deteriorated state, lacking medication, proper clothing, or support, and died shortly after, alone and without legal representation or family.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 2 (right to life), both substantively and procedurally, and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found that Romania had failed to protect Mr. Câmpeanu’s life and to conduct an effective investigation into his death, and that he had no access to remedies. The Court also recognised the CLR’s standing to act on his behalf, given his extreme vulnerability and lack of representation. This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, highlighting the intersectional risks faced by Roma individuals with disabilities and setting a precedent for access to justice for the most marginalised, in a context where Roma communities have long suffered institutional neglect and exclusion.

cases.title: CASE OF KIM v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-4 - Take proceedings);Violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-1 - Lawful arrest or detention;Article 5-1-f - Expulsion);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Kim v. Russia, the applicant, Mr. Kim, was a stateless person born in the Uzbek SSR who had lived in St Petersburg since 1990. While the judgment does not explicitly identify Mr. Kim as belonging to the Roma or Traveller communities, it notes his statelessness and lack of identity documents—circumstances often affecting Roma and Travellers across Europe. The case centered on the harm caused by prolonged detention in inhuman and degrading conditions, as well as the legal uncertainty faced by stateless individuals subject to expulsion proceedings.

On 19 July 2011, Mr. Kim was stopped by police in St Petersburg for an identity check and, lacking documents, was fined and ordered to be expelled. He was detained in a severely overcrowded detention center for aliens, where he spent over two years in cramped cells with inadequate access to water, sanitation, and outdoor exercise. Despite repeated attempts, Russian authorities were unable to secure his removal, as Uzbekistan confirmed he was not a national and would not accept him. Throughout his detention, Mr. Kim was denied effective judicial review of his situation.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) due to the appalling detention conditions, and Article 5 (right to liberty and security), including the lack of lawful basis and judicial review for his prolonged detention. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages and highlighted the need for Russia to adopt general measures to prevent similar violations against stateless persons.

cases.title: CASE OF ZORNIĆ v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+P1-3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 - Stand for election;Right to free elections-{general});Violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 - General prohibition of discrimination;Violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 - General prohibition of discrimination
cases.summary: In Zornić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, the applicant, Ms. Azra Zornić, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Sarajevo, brought a case against the State after being barred from standing for election to the House of Peoples and the Presidency. Ms. Zornić does not declare affiliation with any of the “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats, or Serbs), identifying instead simply as a citizen. This exclusion reflects a broader vulnerability faced by those, including members of Roma and Traveller communities and others, who do not or cannot identify with the three constituent groups recognized by the Constitution. In 2002, Ms. Zornić stood as a candidate for the Social Democratic Party in parliamentary elections but was ineligible for higher office due to her refusal to declare ethnic affiliation. The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaints under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination). The Court found violations of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, holding that the constitutional arrangements unjustifiably discriminated against citizens not affiliated with a constituent people. The judgment reinforced the need for Bosnia and Herzegovina to amend its constitution and electoral laws to ensure equal political participation for all citizens, regardless of ethnic identification.

cases.title: Z.K. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Z.K. v. Slovakia, the applicant, Ms Z.K., is a Slovak national of Roma origin who brought a case against Slovakia, alleging serious violations of her rights as a member of the Roma and Travellers community. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma women to non-consensual sterilisation, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma women in Slovakia and elsewhere, raising grave concerns about discrimination and bodily autonomy. In February 1993, when she was still a minor, Ms Z.K. gave birth by caesarean section at Prešov Hospital. Over a decade later, she discovered a medical record indicating she had been sterilised during that delivery, without her knowledge or consent, and without the involvement of her legal guardians. This revelation led to years of infertility treatment, significant psychological distress, and social ostracism within her community.

Ms Z.K. pursued civil proceedings, seeking an apology and compensation, arguing violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 12 (right to marry and found a family), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the Slovak courts found insufficient evidence that the sterilisation had actually occurred, citing conflicting medical records and the applicant’s refusal to undergo further invasive testing. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately declared the application inadmissible, as the facts could not be established to the required standard.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma women face in seeking justice for alleged forced sterilisation, a practice rooted in historical discrimination and mistrust of Roma and Travellers by state institutions. The decision underscores the evidentiary hurdles that can impede access to remedies for members of vulnerable minorities, even in the face of credible allegations.

cases.title: A.M.B. AND OTHERS v. SPAIN - [English Translation] by European Roma Rights Centre "ERRC"
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of A.M.B. and Others v. Spain, the applicant, Mrs. A.M.B., a Spanish national of Roma origin, brought a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights on behalf of herself and her two minor children against the Spanish state. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing eviction from social housing without adequate safeguards or alternative accommodation, a situation that can exacerbate social exclusion and hardship for already marginalised communities. Mrs. A.M.B. and her children had been living since July 2009 in an uninhabited flat owned by the Madrid Housing Institute (IVIMA), after repeated unsuccessful requests for official housing. In February 2011, IVIMA ordered their eviction without offering alternative housing, and subsequent legal proceedings confirmed the expulsion, despite the applicant’s arguments about her family’s precarious situation and Roma identity. The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly due to the lack of alternative accommodation and the non-suspensive effect of her appeal. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible under Article 35, as domestic remedies had not been exhausted—the applicant’s constitutional appeal was still pending in Spain. This case underscores the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families may face in seeking protection from eviction, reflecting broader challenges in accessing justice and adequate housing in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE WINTERSTEIN ET AUTRES c. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire rejetée (Article 35-1 - Epuisement des voies de recours internes);Partiellement irrecevable;Violation de l'article 8 - Droit au respect de la vie privée et familiale (Article 8-1 - Respect de la vie familiale;Respect du domicile;Respect de la vie privée);Satisfaction équitable réservée
cases.summary:
In Winterstein and Others v. France, the applicants were a group of individuals from the “Gens du voyage” community—part of the broader Roma and Travellers population as defined by the Council of Europe—living in the commune of Herblay, Val d’Oise, France. The case focused on the vulnerability of these families, who faced eviction from land they had occupied for many years, threatening their established homes, family life, and cultural identity as Travellers. Beginning in the early 2000s, the applicants, many of whom were semi-sedentary or had become settled due to repeated expulsions, lived in caravans on land in Herblay. Despite longstanding residence and efforts to regularise their situation, local authorities initiated legal proceedings that resulted in court orders for their eviction, with the threat of force and financial penalties.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found that France had violated Article 8, ruling that the authorities failed to strike a fair balance between the applicants’ rights and the public interest, particularly given their long-term ties to the land and lack of suitable alternative accommodation. The Court reserved the question of just satisfaction for a later stage.

This judgment is significant as it reinforces the protection of Roma and Traveller communities against forced evictions without adequate safeguards, reflecting a broader European context of historical marginalisation and the need for states to respect the specific circumstances of Roma and Travellers when enforcing housing and land regulations.

cases.title: CASE OF WINTERSTEIN AND OTHERS v. FRANCE [Extracts]
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for home;Respect for private life);Just satisfaction reserved
cases.summary:
In Winterstein and Others v. France, the applicants were predominantly Travellers (gens du voyage), a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers, who had lived for many years in the municipality of Herblay, Val d’Oise. The case focused on the vulnerability of these Traveller families, who faced repeated evictions and prohibitions on encampment, threatening their right to maintain their traditional way of life and family unity. The applicants, all French nationals, had established long-standing homes in the “Bois du Trou-Poulet” area, with some families residing there for generations. Despite this, local authorities issued orders in 2003 and 2005 banning the encampment of mobile homes throughout Herblay, and failed to provide sufficient alternative accommodation, even as national and local plans acknowledged the need for dedicated Traveller sites.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life, home, and correspondence. The Court found a violation of Article 8, holding that the evictions and lack of adequate alternative housing disproportionately interfered with the applicants’ rights. The Court reserved the question of just satisfaction for a later stage. This judgment is significant as it affirms the special protection owed to Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, particularly regarding their housing rights, against a backdrop of historical exclusion and forced displacement.

cases.title: CASE OF VONA v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 11 - Freedom of assembly and association (Article 11-1 - Freedom of association)
cases.summary:
In the case of Vona v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. Gábor Vona, was the chairman of the Hungarian Guard Association, an organisation closely linked to the Hungarian Guard Movement. While Mr. Vona himself was not a member of the Roma or Traveller communities, the case directly concerned the rights and safety of Roma populations in Hungary. The central issue was the harm caused to Roma communities by the Movement’s activities, which included uniformed rallies and demonstrations in villages with large Roma populations, accompanied by rhetoric about defending “ethnic Hungarians” against so-called “Gypsy criminality.” These actions generated fear and intimidation among Roma residents, who became a captive audience to exclusionary and hostile messages.

Between 2007 and 2008, the Hungarian Guard Movement, under the auspices of the Association, organised several public events, including a high-profile rally in Tatárszentgyörgy and similar demonstrations in Fadd and Sárbogárd. These events featured military-style uniforms, formations, and commands, and were often staged in areas with significant Roma populations. The authorities, responding to complaints and the evident impact on Roma communities, initiated legal proceedings to dissolve the Association, arguing that its activities infringed the rights of others by generating fear and promoting exclusion.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 11 (freedom of assembly and association) and Article 17 (prohibition of abuse of rights). The Court found no violation of Article 11, holding that the dissolution of the Association was necessary in a democratic society to protect the rights of the Roma minority from intimidation and the threat of exclusion. No remedies were awarded to the applicant.

This case is significant for Roma rights as it affirms that states may take decisive action against organisations whose activities intimidate or threaten vulnerable minorities. Against the backdrop of a history of anti-Roma sentiment and violence in Europe, the judgment underscores the importance of protecting Roma and Traveller communities from organised campaigns of fear and exclusion.

cases.title: CASE OF LAVIDA AND OTHERS v. GREECE - [English Translation] by European Roma Rights Centre "ERRC"
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 14+P1-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to education;Right to education-{general})
cases.summary:
In the case of Lavida and Others v. Greece, the applicants were Roma children and their parents residing in the municipality of Sofades, Thessaly, who brought a complaint against Greece. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma children subjected to ethnic segregation in education, a persistent issue affecting Roma and Traveller communities across Europe. During the 2009–2010 school year, the applicants, all of Roma origin, were assigned to the 4th Primary School of Sofades, a school attended exclusively by Roma pupils, despite living closer to the 1st Primary School, which served non-Roma children. Efforts by the applicants and advocacy groups to address this segregation—including letters to education authorities and the Ombudsman—went unanswered, and Roma children continued to be bused to the segregated school farther from their homes.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding that Greece had violated both provisions by failing to prevent and address the segregation of Roma children. The Court held that this practice amounted to discrimination and ordered Greece to take measures to end such segregation.

This judgment is significant as it reinforces the principle that Roma and Traveller children must have equal, non-discriminatory access to mainstream education, echoing a broader European movement to combat the historical marginalisation and segregation of Roma communities in schools.

cases.title: CASE OF HORVÁTH AND KISS v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 14+P1-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to education-{general})
cases.summary:
In Horváth and Kiss v. Hungary, the applicants, two young Roma men from Nyíregyháza, challenged the Hungarian state after being placed in a remedial school for children with mental disabilities. Both applicants, who identify as Roma, argued that their misdiagnosis and subsequent segregation into special education reflected a broader pattern of discrimination against Roma and Traveller children in Hungary. The heart of the case lay in the vulnerability of Roma children to systemic misdiagnosis, which led to their overrepresentation in special schools and limited their educational and professional opportunities.

The events unfolded in the early 2000s, when the applicants were diagnosed as having mental disabilities and sent to the Göllesz Viktor Remedial Primary and Vocational School, where Roma students made up nearly half the population despite being a small minority in the general student body. This placement restricted their access to mainstream education and the Baccalaureate, curtailing their ambitions and future prospects. The applicants’ parents were not properly informed of the process or their rights, and the diagnostic procedures failed to consider cultural and linguistic differences.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding that Hungary had violated both provisions. The Court held that the state had failed to take adequate safeguards to prevent discrimination against Roma children in the education system. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent issue of educational segregation of Roma and Traveller children in Europe, a practice rooted in decades of systemic discrimination and misdiagnosis.

cases.title: CASE OF SAMPANI AND OTHERS v. GREECE - [English Translation] by European Roma Rights Centre "ERRC"
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 14+P1-2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to education;Right to education-{general});Respondent State to take individual measures (Article 46-2 - Individual measures);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In Sampani and Others v. Greece, the applicants were ninety-eight school-aged children and forty-two adults, all of Romani origin, living in the Psari area near Aspropyrgos. The case focused on the persistent educational segregation and discrimination faced by Roma children, a group historically subjected to exclusion and unequal treatment in Greek schools. Between 2005 and 2010, the applicants’ children were either not enrolled in local schools or were placed in separate preparatory classes and substandard facilities, often in prefabricated buildings that suffered repeated damage and were not fit for use. Despite official measures to integrate Roma and non-Roma students, the authorities continued to assign Roma children to the newly created 12th primary school, which was effectively segregated and lacked adequate infrastructure, while non-Roma parents and local officials resisted their inclusion in ordinary classes.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding that Greece had violated these provisions by failing to ensure equal access to quality education for Roma children. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages and required Greece to take individual measures to remedy the situation. This judgment is significant as it reaffirms the right of Roma and Traveller children to non-discriminatory education and highlights the ongoing struggle against segregation in European schools, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation faced by Roma and Traveller communities across the continent.

cases.title: CASE OF LĂCĂTUŞ AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home);Violation of Article 6 - Right to a fair trial (Article 6 - Civil proceedings;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing);Violation of Article 14+6 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 6 - Right to a fair trial;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing);Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
cases.summary: In the case of Lăcătuş and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Ms. Voichiţa (Rostaş) Lăcătuş and her daughters, Ms. Speranţa-Lămâiţa Rostaş and Ms. Rada-Codruţa Rostaş—are members of the Roma community, as defined by the Council of Europe, who brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case centred on the extreme vulnerability of Roma families subjected to violent attacks, destruction of their homes, and subsequent homelessness, compounded by the authorities’ failure to provide protection or redress. On 20 September 1993, in the village of Hădăreni, a violent confrontation led to the death of a non-Roma man, after which a mob, including police officers, attacked Roma residents. The applicants’ home was destroyed, and they were forced to flee and live in overcrowded, inadequate conditions for years, receiving no assistance from the authorities. The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding that Romania had violated all these rights, both substantively and in terms of discrimination. The Court awarded remedies for the harm suffered. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent discrimination and violence faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, particularly in the post-communist context of the 1990s, and affirms the responsibility of states to protect minority communities from both private and institutional harm.

cases.title: CASE OF I.G. AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objections dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Preliminary objections dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for private life);No violation of Article 13 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of I.G. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants—Ms. I.G., Ms. M.K., and Ms. R.H.—were women of Roma origin who brought a case against Slovakia. The heart of the case was the forced sterilisation of these Roma women without their full and informed consent, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma and Traveller women in Europe and left them particularly vulnerable to violations of their bodily autonomy and dignity. The events took place between 1999 and 2002 at Krompachy Hospital, where each applicant, while still a minor and during childbirth by Caesarean section, was sterilised by tubal ligation. None of the women, nor their legal guardians, were properly informed or gave valid consent before the procedures. The applicants only discovered the sterilisation years later, often after suffering social stigma, relationship breakdowns, and psychological trauma.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Slovakia had violated both articles, both substantively and procedurally, due to the degrading treatment suffered and the lack of effective investigation. The applicants were awarded compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is a landmark for Roma and Traveller rights, highlighting the historical context of forced sterilisation policies targeting Roma women in Central and Eastern Europe, and affirming the need for robust safeguards to protect the reproductive rights and dignity of Roma and Traveller communities.

cases.title: BRAJDIČ v. SLOVENIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Brajdič v. Slovenia, the applicant, Mr. Astor Brajdič, is a Slovenian national of Roma ethnic origin who brought a complaint against Slovenia. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers in detention, specifically alleging discrimination and inadequate protection from harm due to his Roma identity while imprisoned. Mr. Brajdič had been serving a sentence in Dob Prison since December 2008, where he claimed to have suffered from overcrowded conditions, poor sanitation, limited access to the outside world, and insufficient psychological support. He further alleged that he experienced mental distress as a result of discrimination by fellow inmates on account of his Roma origin, and that the authorities failed to provide adequate assistance or remedies.

The European Court of Human Rights examined his complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the Court found that Mr. Brajdič had not provided sufficient evidence or details to substantiate his claims of discrimination or inadequate care, and noted that there was no record of ethnic conflict or discrimination in the prison. As a result, the application was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded.

This case highlights the evidentiary challenges Roma and Traveller applicants may face in substantiating claims of discrimination in detention, reflecting broader historical difficulties in addressing the systemic marginalisation of Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: ROMA c. ITALIE ET AUTRES REQUÊTES
cases.conclusion: Radiation du rôle
cases.summary: In the case of Roma v. Italy and Others, the applicants included Guido Roma and several other individuals, some of whom identified as Roma or Travellers, bringing their claims against the Italian state. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities in Italy, who have historically faced discrimination and obstacles in accessing justice and property rights. The applicants, residing in various Italian cities such as Salerno, Brescia, Palermo, and Milan, lodged their complaints between 2010 and 2011, alleging violations of their rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically concerning fair trial guarantees, effective remedies, and protection of property. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 6 (right to a fair trial), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). However, before a full judgment was rendered, the parties reached a friendly settlement, which the Court found to be consistent with respect for human rights. As a result, the Court struck the case from its list in accordance with Article 39 of the Convention. This outcome reflects the ongoing importance of negotiated solutions in addressing the longstanding challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Italy, against a backdrop of persistent marginalisation across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF FEDORCHENKO AND LOZENKO v. UKRAINE
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 14+2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 2 - Right to life;Article 2-1 - Effective investigation)
cases.summary:
In the case of Fedorchenko and Lozenko v. Ukraine, the applicants, Mr. Fedorchenko and Ms. Lozenko, are members of the Roma community living in Ukraine. Their case brought to the European Court of Human Rights centred on the vulnerability of Roma families to violent attacks and the failure of state authorities to protect their lives and investigate such crimes effectively. On 28 October 2001, the applicants’ home was set on fire in an arson attack in the town of Novi Sanzghary. The first applicant survived with injuries, but five family members, including children, died as a result of the fire or from burns sustained. The applicants alleged that a police officer, Major I., was involved in the attack, motivated by extortion and previous threats, and that the authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation, ignoring evidence and not questioning key witnesses.

The Court examined the case under Article 2 (right to life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. It found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2, as the investigation into the deaths was inadequate, and a violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 2, recognising that the authorities failed to take into account possible racist motives behind the attack. No violation was found regarding the substantive aspect of Article 2. The Court awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent dangers faced by Roma and Traveller families in Europe and the historical failure of authorities to protect them or investigate crimes against them with due diligence and without discrimination.

cases.title: CASE OF BUCKLAND v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
cases.summary:
In Buckland v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Maria Buckland, identified as a Gypsy and thus fell within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. She brought a case against the United Kingdom after being evicted from the Cae Garw caravan site in Port Talbot, Wales, where she had lived with her two children since 1999. The harm at the centre of the case was the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to eviction from their homes, often without sufficient procedural safeguards or consideration of their specific needs and way of life.

Ms. Buckland’s licence to occupy her pitch was terminated by the Gypsy Council in December 2004, with no detailed reasons provided. Although allegations of nuisance were later raised, the domestic court found that Ms. Buckland herself had not engaged in serious misconduct, apart from minor arrears in water charges. Nevertheless, a possession order was made against her, suspended only briefly, and she was ultimately required to leave her home. The courts relied on domestic law that did not allow her to challenge the proportionality of her eviction in light of her right to respect for her home.

The European Court of Human Rights examined Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found a violation of Article 8, holding that Ms. Buckland had not been given the opportunity to have the proportionality of her eviction determined by an independent tribunal. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, reinforcing the principle established in earlier cases that evictions affecting these communities must be subject to meaningful judicial scrutiny, especially given their long history of marginalisation and insecure housing across Europe.

cases.title: SIMION v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Simion v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Simion, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma individuals in Romania, who often face discrimination and other human rights violations, though the specific harm alleged by Mr. Simion is not detailed in the Court’s published decision. According to the available facts, Mr. Simion lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights, raising issues under several articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including Articles 3, 4, 10, and 14, which address the prohibition of torture, prohibition of slavery, freedom of expression, and prohibition of discrimination, respectively. However, before the Court could examine the merits of his claims, Mr. Simion indicated that he no longer wished to pursue his application. As a result, on 11 September 2012, the Court struck the case out of its list, finding no special circumstances requiring further examination. While no violation was found or remedy awarded, the case highlights the procedural challenges that can arise for Roma and Traveller applicants seeking justice at the European level, reflecting broader historical difficulties in accessing effective remedies for rights violations.

cases.title: CASE OF M. AND OTHERS v. ITALY AND BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection partially dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Preliminary objection partially allowed (Article 34 - Victim);Remainder inadmissible;No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect) (Italy);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect) (Italy)
cases.summary:
In the case of M. and Others v. Italy and Bulgaria, the applicants—a Roma family from Novo Selo in Bulgaria—brought a complaint against both Italy and Bulgaria. The applicants, who are of Roma ethnic origin, included a minor and her parents, highlighting the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to exploitation and abuse, especially when seeking work abroad. In May 2003, the family travelled to Italy after being promised employment by another Roma individual. Upon arrival, they were accommodated in a villa in Ghislarengo, where the minor was allegedly subjected to forced labour, physical abuse, and repeated sexual violence, while her parents were threatened and forced to return to Bulgaria. The mother later returned to Italy to report the kidnapping and abuse to the police, but the authorities responded slowly, and the minor was only rescued after an eighteen-day delay. During police questioning, the applicants alleged further mistreatment and inadequate interpretation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights. While the Court found no substantive violation of Article 3 by Italy regarding the treatment itself, it held that Italy had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the applicants’ allegations, thus violating the procedural aspect of Article 3. This case is significant as it underscores the persistent risks of trafficking and abuse faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, and the critical importance of prompt, thorough investigations by authorities—a concern that remains highly relevant given the historical marginalisation of Roma and Travellers across the continent.

cases.title: CASE OF FÁBER v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 10 - Freedom of expression -{General} (Article 10-1 - Freedom of expression) read in the light of Article 11 - (Art. 11) Freedom of assembly and association (Article 11-1 - Freedom of peaceful assembly);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In Fáber v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. János Fáber, a Hungarian national, challenged his conviction for holding an Árpád-striped flag during a public demonstration in Budapest on 9 May 2007. The case did not involve a Roma or Traveller applicant, but the context is relevant to minority rights, as the demonstration organized by the Hungarian Socialist Party was specifically protesting against racism and hatred, issues central to Roma and Traveller communities in Hungary. On the day in question, Mr. Fáber stood silently with the flag near the Socialist Party’s anti-racism event, close to a simultaneous right-wing Jobbik party gathering. Police, acting on instructions not to tolerate the flag within 100 metres of the Socialist demonstration, ordered Mr. Fáber to remove it or leave. When he refused, he was detained for six hours and later fined for disobeying police instructions. His appeals in domestic courts were unsuccessful, with the courts finding his conduct provocative and likely to disturb public order.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 10 (freedom of expression), read in light of Article 11 (freedom of assembly). The Court found that Hungary had violated Mr. Fáber’s right to freedom of expression, ruling that the authorities’ response was disproportionate and not justified by a pressing social need. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to Mr. Fáber. This judgment is significant for its emphasis on the high level of protection afforded to political expression, even when it is provocative or offensive, provided it does not incite violence or hatred.

cases.title: CASE OF KURIĆ AND OTHERS v. SLOVENIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objections dismissed (Article 35-1 - Effective domestic remedy;Continuing situation;Article 35-3 - Ratione materiae;Ratione temporis);Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Preliminary objection allowed (Article 35-1 - Effective domestic remedy);Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for private life);Violation of Article 13+8 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life);Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life);Respondent State to take measures of a general character (Article 46 - Pilot judgment;General measures);Pecuniary damage - reserved;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Kurić and Others v. Slovenia, the applicants were eight individuals, including Mr. Mustafa Kurić, who identified as members of the Roma and other minority groups from the former Yugoslavia, residing in Slovenia at the time of its independence. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and other minorities who, following Slovenia’s independence in 1991, became victims of the so-called “erasure”—the removal of their names from the register of permanent residents. This act left thousands, including the applicants, stateless or without legal status, depriving them of basic rights such as healthcare, employment, and social security.

After Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991, the applicants, who had been lawful residents, failed to acquire Slovenian citizenship within a short legal window. As a result, in February 1992, their names were erased from the register, stripping them of residency rights and rendering them undocumented. Many, including Roma and other minorities, faced expulsion, loss of homes, and severe social exclusion for years.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Slovenia had violated these rights and ordered both individual compensation and general measures to remedy the situation.

This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it addressed the long-standing exclusion and discrimination faced by minorities in post-Yugoslav states, setting a precedent for the protection of stateless and marginalised groups in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF BORBALA KISS v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of Borbala Kiss v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms. Borbala Kiss, is a Hungarian national of Roma origin who brought a complaint against the Hungarian state. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the lack of effective legal protection when such abuses occur. On 4 September 2010, during a family gathering in Tiszalúc attended by around fifty people, police officers intervened twice due to noise complaints. After a heated exchange, Ms. Kiss was verbally abused by an officer, threatened with arrest, grabbed, and pepper-sprayed in the eyes. She was then dragged by several male officers to a police car, during which her clothing was torn and she suffered physical injuries and humiliation. Despite her complaints and medical evidence, the authorities repeatedly discontinued investigations into the police conduct, relying mainly on police testimony and failing to hear key witnesses or the officers involved.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found both a substantive violation, due to the degrading treatment inflicted on Ms. Kiss, and a procedural violation, due to the lack of an effective investigation. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent risks of police abuse faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe and the systemic failures in ensuring accountability, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination against these communities.

cases.title: CASE OF KOKY AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage)
cases.summary:
In Koky and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were members of the Roma community living in the village of Gánovce-Filice, Slovakia. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma residents who were subjected to a violent, racially motivated attack and the subsequent failure of the authorities to conduct an effective investigation. On the evening of 28 February 2002, following an argument in a local bar where a Roma man was refused service, a group of at least twelve masked and armed individuals entered the Roma settlement, shouting racist language, breaking into homes, damaging property, and physically assaulting several Roma residents, including Mr Ján Koky, Mr Martin Kočko, and Mr Rastislav Koky. Despite the serious nature of the attack and the injuries sustained, the police response was delayed and the ensuing investigation was inadequate, failing to identify or prosecute those responsible.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, focusing on the procedural obligation to investigate such acts. The Court found a violation of Article 3 due to the authorities’ failure to carry out an effective investigation into the racially motivated violence. The applicants were awarded non-pecuniary damages as just satisfaction.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent problem of anti-Roma violence and the duty of states to protect Roma and Traveller communities from racially motivated attacks, especially in light of Europe’s long history of discrimination against these groups.

cases.title: CASE OF N.B. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of N.B. v. Slovakia, the applicant, Ms. N.B., is a woman of Roma origin living in Nálepkovo, Slovakia. Her case brought to the European Court of Human Rights highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma women to non-consensual sterilisation, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma and Traveller communities in Europe. On 25 April 2001, at the age of 17 and while in labour with her second child at Gelnica Hospital, Ms. N.B. was sterilised without her full and informed consent. Under the influence of sedative medication and in a highly vulnerable state, she was asked to sign documents authorising the procedure, without any explanation and without the involvement or consent of her mother, who was her legal representative as she was still a minor. Ms. N.B. only learned of the sterilisation’s nature over a year later, suffering significant psychological harm and social ostracism as a result.

The Court examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. It found that Slovakia had violated both articles, recognising the sterilisation as inhuman and degrading treatment and a breach of her private and family life. The Court awarded Ms. N.B. non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it addresses the historical pattern of forced sterilisation of Roma women in Central and Eastern Europe, affirming the need for robust safeguards to protect the reproductive rights and dignity of Roma and Traveller women.

cases.title: CASE OF NACIC AND OTHERS v. SWEDEN
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Expulsion) (Conditional) (Serbia);No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Expulsion;Article 8-1 - Respect for family life)
cases.summary: In the case of Nacic and Others v. Sweden, the applicants—Mr. Sladjan Nacic, his wife Jelena Nacic, and their two sons—are a family of Roma descent who fled Kosovo in 1999 due to threats and violence linked to the conflict and their ethnicity. The core vulnerability in this case was the risk of harm the family faced as Roma, including discrimination and difficulties accessing health care if returned to Kosovo or Serbia, compounded by serious mental health issues within the family. After hiding in Kosovo for several years, the family arrived in Sweden in 2006 and sought asylum, citing both past trauma and ongoing psychological distress. Swedish authorities rejected their applications, questioning their Roma identity and finding insufficient evidence of persecution or risk upon return, despite medical reports indicating depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and suicide attempts among the applicants. The European Court of Human Rights examined their complaints under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the Convention. The Court found no violation of either article, concluding that the applicants had not demonstrated a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 or a breach of their family life under Article 8 if returned. This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller families face in proving both their identity and the specific risks of discrimination and exclusion in asylum proceedings, against a backdrop of persistent marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF KLEYN AND ALEKSANDROVICH v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible (Article 35-1 - Six month period);No violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Kleyn and Aleksandrovich v. Russia, the applicants were Mr. Kleyn, a Russian national, and his son, both of whom are Russian nationals living in the Pskov Region. The case concerned the death of Ms. Fatsima Aleksandrovich, Mr. Kleyn’s late wife and the mother of his son, who was a Belarus national of Roma ethnicity. The applicants’ Roma identity is central, as the events unfolded against a backdrop of ethnic prejudice.

The vulnerability at the heart of the case was the discriminatory treatment and lack of protection afforded to Ms. Aleksandrovich as a Roma woman in police custody, culminating in her death and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. The harm was compounded by the police officer’s assumption of guilt based on her ethnicity and the subsequent inadequate response by the authorities.

On 20 May 2002, Ms. Aleksandrovich was arrested on a bus in Pskov after a police officer’s purse went missing. Despite the purse being found, she was accused of theft solely because of her Roma background, struck on the head, and taken to the police station. While in custody, she complained of severe pain and was later found unconscious in the police yard, having apparently jumped from a window. She died four days later from her injuries. The ensuing investigation was marked by delays and significant shortcomings.

The European Court of Human Rights examined Article 2 (right to life) of the Convention. While it found no substantive violation regarding the cause of death, it held that Russia had violated the procedural aspect of Article 2 by failing to conduct an effective investigation. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent risks Roma and Traveller individuals face in police custody and the critical importance of thorough, unbiased investigations into deaths involving vulnerable minorities. It reflects a broader historical context of systemic discrimination against Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF YORDANOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Respect for home;Respect for private life) (Conditional);Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient;Respondent State to take individual measures (Article 46-2 - Individual measures)
cases.summary:
In Yordanova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were residents of Batalova Vodenitsa, a neighbourhood in Sofia, who identified themselves as being of Roma origin. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma families facing eviction from homes they had built and lived in for decades, highlighting the precariousness of their housing situation and the risk of homelessness. Many of the applicants or their families had settled in Batalova Vodenitsa from the late 1960s onwards, constructing homes on state land that was never formally allocated or regularised, and living in conditions lacking basic infrastructure such as sewage and plumbing.

Tensions grew in the area as non-Roma neighbours and local authorities increasingly pressured for the removal of the Roma settlement, citing sanitary and aesthetic concerns. In 2005, the Sofia municipality issued removal orders to the applicants, threatening forcible eviction and demolition of their homes. Despite an agreement to provide alternative housing, the municipality took no action, and the courts upheld the removal orders solely on the basis of the applicants’ lack of legal title to the land.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the Convention, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found a violation of Article 8, ruling that the authorities had failed to balance the applicants’ interests against the public interest and had not considered their vulnerability or the consequences of eviction. The Court required Bulgaria to take individual measures to remedy the situation. This judgment is significant as it affirms the need for procedural safeguards and proportionality in eviction cases, especially given the historical marginalisation of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF KALUCZA v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations)
cases.summary: In the case of Kalucza v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms. Kalucza, a woman of Roma origin living in Budapest, brought a complaint against the Hungarian state. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller women facing domestic violence, and the difficulties they encounter in obtaining effective protection from the authorities. Between 2005 and 2010, Ms. Kalucza endured repeated physical assaults and threats from her partner, Gy.B., with whom she shared an apartment. Despite numerous criminal complaints, medical reports documenting her injuries, and repeated requests for restraining orders, the Hungarian authorities failed to provide her with adequate protection. The courts often dismissed her requests for restraining orders, citing mutual animosity or lack of evidence, and criminal proceedings were frequently delayed or discontinued. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found that Hungary had violated its positive obligations under Article 8 by failing to protect Ms. Kalucza from domestic violence and to provide an effective legal framework for her protection. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the need for states to address the intersectional vulnerabilities faced by Roma women, who have historically been at heightened risk of violence and institutional neglect in Europe.

cases.title: MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Moldovan and Others v.
