Romania (2012), the applicants—Mr. Luşca Moldovan, Mrs. Monica Simona Moldovan, Ms. Olguţa, Ms. Sanda and Mr. Traian Florin Lăcătuş, and Mr. Lucian-Gruia Rostaş—were Romanian nationals of Roma origin from the village of Hădăreni. Their case concerned the aftermath of the violent inter-ethnic clashes of 20 September 1993, which resulted in the killing of three Roma individuals and the destruction of eighteen Roma homes. The applicants, all members of the Roma community, suffered the loss of family members, destruction of property, and years of displacement and hardship, including being forced to live in overcrowded and inadequate conditions, both in Romania and later as refugees in Belgium.

The core harm at issue was the severe and lasting impact of anti-Roma violence, compounded by alleged failures of the Romanian authorities to provide redress or adequate living conditions, and the applicants’ subsequent vulnerability as refugees. The applicants described ongoing trauma, health problems, and persistent threats, which led them to seek asylum abroad.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the applicants had not exhausted available domestic remedies in Romania, as required by Article 35 of the Convention, distinguishing their situation from earlier successful cases where applicants had pursued all legal avenues domestically.

This decision highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller applicants may face in accessing justice at the European level, even in the context of well-documented anti-Roma violence. It underscores the importance of exhausting national remedies—a requirement that has historically posed challenges for Roma communities seeking redress for systemic discrimination and violence in Europe.

cases.title: COSTACHE v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Costache v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Mitică Costache, is a Romanian national of Roma origin living in Slobozia. His case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing inadequate housing and the compounded difficulties experienced by those with severe health conditions. After suffering a stroke in 2005, Mr. Costache was left paralysed on one side and later diagnosed with chronic hepatitis, brain damage, and epilepsy. Unable to secure proper accommodation, he and his partner, C.C., lived for several years in a deserted horse stable lacking basic amenities such as water, electricity, and sanitation—conditions repeatedly documented by social services as unsuitable for human habitation.

Mr. Costache complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the authorities’ failure to provide adequate housing, given his health and vulnerability, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 and a violation of his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the Court ultimately found the application inadmissible, reasoning that Article 8 does not guarantee a right to housing and that the authorities had eventually provided social accommodation once it became available.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent housing insecurity faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, particularly those with disabilities, and clarifies the limited scope of positive obligations under the Convention regarding social housing, even amid ongoing marginalisation of Roma communities.

cases.title: CASE OF KONSTANTIN MARKIN v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 37-1-b - Matter resolved);Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8-1 - Respect for family life;Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life);No violation of Article 34 - Individual applications (Article 34 - Hinder the exercise of the right of petition);Non-pecuniary damage - award;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed
cases.summary:
The case of Konstantin Markin v. Russia concerned Mr. Markin, a Russian national and military serviceman, who sought three years’ parental leave to care for his three children after his divorce in 2005. The applicant, who is not identified as belonging to the Roma or Traveller communities, became the sole carer for his children when his former wife moved to St Petersburg. When Mr. Markin requested parental leave from his military unit, his request was denied on the grounds that, under Russian law, only female military personnel were entitled to such leave. He was granted a short period of leave but was soon recalled to duty, prompting him to challenge the decision in Russian courts, which ultimately upheld the restriction.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that denying parental leave to male servicemen, while granting it to servicewomen, constituted unjustified gender discrimination and violated Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8. The Court awarded Mr. Markin compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant for its clear stance that states must avoid gender-based discrimination in parental leave policies, even within the context of military service, and that the special status of the armed forces does not justify blanket exclusions based on sex.

cases.title: CASE OF AKSU v. TURKEY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life)
cases.summary:
In the case of Aksu v. Turkey, the applicant, Mr. Ahmet Aksu, is a Turkish national of Roma origin who brought a complaint against the Turkish state. Mr. Aksu argued that his Roma identity was harmed by the publication of a government-funded book, "The Gypsies of Turkey," and by dictionary definitions that he considered offensive and degrading to Roma and Traveller communities. The core of the case was the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to negative stereotyping and the perpetuation of prejudice through state-supported publications, which Mr. Aksu claimed undermined his dignity and private life.

The events unfolded in 2000, when the Turkish Ministry of Culture published the book in question, which included descriptions and generalisations about Roma people’s physical characteristics and way of life. Mr. Aksu contended that both the book and certain dictionary entries contained language that reflected anti-Roma sentiment and constituted an attack on his identity.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found no violation of Article 8, concluding that the publications did not amount to an unjustified interference with Mr. Aksu’s rights and that there was no evidence of discriminatory intent or effect.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it clarifies the threshold for state responsibility in cases of alleged group defamation, against a backdrop of historical marginalisation of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE HIRSI JAMAA ET AUTRES c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire jointe au fond et rejetée (Article 35-1 - Epuisement des voies de recours internes);Exception préliminaire jointe au fond et rejetée (Article 34 - Victime);Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Expulsion) (Conditionnel) (Libye);Violation de l'article 3 - Interdiction de la torture (Article 3 - Expulsion) (Conditionnel) (Eritrea) (Somalie);Violation de l'article 4 du Protocole n° 4 - Interdiction des expulsions collectives d'étrangers-{général} (article 4 du Protocole n° 4 - Interdiction des expulsions collectives d'étrangers);Violation de l'article 13+3 - Droit à un recours effectif (Article 13 - Recours effectif) (Article 3 - Interdiction de la torture;Expulsion);Violation de l'article 13+P4-4 - Droit à un recours effectif (Article 13 - Recours effectif) (article 4 du Protocole n° 4 - Interdiction des expulsions collectives d'étrangers-{général};Interdiction des expulsions collectives d'étrangers);Préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary:
Hirsi Jamaa and Others v. Italy concerned a group of applicants—eleven Somali and thirteen Eritrean nationals—who left Libya by boat in May 2009, aiming to reach Italy. The applicants, described in the judgment as migrants from Somalia and Eritrea, did not claim Roma or Traveller identity, nor does the judgment suggest such a background. Their vulnerability stemmed from the risk of ill-treatment and collective expulsion as irregular migrants intercepted at sea. On 6 May 2009, Italian coastguard and navy vessels intercepted their boats in international waters south of Lampedusa, within Malta’s search and rescue zone. Without any identification or assessment of individual protection needs, the Italian authorities transferred the applicants onto military ships, confiscated their belongings, and returned them to Tripoli, Libya, under bilateral agreements with Libya. The applicants were not informed of their destination and were handed over to Libyan authorities against their will.

The European Court of Human Rights found that Italy had violated Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) by exposing the applicants to the risk of ill-treatment in Libya and possible further refoulement to Somalia or Eritrea. The Court also found violations of Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) in conjunction with both Article 3 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 4. The applicants were awarded compensation for non-pecuniary damage. This landmark judgment established that states cannot avoid their human rights obligations by intercepting migrants on the high seas and returning them without individual assessment.

cases.title: CASE OF HIRSI JAMAA AND OTHERS v. ITALY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objections joined to merits and dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Expulsion) (Conditional) (Libya);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Expulsion) (Conditional) (Eritrea) (Somalia);Violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 - Prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens-{general} (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 - Prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens);Violation of Article 13+3 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture;Expulsion);Violation of Article 13+P4-4 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 - Prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens-{general};Prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
Hirsi Jamaa and Others v. Italy concerned a group of applicants—eleven Somali nationals and thirteen Eritrean nationals—who were part of a larger group intercepted at sea by Italian authorities in May 2009. While the applicants’ Roma or Traveller identity is not mentioned or implied in the judgment, the case is significant for its examination of collective expulsions and the rights of vulnerable migrants, including those who may belong to minority groups.

The applicants, fleeing conflict and persecution, left Libya by boat aiming to reach Italy. When their vessels were 35 nautical miles south of Lampedusa, Italian coastguard and police intercepted them, transferred them onto Italian military ships, and returned them to Tripoli, Libya, without any identification process or opportunity to seek asylum. The applicants’ personal belongings were confiscated, and they were not informed of their destination. Upon arrival in Libya, they were handed over to Libyan authorities, despite their objections and fears of ill-treatment.

The European Court of Human Rights found that Italy had violated Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) in conjunction with both Article 3 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 4. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. This judgment is notable for establishing that states cannot evade their human rights obligations by conducting operations on the high seas, and that collective expulsions without individual assessment are prohibited under the Convention.

cases.title: CASE OF EREMIASOVA AND PECHOVA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In Eremiasova and Pechova v. Czech Republic, the applicants are Ms. Eremiasova and Ms. Pechova, Czech nationals living in Brno who identify as Roma. They challenge the Czech Republic after V.P., the partner of the first applicant, died in police custody.

The case centers on Roma vulnerability in policing. V.P., Roma by origin, died after a police escort, raising questions about treatment of Roma in custody and investigations into deaths tied to law enforcement.

On 18 June 2002, V.P. was detained on suspicion of burglary in Brno. After questioning and fingerprinting, he was escorted; on mezzanine he turned, struck an officer, and jumped through a closed window, dying the next morning. Autopsy linked death to violent injuries from a fall, not excluding third-party involvement. Investigations followed, with conflicting statements on which wrist was held and adequacy of inquiries.

The Court examined Articles 2 and 2-1, finding violations of the substantive right to life and the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation into deaths in police custody.

Significance: The decision reinforces the obligation to protect life and investigate deaths in custody, especially where Roma individuals are involved, within the Court’s broader focus on Roma rights in Europe.

cases.title: PUKY v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of Puky v. Slovakia, the applicant, Mr Ľudovít Puky, is a Slovak national of Romany ethnic origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The case arose from the vulnerability of Roma communities in Eastern Slovakia, particularly in the context of large-scale police operations following protests by Roma against changes in social welfare policy. On 24 February 2004, after disturbances in Trebišov, police surrounded the Roma settlement, and Mr Puky’s brother, Radoslav, fled the scene, reportedly injured. He was last seen running towards a field, and was later found dead in a drainage ditch, with suffocation by drowning identified as the cause of death. The applicant alleged that the police had physically attacked Roma residents and that the investigation into his brother’s death was inadequate, raising issues under Articles 2 (right to life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that domestic remedies had not been fully exhausted. This case highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in seeking accountability and effective protection from state authorities, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and mistrust in law enforcement across Europe.

cases.title: CIUBOTARU AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Ciubotaru and Others v. Romania, the applicants are nine Romanian nationals of Roma identity: Cristian Ciubotaru, Ovidiu Ciubotaru, Vasile Vâtu, Vasile Călin, Ana Ciubotaru, Ana Romaşcu, Eva Ciubotaru, Aurel Călin and Elena Avădanii, who were represented before the Court by Romani Criss, a Roma rights NGO. They brought their case against Romania, asserting violations connected with the treatment of Roma during police action and the subsequent investigation.

The central vulnerability concerns Roma-related harm alleged during a police operation: the disproportionate use of force by state agents in December 2002, which led to deaths and serious injuries, and the claim that protections against such harm were undermined by discrimination against Roma. The applicants argued that their ethnic background as Roma underpinned the authorities’ conduct and the inadequacy of the ensuing investigation, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination faced by Roma communities in Romania.

The facts describe a police operation on 3 December 2002 in Buhuşi to capture suspects, followed on 5 December by a violent confrontation as tear gas was used and shots were fired after suspects emerged from a house. Florin Călin and Gelu Ciubotaru died, others were injured, including police and bystanders, and questions arose about representation and the criminal proceedings that followed. The applicants’ complaints were framed under Articles 2, 3 and 14 of the Convention, among others, with Romani Criss authorised to act on their behalf; the Government argued admissibility issues.

The Court examined Articles 2, 3 and 14 but, in view of the arguments about admissibility and representation, declared the application inadmissible, offering no merits-based findings or remedies. This decision sits within a broader trajectory of Roma-rights jurisprudence, underscoring procedural hurdles in some Roma-related cases and the ongoing scrutiny of police conduct in Romania during the early 2000s.

cases.title: CASE OF AJDARIC v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 6-1;Non-pecuniary damage - award;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed
cases.summary:
In Ajdarić v. Croatia, the applicant, Mr. Nedjeljko Ajdarić, was described in the judgment as having connections to a Roma settlement near Banja Luka, though his Roma identity is implied rather than explicitly confirmed. The case centered on the applicant’s vulnerability as a detainee whose conviction for a triple murder in Kutina in 1998 was based primarily on the testimony of a fellow inmate, S.Š., who claimed to have overheard incriminating conversations between Ajdarić and another accused while they were all held in Zagreb Prison Hospital in late 2005 and early 2006. S.Š. later contacted the police and provided detailed statements, including references to a Roma settlement, which played a significant role in the prosecution.

Ajdarić argued that his right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights had been violated, as his conviction relied heavily on uncorroborated prison testimony, and he was unable to effectively challenge this evidence. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1, concluding that the proceedings had not been fair due to the decisive reliance on the prison witness without sufficient safeguards for the defense. The Court awarded Ajdarić non-pecuniary damages but dismissed his claim for pecuniary loss. This judgment is notable for its scrutiny of the use of prison informant testimony and the procedural protections required to ensure a fair trial.

cases.title: CASE OF V.C. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect);No violation of Art. 3 (procedural aspect);Violation of Art. 8;No violation of Art. 13;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
The applicant, Ms V.C., born in 1980, is a Roma woman from Jarovnice, Slovakia, with Slovakia as the State respondent before the European Court of Human Rights. She identifies as Roma, and Slovakia is the State against which the case was brought.

Her vulnerability centers on forced sterilisation of a Roma woman, an irreversible medical intervention carried out under coercive circumstances, accompanied by segregation in hospital facilities.

On 23 August 2000 she was admitted for delivery at Prešov Hospital. During labour she requested sterilisation; she was told a further pregnancy could be fatal. In fear she signed the record "Patient requests sterilisation" and the tubal ligation was performed at 12:10 p.m. The record notes her Roma origin; she was placed in a Roma-only ward. Later she faced infertility and psychological distress, including a false pregnancy (2007–2008) and psychiatric treatment in 2008, with divorce in 2009.

The Court examined Articles 3, 8, 8-1 and 13, and awarded non-pecuniary damages under Article 41, finding a violation of Article 3, substantive, and of Article 8; it found no violation of Article 3 procedural or Article 13.

Significance: The ruling affirms Roma bodily integrity and private life against coercive medical practices, highlighting ongoing discrimination; it sits within a broader history of forced sterilisation of Roma women in Slovakia.

cases.title: AFFAIRE V.C. c. SLOVAQUIE [Extraits]
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'art. 3 (volet matériel);Non-violation de l'art. 3 (volet procédural);Violation de l'art. 8;Non-violation de l'art. 13;Préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary:
The applicant is V.C., a Romani woman born in 1980 and residing in Jarovnice, Slovakia. She identifies as Roma, speaks Romani, and challenged Slovakia before the European Court of Human Rights. The case centers on Roma identity within the framework of the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers, with Slovakia as the respondent state.

Her vulnerability lies in a Roma-related harm: a sterilization performed during childbirth, reportedly without freely given, informed consent, and accompanied by Roma-specific hospital practices, including placement in a Romani-only ward and denial of access to shared facilities for non-Romani patients.

Chronology: On 23 August 2000, at the Prešov hospital, during a cesarean for her second child, she reportedly asked for sterilization; the request was noted and she signed under a tremulous hand. Anesthesia began at 11:30 and the tubal ligation ended at 12:10. She had previously delivered in 1998 by cesarean. Post-operatively she suffered infertility and psychological distress, faced social ostracism within the Roma community, and her marriage ended in 2009.

The Court examined Articles 3 and 8, and Article 13. It found a violation of Article 3 in its substantive, or material, aspect for the inhumane treatment of sterilization; it did not find a procedural violation of Article 3. It also found a violation of Article 8 (respect for private life and family life) and no violation of Article 13, awarding moral damages. The judgment underscores state responsibility for coercive medical practices targeting Roma women.

This case matters for Roma rights as a sustained Court endorsement that coercive sterilization and discriminatory hospital treatment of Roma women violate core human rights, reinforcing the imperative to protect bodily autonomy and dignity; it sits in a broader post-communist European context, with Slovakia addressing Roma rights in the early 2000s and the Court delivering its ruling in 2011.

cases.title: HAMIDOVIC c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Partiellement irrecevable
cases.summary:
In Hamidovic v. Italy, Nevresa Hamidovic, a Bosnian Roma woman born in 1975, lives in the Castel Romano camp in Rome and challenges Italy before the European Court of Human Rights. Represented by Luca Santini.  

Her vulnerability stems from Roma identity and precarious residence. She and her husband, also Bosnian Roma, have five children born 1992, 1993, 1995, 2001 and 2002; three attended school in 1999/2000 and 2002/2003. In 2005 Italy ordered expulsion for irregular residence, and she was detained.  

Her lawful stay began with a humanitarian permit in 1996, revoked in 1997; renewal requests in 1998 were refused after criminal penalties. In 2005 a Teramo prefect issued an expulsion order for irregular residence; she was held at Ponte Galeria. She challenged under Article 8; the Teramo judge rejected on 24 August 2005.  

At the Court, she invoked Article 8, arguing expulsion would breach private and family life. The Government argued non-exhaustion of remedies and lack of entitlement to family regrouping. The Court found the grievance raised serious questions warranting merits evaluation; the overall result was partial inadmissibility.  

Significance: The Hamidovic case highlights Roma family life in expulsion decisions and contributes to the Court’s mid-2000s Roma rights jurisprudence in Italy.

cases.title: CASE OF ĐURĐEVIĆ v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 3 (procedural aspect);Remainder inadmissible;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Đurđević v. Croatia, the applicants are three individuals, born in 1967, 1966 and 1994, who live in Kloštar-Ivanić and who are Roma. They challenged the Croatian authorities before the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of the European Convention on Human Rights. The state named is Croatia.

The vulnerability at issue concerns Roma-related harm: the events revolve around violence against a Roma family and the state’s corresponding responsibility to protect individuals from such harm and to investigate ill-treatment, with particular attention to whether authorities properly addressed incidents connected with Roma individuals and Roma-origin suspects or victims. The case examines whether Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and of inhuman or degrading treatment) was violated in both private- and police-violence contexts.

Chronology and facts: On 16 June 2009, in Ivanić Grad, a confrontation outside the Yogi restaurant involved the third applicant and his brother against a man who insulted them because of their Roma origin; a group of Roma subsequently returned to the scene, and the third applicant was beaten. Police intervened; the second applicant sustained contusions during the incident at the police station. The private-violence events were followed by medical assessments and divergent official accounts, with the Government’s version emphasizing the involvement of a Roma group, while the applicants reported police involvement in the aftermath.

The Court examined Article 3, finding no violation in the 9:30 p.m. incident involving private individuals (the authorities’ findings and penalties were deemed sufficient). However, regarding the incident at about 10:30 p.m. and the alleged ill-treatment by police, the Court found a procedural violation of Article 3, and awarded non-pecuniary damages. The remainder of the complaints were deemed inadmissible.

This case matters for Roma rights because it underscores the obligation of states to ensure effective investigations into alleged police ill-treatment and to address risks of violence against Roma communities; it sits within a broader pattern of Roma minority protection in Europe, including ongoing scrutiny of Croatia’s handling of Roma incidents in the early 2010s.

cases.title: LAKATOSH AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Lakatosh and Others v. Russia, the applicants, identified as members of the Roma community, brought a case against the Russian Federation. The case concerned the applicants’ vulnerability stemming from their inability to access basic rights due to a lack of identity documents, a common issue affecting Roma and Traveller populations. This lack of documentation prevented them from opening bank accounts and accessing social and legal protections. The applicants sought redress for these hardships, highlighting systemic barriers faced by Roma individuals in Russia.

The case was resolved through a friendly settlement between the parties, in which the Russian government agreed to pay each applicant 30,000 euros in compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, as well as costs and expenses. The payments were to be made in Russian roubles and were exempt from taxes. Due to the applicants’ inability to open bank accounts in their own names, the sums were transferred to their legal representative’s account. The European Court of Human Rights, satisfied that the settlement respected human rights standards under the Convention, struck the case out of its list, ending further examination.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma communities face regarding identity documentation and access to rights in Europe. It reflects broader historical patterns of marginalisation and the importance of legal remedies to address systemic discrimination against Roma and Travellers.

cases.title: CELANO AND OTHERS v. ITALY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Celano and Others v. Italy, the applicants were a group of Italian nationals, all medical graduates undergoing specialist training at the University of La Sapienza in Rome. Although the case metadata does not specify their Roma or Traveller identity, the Council of Europe definition requires that the term "Roma and Travellers" be applied only when explicitly stated; here, no such identity is indicated. The applicants challenged the Italian State over the denial of social security coverage and salary adjustments during their specialist training period, which lasted until 2006. The vulnerability at the heart of the case concerned the applicants’ lack of social security protection and pay increases due to legislative delays and government measures that suspended relevant provisions of Law no. 368/1999. Despite legal provisions entitling them to remuneration adjustments and social security registration with the Italian welfare institution INPS, these rights were not implemented until 2006-2007, leaving the applicants without coverage for several years.

The applicants initiated domestic proceedings in 2005, which were dismissed by the Rome Labour Court in 2006. The Court held that the relevant EU directive did not guarantee specific salary rights for medical trainees and that the suspension of national legal provisions meant no enforceable rights had arisen. The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, examining Articles 14 (prohibition of discrimination) and Protocol 1, Article 1 (protection of property), but found no violation. This case highlights the challenges faced by medical trainees in Italy regarding social security and remuneration, though it does not directly address Roma or Traveller rights. Historically, the European Court has played a crucial role in protecting minority rights, but here the Court’s decision reflects the limits of its jurisdiction when no discrimination or Convention breach is established.

cases.title: DAUTAJ v. SWEDEN
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Dautaj v. Sweden, the applicants, members of the Roma community originally from Kosovo, brought a case against the Swedish state. The case concerned their vulnerability as Roma facing potential harm upon return to Kosovo, a context marked by ongoing challenges for Roma and other minorities. The applicants sought protection under several articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including the right to life (Article 2), prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment (Article 3), and respect for private and family life (Article 8). The facts of the case involved the applicants’ asylum claims in Sweden, which were ultimately not pursued further by them. On May 10, 2011, the European Court of Human Rights decided to strike the case out of its list, concluding that the applicants no longer wished to pursue their application and that no exceptional human rights concerns required continued examination. No violations were formally found, and no remedies were awarded. This case highlights the complex and often precarious situation of Roma individuals seeking asylum in Europe, reflecting broader historical patterns of displacement and discrimination faced by Roma communities across the continent.

cases.title: HORIE v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Horie v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Sharon Horie, is a British national identifying as a New Traveller, a subgroup within the broader category of Travellers. She has lived a nomadic lifestyle since 1982, residing in vehicles with her three children. The case concerns her and a group of New Travellers who established an unauthorised encampment in January 2007 on Hethfelton Wood, Dorset, land owned by the Secretary of State for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (SSEFRA) and managed by the Forestry Commission.

The central issue was the eviction and prevention of future trespassing on multiple woodlands in Dorset. SSEFRA sought possession orders and an injunction to bar the applicant and others from entering or occupying these lands. After initial mixed rulings, the Court of Appeal granted a wide injunction preventing entry to several woods, but the Supreme Court later ruled that possession orders could not extend to land not currently occupied. However, it upheld the injunction to prevent future trespass. The Court examined Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, concerning respect for private and family life, but declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation.

This case highlights the legal tensions between the rights of New Travellers to a nomadic lifestyle and landowners’ rights to protect property. It reflects ongoing challenges faced by Traveller communities in the UK regarding unauthorised camping and eviction, set against evolving legal interpretations of possession and injunctions.

cases.title: CASE OF DIMITROVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 2;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary: In the case of Dimitrova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants are members of the Roma community: the first and second applicants are the mother and wife, respectively, and the third and fourth applicants are brothers of Mr. Georgi Gerasimov, a Roma man who died following a violent attack. The case concerns the Bulgarian State’s responsibility for the death of Mr. Gerasimov and the subsequent investigation. On 30 May 2003, Mr. Gerasimov and three other Roma men were digging coal in an abandoned mine near Pernik when they were confronted by a group led by Mr. B.I., with whom one of the men had a debt dispute. A violent fight ensued, during which Mr. Gerasimov was severely beaten with bats and sustained fatal head injuries. He was hospitalized in a coma and died on 4 June 2003. The police investigation was criticized for its shortcomings, including the discontinuation of criminal proceedings against the suspects. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 (right to life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found a violation of Article 2, holding that the State failed to conduct an effective investigation into Mr. Gerasimov’s death, but did not find a violation of Article 14. This judgment highlights the ongoing challenges Roma face regarding protection of their right to life and effective investigation of violence against them, reflecting a broader historical context of systemic discrimination and impunity in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF MILANOVIC v. SERBIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 3;Violation of Art. 14+3;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary: In the case of Milanović v. Serbia, the applicant, Mr. Života Milanović, a member of the Roma community and a follower of the Vaishnava Hindu (Hare Krishna) faith, brought a case against Serbia. The case concerned repeated violent attacks against Mr. Milanović, motivated by his religious and ethnic identity, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma and religious minorities to hate crimes. Between 2001 and 2007, Mr. Milanović was assaulted multiple times in Jagodina and its vicinity, suffering serious injuries including stabbings and beatings. Despite reporting these attacks and filing criminal complaints, the police investigations were ineffective, with authorities failing to identify or prosecute the perpetrators, who were linked by the applicant to far-right extremist groups. The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) taken together with Article 3. The Court found that Serbia had violated these provisions by failing to protect Mr. Milanović from ill-treatment and by not conducting an effective investigation into the hate-motivated attacks. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicant. This judgment is significant as it underscores the ongoing risks faced by Roma and religious minorities in Serbia and the obligation of states to ensure effective protection and investigation of hate crimes. Historically, Roma communities have endured systemic discrimination, making this ruling a crucial affirmation of their right to security and equal treatment under the law.

cases.title: CASE OF MIŽIGÁROVÁ v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 2 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 2 (procedural aspect);No violation of Art. 14+2;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary: In the case of Mižigárová v. Slovakia, the applicant, Mrs. Miluša Mižigárová, a Slovak national of Roma origin, brought a case against Slovakia concerning the death of her husband, Mr. Ľubomír Šarišský. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the failure of authorities to protect their right to life. On the evening of 12 August 1999, Mr. Šarišský was arrested on suspicion of bicycle theft and taken to the District Police Department in Poprad. During interrogation by Lieutenant F., an off-duty officer, Mr. Šarišský was handcuffed, left alone, and later shot in the abdomen with the officer’s service pistol. He died four days later in hospital from complications related to the gunshot wound. Despite medical evidence and witness accounts indicating police ill-treatment, the investigation was delayed and incomplete. The European Court of Human Rights examined Articles 2 (right to life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. It found violations of Article 2 both substantively and procedurally, concluding that the State failed to protect Mr. Šarišský’s life and conduct an effective investigation. No violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 2 was found. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages but dismissed the claim for pecuniary damage. This judgment highlights the persistent risks faced by Roma in police custody and the critical need for accountability, reflecting ongoing concerns about police violence against Roma in Slovakia at the turn of the century.

cases.title: HORVATH AND VADASZI v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Horváth and Vadászi v. Hungary, the applicants, Mr. Tibor Horváth and Mr. Géza Vadászi, are Hungarian nationals of Roma origin. They challenged their placement in a physically segregated special school class in Kesznyéten, alleging that it amounted to racial segregation and violated their rights. The applicants had been classified as having mild intellectual disabilities in 1994 and placed in a special class taught by an unqualified teacher. They argued that this placement endangered their mental and educational development and was discriminatory.

The applicants pursued criminal proceedings against school officials, accusing them of endangering minors by placing Roma children in segregated classes. However, the Hungarian authorities discontinued the investigation, finding no grave breach of duty, and dismissed a private prosecution on procedural grounds. The applicants did not pursue available civil remedies for compensation under domestic law.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of degrading treatment), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court declared the application inadmissible, primarily because the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and had lodged their complaint outside the six-month time limit. The Court acknowledged that segregated education of Roma children raises a presumption of discrimination but did not assess the merits due to procedural shortcomings.

This case highlights ongoing challenges faced by Roma children in education and the importance of exhausting domestic remedies before seeking international redress. It reflects a broader historical context of Roma segregation in European schools and the evolving legal scrutiny of such practices.

cases.title: CASE OF KAY AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 8;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Kay and Others v. the United Kingdom, the applicants were eight British nationals and one Irish national living in London, all of whom were part of the Traveller community. They challenged the London Borough of Lambeth’s decision to evict them from properties provided under a “singles scheme” managed by a housing trust. These properties, owned by Lambeth, were designated as “short life” and scheduled for demolition or redevelopment. The applicants had been granted temporary accommodation but did not have secure tenancy rights under the Housing Act 1985.

The core issue concerned the applicants’ vulnerability as Travellers facing eviction from their homes without adequate legal protection or consideration of their personal circumstances. Between 1999 and 2004, Lambeth terminated leases with the housing trust and sought possession orders against the applicants. The applicants argued that eviction would violate their right to respect for their homes under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, domestic courts ruled that Lambeth had an unqualified right to possession and struck out the Article 8 defence, citing the absence of secure tenancy and the lawful basis for possession.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, recognising that the applicants’ eviction engaged their right to respect for their homes and that the authorities had failed to adequately balance this right against Lambeth’s property interests. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages. This case is significant as it highlights the precarious housing situation of Roma and Traveller individuals in the UK and affirms the need for authorities to consider their specific vulnerabilities before eviction, reflecting ongoing challenges faced by these communities in securing stable housing.

cases.title: YORDANOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Yordanova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants, including Ms. Lyubka Yordanova Yordanova and 22 others, are Bulgarian nationals who identify as Roma and reside in the Batalova Vodenitsa neighbourhood of Sofia. They live in informal housing built without authorization on state-owned land, forming a small Roma settlement with limited infrastructure and poor living conditions. The case centers on the vulnerability of Roma communities facing forced eviction and demolition of their homes, raising concerns about inhuman and degrading treatment and violations of their right to respect for their homes.

The applicants’ families settled in the area from the late 1960s onwards, constructing makeshift houses on land designated for green space but never developed. Despite longstanding occupation, their homes do not comply with building regulations and cannot be legalized without major reconstruction. Tensions grew between Roma residents and non-Roma neighbours, with complaints about sanitation, animal keeping, and alleged criminal behaviour. In response, Sofia municipality planned to remove the settlement to build new housing, prompting the applicants to challenge the proposed eviction.

The European Court of Human Rights examined alleged violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for home), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found the application partly admissible but did not establish a violation of these rights, emphasizing the authorities’ efforts to balance enforcement of land-use laws with social integration policies.

This case highlights the complex challenges Roma communities face regarding housing rights and discrimination in Europe. It reflects ongoing struggles since the late 20th century to secure adequate living conditions for Roma populations amid urban development pressures and societal prejudice.

cases.title: CASE OF AKSU v. TURKEY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (victim);No violation of Art. 14+8
cases.summary:
In the case of Aksu v. Turkey, the applicant, Mr. Faik Aksu, a Turkish national of Roma (Gypsy) origin, brought a complaint against Turkey concerning the publication of a book titled “The Gypsies of Turkey” by the Ministry of Culture. Mr. Aksu argued that the book contained numerous derogatory stereotypes about Roma and Gypsies, including descriptions of them as thieves, swindlers, and beggars, which he claimed were deeply offensive and damaging to his identity as a member of the Roma and Traveller communities.

The harm at the centre of the case was the perpetuation of negative stereotypes and the resulting stigmatisation of Roma people in Turkey through a state-published book, raising concerns about discrimination and the protection of minority dignity. Mr. Aksu, acting on behalf of Turkish Gypsy associations, sought to have the book withdrawn and compensation awarded for non-pecuniary damage, arguing that the language used amounted to an attack on his ethnic identity.

The events unfolded between 2000 and 2004, beginning with the book’s publication and Mr. Aksu’s subsequent petitions and legal actions against both the Ministry of Culture and the book’s author. Turkish courts ultimately dismissed his claims, finding the book to be academic research rather than an insult.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found no violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, concluding that the domestic authorities had struck a fair balance between freedom of expression and the applicant’s right to respect for his private life.

This case is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it highlights the ongoing struggle against negative stereotyping in public discourse and the challenges of balancing minority protection with academic freedom, set against a backdrop of historical prejudice faced by Roma communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF CARABULEA v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 2 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 2 (procedural aspect);Violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 3 (procedural aspect);Violation of Art. 13 (procedural aspect);Pecuniary damage - award;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Carabulea v. Romania, the applicant, Viorel Carabulea, a Romanian national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Romanian state following the death of his brother, Gabriel Carabulea, in police custody. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective investigations into deaths in custody, which disproportionately affect these communities. On 13 April 1996, Gabriel Carabulea was arrested in Bucharest and transferred between police stations. Initially in good health, he soon showed signs of severe physical distress, and his family observed a rapid deterioration. Despite repeated requests for information and medical attention, Gabriel died on 3 May 1996. The authorities attributed his death to natural causes, but the family contested this, pointing to evidence of injuries and procedural irregularities in the investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 2 (right to life), Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found both substantive and procedural violations of Articles 2 and 3, as well as a violation of Article 13, and awarded pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages to the applicant. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in police custody and the historical failure of authorities in Europe to provide effective protection and accountability for these communities.

cases.title: CASE OF KURIĆ AND OTHERS v. SLOVENIA
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Art. 8;Violation of Art. 13;Respondent State to take individual measures;Respondent State to take measures of general character;Just satisfaction reserved
cases.summary:
In the case of Kurić and Others v. Slovenia, the applicants were eleven individuals, including Mr. Mustafa Kurić, who identified as members of the Roma and Traveller communities or other minorities from the former Yugoslavia, challenging the actions of Slovenia. The case focused on the vulnerability of these individuals, who, after Slovenia’s independence in 1991, were “erased” from the Register of Permanent Residents in 1992, leaving many stateless or without legal status, and disproportionately affecting Roma and Traveller groups who already faced marginalisation. The applicants had lived in Slovenia for years, some since childhood, and had built their lives there. Following the erasure, they lost access to employment, healthcare, housing, and social benefits, with some forced into homelessness or unable to regularise their status despite repeated attempts.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Slovenia had violated both articles, recognising the severe and lasting impact of the erasure on the applicants’ lives. The Court ordered Slovenia to take both individual and general measures to remedy the situation, with just satisfaction to be determined later.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it highlights the dangers of administrative measures that disproportionately harm vulnerable minorities. The case reflects the broader historical context of post-Yugoslav transitions, where Roma and Travellers often faced exclusion and statelessness.

cases.title: CASE OF VASIL SASHOV PETROV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (six month period);Violation of Art. 2 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 2 (procedural aspect);Violation of Art. 13;No violation of Art. 14+2 (substantive aspect);No violation of Art. 14+2 (procedural aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Vasil Sashov Petrov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Vasil Sashov Petrov, identified himself as being of Roma (Gypsy) ethnic origin and brought a complaint against the Bulgarian state. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to excessive police force and the lack of effective investigation into such incidents, reflecting broader concerns about the treatment of Roma communities by law enforcement in Europe.

On 14 January 1999, in Velingrad, Mr. Petrov was shot by police officers while fleeing after being suspected of attempting to steal hens. Despite warnings, he ran towards the Roma neighbourhood and was shot in the stomach at close range. The officers took him to hospital but did not disclose the use of firearms, resulting in delayed and inadequate medical care. Mr. Petrov suffered severe injuries, including the loss of a kidney and part of his liver. The subsequent investigation was marred by significant shortcomings, including failure to conduct key forensic tests and a lack of proper scene reconstruction, leading to the discontinuation of proceedings against the officers.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 (right to life) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), finding violations of both the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 2, as well as Article 13. The Court awarded Mr. Petrov non-pecuniary damages for the harm suffered. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in their interactions with law enforcement and the importance of thorough, impartial investigations, especially given the historical context of discrimination against Roma communities in Bulgaria and across Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE UDOROVIC c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'art. 6-1;Violation de l'art. 6-1;Préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary:
In the case of Udorovic v. Italy, the applicant, Mr. Udorovic, is an Italian national belonging to the Sinti community, a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case focused on the vulnerability of Sinti families living in authorized and informal camps in Rome, who faced the threat of eviction and alleged discrimination by local authorities. In November 1995, municipal police conducted inspections of all nomadic camps in Rome, including the camp on Via Luigi Nono where Mr. Udorovic lived. Subsequent decisions by the mayor in 1996 and 1999 imposed strict residency criteria for Roma and Sinti families and ultimately ordered the evacuation of the Nono camp, citing inadequate sanitary conditions and over-occupancy.

Mr. Udorovic challenged these decisions before Italian courts, arguing they were discriminatory and violated his rights. However, both the civil tribunal and the court of appeal rejected his claims, finding no discriminatory intent. He then brought his case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a violation of Article 6 (right to a fair trial) due to the lack of public hearings in his discrimination proceedings. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the absence of public hearings in a case concerning civil rights was unjustified, and awarded Mr. Udorovic compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant as it reinforces the procedural rights of Roma and Traveller individuals in discrimination cases, highlighting the importance of transparency and fairness in legal proceedings. The case reflects ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Sinti communities in Italy during the late 1990s and early 2000s, particularly regarding housing rights and access to justice.

cases.title: GASHI v. SWEDEN
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Gashi v. Sweden, the applicants—Mr. Besim Gashi, Ms. Sylvana Osmanis, and their four children—are Serbian nationals of Roma origin, with the first applicant born in Kosovo. They sought asylum in Sweden, arguing that, as Roma, they would face harassment and discrimination if returned to Serbia or Kosovo. The core vulnerability in this case was the risk of inhuman or degrading treatment due to their Roma identity, a group historically subjected to widespread discrimination and violence in the region.

The family arrived in Sweden in 2004 and repeatedly applied for asylum, citing fears of persecution as Roma. Their applications were consistently rejected by Swedish migration authorities, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. Despite efforts to obtain travel documents, Serbia would not accept them, and the exact country of potential deportation remained uncertain, though Sweden intended to focus on Serbia unless another country agreed to receive them.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found that the applicants had not demonstrated a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 if deported to Serbia or Kosovo, and declared the application inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded.

This case highlights the high evidentiary threshold required for Roma and Traveller applicants to demonstrate a real risk of Article 3 violations in expulsion cases, reflecting ongoing challenges for Roma communities seeking protection in Europe amid persistent discrimination.

cases.title: CASE OF STEFANOU v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 6-1;Remainder inadmissible;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Stefanou v. Greece, the applicant, Mr. Stefanou, is a Greek national of Roma origin who was sixteen years old at the time of the events. His case against Greece highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective remedies for such abuses. On 5 August 2001, following a theft report in Argostoli, Cephalonia, four Roma youths were taken to the police station; Mr. Stefanou, a friend, voluntarily presented himself at the station. Although not identified by the victim, he was questioned and, according to his account, punched and slapped by a police officer in an attempt to force a confession. He was released but soon after sought medical attention for head injuries, which were documented by hospital staff. Despite his complaints and supporting medical evidence, the ensuing investigations by police and prosecutors were superficial and ultimately dismissed his allegations as unfounded.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Mr. Stefanou had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment at the hands of the police and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, thus violating Article 3. It also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the lack of a fair hearing. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to Mr. Stefanou.

This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent risks of police ill-treatment faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe and the importance of effective investigations, especially given the historical context of systemic discrimination against these communities.

cases.title: CASE OF LASKA AND LIKA v. ALBANIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 6-1;Remainder inadmissible;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Laska and Lika v. Albania, the applicants, Mr. Laska and Mr. Lika, both of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Albanian state. Their case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals in the criminal justice system, especially regarding procedural safeguards and fair trial rights. On 31 March 2001, following an armed robbery of a minibus near Tirana, police searched Mr. Lika’s home, where both applicants were present. The search and subsequent identification procedures were conducted without the presence of a lawyer, despite explicit requests and the fact that one of those questioned was a minor. The applicants were identified by victims in a line-up and with objects allegedly used in the crime, again without legal representation. They were convicted largely on the basis of these identifications and sentenced to lengthy prison terms.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair trial. The Court found that the applicants’ rights had been violated due to the absence of legal assistance during crucial stages of the investigation and identification, rendering the proceedings unfair. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. This judgment is significant as it underscores the importance of procedural fairness for Roma and Traveller individuals, who have historically faced systemic discrimination and are particularly at risk of rights violations in criminal proceedings.

cases.title: CASE OF PARASKEVA TODOROVA v. BULGARIA - [English Translation] by European Roma Rights Centre "ERRC"
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 14+6-1;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary: In the case of Paraskeva Todorova v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Ms. Paraskeva Todorova, is a Bulgarian citizen of Roma origin living in the village of Trud, Plovdiv region. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to discriminatory treatment within the criminal justice system, particularly when courts rely on ethnic stereotypes in their reasoning. In 2005, Ms. Todorova was prosecuted for fraud involving the alleged appropriation of money and jewellery from a local resident. Despite presenting an alibi and medical evidence, she was convicted by the Plovdiv District Court in May 2006 and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. Notably, the court explicitly referenced her Roma origin in its judgment and justified the refusal to suspend her sentence by invoking a supposed “feeling of impunity, especially among members of minority groups,” suggesting that conditional sentences were ineffective for Roma. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 6 § 1. The Court awarded Ms. Todorova non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it condemns the use of ethnic stereotypes in judicial decisions and affirms the right of Roma and Travellers to equal treatment before the law, against a backdrop of persistent discrimination in Europe’s courts.

cases.title: CASE OF ORŠUŠ AND OTHERS v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed;Violation of Art. 6-1;Violation of Art. 14+P1-2;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In Oršuš and Others v. Croatia, the applicants were fifteen Croatian nationals of Roma origin, all of whom attended primary schools in the villages of Podturen and Macinec in Međimurje County. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma children subjected to educational segregation, as they were placed in separate classes consisting only of Roma pupils, which the applicants argued amounted to discrimination and hindered their educational development. Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, the applicants were assigned to Roma-only classes, often following a reduced curriculum and with limited opportunities to transfer to mixed classes, primarily due to their insufficient command of the Croatian language. Despite some measures such as the introduction of Roma assistants and preparatory programmes, the applicants faced significant barriers, including high dropout rates and lower educational attainment compared to the general population.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 14 in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. The Court held that the placement of Roma children in separate classes constituted discrimination and awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it established that segregating Roma children in education, even if based on language needs, can perpetuate systemic discrimination—a persistent issue in Europe’s history of marginalising Roma and Traveller communities.

cases.title: AFFAIRE ORŠUŠ ET AUTRES c. CROATIE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire rejetée;Violation de l'art. 6-1;Violation de l'art. 14+P1-2;Préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary:
In Oršuš and Others v. Croatia, the applicants were fifteen Croatian nationals, all children belonging to the Roma community, who brought a case against Croatia. The heart of the case was the vulnerability of Roma children facing systemic educational segregation, which placed them in separate classes and limited their educational opportunities compared to non-Roma peers. Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, the applicants attended primary schools in the villages of Podturen and Macinec, in the Međimurje region. During their schooling, they were assigned to Roma-only classes, often following a reduced curriculum—up to 30% less than the standard programme. This segregation led to high dropout rates among Roma children and significantly lower educational attainment compared to the general population.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 due to excessive length of domestic proceedings, and of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, concluding that the applicants had suffered discrimination in access to education. The Court awarded moral damages to the applicants.

This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it was the first time the Court condemned the practice of educational segregation of Roma children in Europe, highlighting the persistent legacy of exclusion and discrimination faced by Roma communities.

cases.title: ILJAZOVIC v. SWEDEN
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Iljazovic v. Sweden, the applicants—Aleksander, Stefan, Marija, and Filip Iljazovic—are Serbian nationals who identified themselves as Roma, a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma children facing the threat of deportation to Serbia, where they alleged a lack of family support and inadequate state protection due to their ethnicity. The Iljazovic children arrived in Sweden with their parents in December 2006 and sought asylum, citing years of ethnic persecution in Serbia and the authorities’ refusal to protect them. After their father was murdered in 2008 and their mother was imprisoned for complicity, the children were placed with relatives in Sweden. Despite these traumatic events and their claims of having no caregivers in Serbia, Swedish authorities repeatedly rejected their asylum requests, concluding that Serbian authorities could provide adequate protection. The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to family life), fearing separation from their mother and lack of care if deported. However, after the Swedish Migration Board granted them permanent residence permits in October 2009, the Court struck the case out, as the applicants no longer faced deportation. This case underscores the precarious situation of Roma children in asylum proceedings and reflects ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Traveller families seeking protection in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE SASHOV ET AUTRES c. BULGARIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'art. 3 (volet matériel);Violation de l'art. 3 (volet procédural);Partiellement irrecevable;Préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary:
In Sashov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants—Mr. Sashov, Mr. Simeonov, and Mr. Yankov—are Bulgarian nationals from Sofia who belong to the Roma community, as defined by the Council of Europe. Their case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the lack of effective state protection against such abuse. On 18 July 2001, following a report of alleged theft by Roma individuals, plainclothes police officers apprehended the three men in the Ovcha Kupel district of Sofia. During and after their arrest, the applicants were subjected to repeated beatings with batons and other objects, forced into the trunk of a police car, and insulted with anti-Roma slurs. Medical examinations conducted immediately after their release documented significant injuries consistent with their account of police brutality.

Despite their complaints and supporting medical evidence, the Bulgarian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the alleged ill-treatment. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found a violation of Article 3, both in its substantive and procedural aspects, and awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent problem of police violence against Roma and the failure of state authorities to provide effective remedies, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination and marginalisation of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF SEJDIĆ AND FINCI v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 14+P1-3;Violation of P12-1;Remainder inadmissible;Non-pecuniary damage - finding of a violation sufficient
cases.summary:
In the landmark case of Sejdić and Finci v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, the applicants, Mr. Dervo Sejdić, of Roma origin, and Mr. Jakob Finci, of Jewish origin, challenged the constitutional arrangements of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Sejdić, a prominent Roma leader and public official, and Mr. Finci, a distinguished Jewish community representative, both identified as members of groups classified as “others” rather than as one of the three “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats, and Serbs) under the country’s constitution. The case centred on the exclusion of Roma and other minorities from standing for election to the House of Peoples and the Presidency, positions reserved exclusively for the “constituent peoples.” In 2006 and 2007, both applicants were officially barred from running for these high offices solely due to their ethnic identities, despite their significant public service.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination). The Court found that Bosnia and Herzegovina had violated these provisions by discriminating against the applicants on the basis of their ethnic origin. No financial compensation was awarded, as the finding of a violation was deemed sufficient.

This judgment is a milestone for Roma and Traveller rights, highlighting the need for genuine political participation for all minorities in post-conflict societies. It remains a crucial reference point in the ongoing struggle against entrenched ethnic discrimination in Europe’s constitutional frameworks.

cases.title: CASE OF MUÑOZ DÍAZ v. SPAIN
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Art. 14+P1-1;Pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary: In the case of Muñoz Díaz v. Spain, the applicant, Ms. María del Rosario Muñoz Díaz, a Spanish national belonging to the Roma community, brought a complaint against Spain after being denied a survivor’s pension following her husband’s death. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma individuals whose marriages, solemnised according to their community’s customs, are not recognised by state authorities, leading to exclusion from social security benefits. Ms. Muñoz Díaz and her late husband were married in 1971 in a Roma ceremony, a union fully recognised within their community and by Spanish society, as evidenced by their family record book and large-family status. However, when her husband died in 2000 after nearly two decades of social security contributions, Ms. Muñoz Díaz’s application for a survivor’s pension was rejected solely because their marriage was not registered under Spanish civil or religious law. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), finding that Spain’s refusal amounted to discrimination based on her Roma identity and marital status. The Court awarded both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it recognises the rights of Roma and Travellers to have their family life and community traditions respected, addressing a long history of legal and social marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF KARSAI v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 10;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In Karsai v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. László Karsai, is a historian and university professor whose research focuses on the Second World War and the extermination of Jews and Roma. Although Mr. Karsai is not himself identified as Roma, his work addresses issues central to Roma and Jewish history in Hungary. The case arose from a 2004 public debate over whether to erect a statue of Pál Teleki, a controversial Hungarian prime minister associated with anti-Semitic and anti-Roma legislation. In a published article, Mr. Karsai criticized right-wing media and a specific journalist, Mr. B.T., for downplaying Teleki’s responsibility for such laws and for using language that, in Karsai’s view, amounted to “cautious Jew-bashing.” Mr. B.T. sued for defamation, claiming the article implied he personally engaged in anti-Semitic rhetoric. While the first-instance court dismissed the claim, the Budapest Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court ruled against Mr. Karsai, ordering him to publish a rectification and pay legal costs.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 10 (freedom of expression) and found a violation. The Court held that Mr. Karsai’s statements were part of a debate on matters of significant public interest, including Hungary’s historical treatment of Jews and Roma, and that the interference with his freedom of expression was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The Court awarded Mr. Karsai non-pecuniary damages, emphasizing the importance of robust public debate on sensitive historical issues.

cases.title: MIŽIGÁROVÁ v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary: In the case of Mižigárová v. Slovakia, the applicant, Mrs. Miluša Mižigárová, a Slovak national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Slovakia following the death of her husband, Mr. Ľubomír Šarišský, in police custody. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective investigations into such incidents, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination and mistrust between Roma communities and law enforcement. On the evening of 12 August 1999, Mr. Šarišský, then 21 and in good health, was arrested in Poprad on suspicion of bicycle theft. During his interrogation at the police station, he was taken to a separate office by an off-duty officer, handcuffed to a radiator, and later shot in the abdomen with the officer’s service pistol. Despite being hospitalized, Mr. Šarišský died four days later from his injuries. Conflicting accounts emerged regarding the circumstances of the shooting and the presence of physical injuries, with the applicant reporting visible bruises and swelling on her husband’s body. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found the application admissible and scrutinized the adequacy of the investigation into Mr. Šarišský’s death. This case is significant as it underscores the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in police custody and the urgent need for independent, thorough investigations into allegations of police violence, set against a historical backdrop of systemic abuse and impunity in Slovakia and across Europe.

cases.title: EVANGELOS TZAMALIS AND OTHERS v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Evangelos Tzamalis and Others v. Greece, the applicants—Evangelos Tzamalis, Emmanouil Tzamalis, Kostas Petropoulos, and Sofia Markopoulou—are Greek nationals of Roma origin, represented by the Greek Helsinki Monitor. Their case was brought against the Greek state, highlighting the persistent vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to forced evictions and inadequate housing protections. The applicants, along with other Roma families, moved in late 2005 from Megara (Attica) to the Kladissos area in Crete, where they set up makeshift homes on unused public and private land. Local authorities deemed their living conditions unsanitary and, after complaints from landowners and officials, police and municipal workers demolished several of their sheds in July 2006, warning that further evictions would follow. The applicants, supported by an NGO, lodged criminal complaints alleging racially motivated eviction, destruction of property, and lack of alternative accommodation, but these were dismissed by Greek prosecutors on procedural grounds, including late filing and lack of proper authorisation at the time of the first complaint.

The European Court of Human Rights examined alleged violations of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies, as required by Article 35 of the Convention, due to procedural errors in their appeals. This case underscores the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller communities often face when seeking redress for housing rights violations, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and legal obstacles in Europe.

cases.title: I.G., AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary: In the case of I.G. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants—Ms I.G., Ms M.K., and Ms R.H.—are Slovakian nationals of Roma ethnic origin who brought a complaint against Slovakia. The case centres on the profound vulnerability of Roma women subjected to sterilisation without their full and informed consent, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma and Traveller women in Europe and raises serious concerns about discrimination and bodily autonomy. The applicants were sterilised at Krompachy Hospital during or after childbirth between 1999 and 2000, when two of them were still minors. They allege that they were neither properly informed about the procedure nor gave valid consent, and in some cases only discovered they had been sterilised years later when reviewing their medical records.
