Despite their complaints, Slovak authorities repeatedly discontinued criminal investigations, concluding that the procedures were medically justified and that consent had been obtained, though the applicants and their representatives strongly disputed this. The European Court of Human Rights declared the case admissible and examined potential violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 12 (right to marry and found a family), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. While the final judgment on the merits was pending at this stage, the admissibility decision marked a crucial step in recognising the gravity of forced sterilisation claims. This case is significant as it highlights the historical pattern of reproductive rights violations against Roma and Traveller women in Europe, underscoring the need for robust legal protections and accountability.

cases.title: KOKY AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Koky and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were ten Slovak nationals of Roma ethnic origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Center and the League of Human Rights Advocates, who brought a case against Slovakia. The heart of the case lay in the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to racially motivated violence and the failure of state authorities to provide effective protection and investigation. On the night of 28 February 2002, following a dispute in a bar in the village of Gánovce-Filice, a group of around 30 young men—believed to be linked to extremist “skinhead” groups—attacked the Roma settlement where the applicants lived. Armed with baseball bats and iron bars, the attackers shouted racist threats, broke into homes, physically assaulted residents, and caused significant property damage. Two applicants suffered serious injuries requiring hospitalisation. Although the police were called, they arrived an hour after the attack and the subsequent investigation was repeatedly suspended, despite evidence and identification of suspects by the victims.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), including their combinations. The case was declared admissible, but the Court ultimately did not find a violation, as domestic remedies had not been exhausted.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent risks of racially motivated violence faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe and the crucial need for effective state responses. It reflects the historical context of systemic discrimination and the ongoing struggle for equal protection under the law for Roma communities.

cases.title: CASE OF BEGANOVIĆ v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 3;No violation of Art. 14+3;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Beganović v. Croatia, the applicant, Mr. Darko Beganović, is of Roma origin and resides in Luka, Croatia. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma individuals to violent attacks and the failure of state authorities to provide effective protection and investigation, particularly when the victim belongs to a minority group. On 23 April 2000, Mr. Beganović was attacked by a group of young men, some of whom had previously been involved in a conflict with him. The assailants, who had planned the attack, beat him severely, causing him to lose consciousness and sustain grievous bodily injuries, as confirmed by hospital records. Despite Mr. Beganović’s repeated complaints and the clear evidence of serious harm, the Croatian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the incident, especially regarding any possible racist motives behind the attack.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. The Court found a violation of Article 3 due to the authorities’ failure to investigate the attack effectively but did not find a separate violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 3. Mr. Beganović was awarded non-pecuniary damages for the harm suffered.

This judgment is significant as it reinforces the obligation of states to protect Roma and Traveller individuals from violence and to ensure prompt, thorough investigations, reflecting ongoing concerns about the treatment of Roma communities in Europe.

cases.title: V.C. v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of V.C. v. Slovakia, the applicant, Ms. V.C., is a Slovak national of Roma origin living in Šarišská Poruba. Her case was brought against Slovakia, highlighting the specific vulnerabilities faced by Roma women in the healthcare system. The central harm in this case was the non-consensual sterilisation of Ms. V.C., a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma women and is rooted in a broader context of discrimination and marginalisation.

On 23 August 2000, while in labour with her second child at Prešov Hospital, Ms. V.C. was sterilised without her full and informed consent. During the final stages of labour and in considerable pain, she was told by medical staff that another pregnancy would be fatal for her or her baby. Under duress and without understanding the term "sterilisation," she signed a form authorising the procedure. The operation was performed immediately after her Caesarean section. The medical records noted her Roma origin, and following the procedure, Ms. V.C. suffered significant psychological and social consequences, including ostracism from her community and the breakdown of her relationship.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 12 (right to marry and found a family), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The case was declared admissible, allowing the Court to consider whether Slovakia had violated these fundamental rights.

This case is significant as it addresses the legacy of forced sterilisation policies targeting Roma women in Central and Eastern Europe, reflecting a history of systemic discrimination. The Court’s scrutiny of such practices marks an important step in affirming the reproductive rights and dignity of Roma and Traveller women across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF TANASE AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list (Article 37-1 - Striking out applications)
cases.summary:
In the case of Tanase and Others v. Romania, the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin who lived in the village of Bolintin Deal, Giurgiu County. The case arose from a series of violent attacks against the Roma community following the killing of a non-Roma villager by a Roma individual on the night of 6–7 April 1991. In retaliation, over two thousand non-Roma residents, joined by local officials, burned and destroyed the applicants’ homes and belongings, forcing the entire Roma community to flee and leaving them homeless. When the Roma attempted to return a month later, further violence ensued, resulting in additional homes being burned and the community being denied access to the village, church, and cemetery. The applicants lost all their possessions and were forced to relocate multiple times, often without legal documentation of residence.

The applicants sought justice through the Romanian courts, but the criminal proceedings resulted in only suspended sentences for the perpetrators and limited compensation, which was further reduced due to alleged provocation. The courts also used derogatory language, referring to the applicants as “gypsies.” The European Court of Human Rights was prepared to examine violations of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13, and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but the case was struck out after the Romanian government acknowledged these violations, offered substantial compensation, and committed to a range of general and individual measures to address discrimination and improve conditions for Roma in Bolintin Deal.

This case is significant as it highlights the systemic violence and discrimination faced by Roma communities in post-communist Romania, and it underscores the importance of both individual redress and broader structural reforms to protect Roma and Traveller rights under the European Convention on Human Rights.

cases.title: CASE OF K.H. AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 8;Violation of Art. 6-1;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary: In the case of K.H. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were eight Slovakian women of Roma origin who brought a case against Slovakia. The heart of the case lay in the applicants’ vulnerability as Roma women who suspected they had been sterilised without their full and informed consent during caesarean deliveries in two hospitals in eastern Slovakia. After their hospital stays, none of the women was able to conceive, and they sought access to their medical records to understand the reasons for their infertility and to pursue possible legal remedies. In 2002 and 2003, the applicants, represented by lawyers from the Centre for Civil and Human Rights, requested to consult and photocopy their medical records, but the hospitals refused, citing restrictive interpretations of Slovak law. Although courts allowed the women and their representatives to view the records and make handwritten notes, they denied the right to make photocopies, which limited the applicants’ ability to obtain independent medical analysis and to safeguard evidence for potential legal proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial), awarding non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it affirms the right of Roma and Traveller women to access essential personal information, particularly in the context of a history of forced sterilisation and systemic discrimination in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF F.H. v. SWEDEN
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 2;No violation of Art. 3
cases.summary:
In the case of F.H. v. Sweden, the applicant, F.H., an Iraqi national of Roma origin, sought asylum in Sweden after fleeing Iraq with his children in 1993, later joined by his wife. The case focused on the applicant’s vulnerability as a member of the Roma and Travellers community, who faced heightened risks of persecution and violence in Iraq, particularly given his background as a former officer in the Republican Guard and his desertion from the military. F.H. claimed that, as a Roma and a deserter, he would be at risk of execution or ill-treatment if returned to Iraq, citing both his ethnicity and his perceived association with the former regime as grounds for protection.

Upon arrival in Sweden, F.H. applied for asylum, detailing his military service, desertion, and subsequent flight from Iraq. Swedish authorities conducted several interviews and ultimately rejected his asylum claim, doubting the credibility of his account and the immediacy of the risks he described. F.H. argued before the European Court of Human Rights that his removal to Iraq would violate Article 2 (right to life) and Article 3 (prohibition of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The Court examined the evidence and concluded that there was insufficient proof that F.H. faced a real and personal risk of death or ill-treatment upon return to Iraq. Accordingly, it found no violation of Articles 2 or 3 and did not award any remedies. This case is significant for Roma and Travellers’ rights as it highlights the challenges Roma applicants face in substantiating claims of vulnerability and risk in asylum proceedings, against a backdrop of historical marginalisation and ongoing discrimination in Europe and beyond.

cases.title: CASE OF RENOLDE v. FRANCE
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 2 (procedural aspect);Violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect)
cases.summary: In the case of Renolde v. France, the applicant, Ms. Renolde, is the sister of Joselito Renolde, both members of a Traveller family, who brought a case against France following her brother’s death in custody. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals in detention, especially those with mental health issues, and the risks they face when their specific needs are not adequately addressed by authorities. Joselito Renolde, who had a history of psychiatric problems, was placed in pre-trial detention in April 2000 and later transferred to Bois-d’Arcy Prison. Despite a suicide attempt and clear signs of acute mental distress, he was placed in a punishment cell for 45 days after a disciplinary incident, with insufficient supervision of his medication and mental health. On 20 July 2000, Joselito Renolde died by suicide in his cell. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 (right to life) and Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found France in violation of both articles, citing failures in the authorities’ duty to protect Joselito’s life and to ensure humane treatment. This judgment is significant as it underscores the heightened duty of care owed to vulnerable detainees, particularly from Roma and Traveller backgrounds, in a context where such minorities have historically faced neglect and discrimination in European custodial settings.

cases.title: HRISTOV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Hristov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Ilcho Zoev Hristov, a Bulgarian national of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Bulgarian state. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face procedural obstacles and risks of arbitrary detention within the criminal justice system. In October 1999, Mr. Hristov was charged with petty theft in Sofia. Due to a miscommunication—his court summons was served to another person—he missed his hearing on 4 September 2001, leading the Sofia District Court to order his remand in custody. After reaching a plea bargain on 23 October 2001, which resulted in a suspended sentence, the court failed to explicitly order his release, and Mr. Hristov remained in detention until 30 October 2001, despite a letter from the court on 25 October instructing his immediate release. Mr. Hristov complained under Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alleging that his detention during this period was unlawful and arbitrary. However, the European Court of Human Rights ultimately struck the case out of its list, as Mr. Hristov and his representatives ceased communication and did not pursue the application further. This case illustrates the procedural barriers Roma individuals may encounter in seeking justice, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and the importance of effective legal remedies for Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE PETRULIAN IOANOVICI c. ROUMANIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 1 du Protocole n° 1 - Protection de la propriété
cases.summary:
In Petrulian Ioanovici v. Romania, the applicant, Ms. Petrulian Ioanovici, brought a case against Romania concerning the loss of property rights over an apartment and adjoining land in Bucharest. The judgment does not explicitly state that Ms. Ioanovici is a member of the Roma or Traveller communities, but the property in question was located on Roma Street in Bucharest, suggesting a possible connection to a Roma settlement.

The harm at the heart of the case was Ms. Ioanovici’s inability to regain possession of her family’s apartment and land, which had been nationalized by the state in 1950 and later sold to third parties, despite a 1996 court judgment recognizing her ownership. After the state transferred the property to a government agency, it was sold in 1996 to former tenants. Ms. Ioanovici’s repeated legal efforts to reclaim the property or obtain compensation were unsuccessful, and her administrative requests for restitution remained unaddressed for years.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), holding that the state’s actions amounted to a de facto deprivation of property without compensation. The Court ordered restitution of the property or, if not possible, payment of compensation. This case follows established ECtHR precedent on property restitution in Romania, emphasizing the incompatibility of such uncompensated deprivation with the Convention.

cases.title: CASE OF ORŠUŠ AND OTHERS v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 6-1;No violation of P1-2;No violation of Art. 14+P1-2;Remainder inadmissible;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In the case of Oršuš and Others v. Croatia, the applicants were fifteen schoolchildren from the Roma community, living in the villages of Orehovica, Podturen, and Trnovec. They brought a case against Croatia, arguing that their placement in Roma-only classes in local primary schools amounted to discrimination. The core harm at issue was the segregation of Roma pupils into separate classes, which the applicants claimed resulted in an inferior education and reinforced their social exclusion, a vulnerability long experienced by Roma and Traveller communities across Europe.

Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, the applicants attended primary schools where, at various times, they were placed in classes composed exclusively of Roma children. The authorities justified this separation on the grounds that many Roma pupils lacked sufficient knowledge of Croatian, the language of instruction. However, the applicants argued that this practice led to educational disadvantage and stigmatisation, as they were not given adequate opportunities to integrate into mixed classes or to overcome language barriers.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, concluding that the applicants had not received a fair hearing before the domestic courts. However, it found no violation of the right to education or of the prohibition of discrimination in conjunction with the right to education. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to the applicants.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma children in accessing equal education in Europe. Against a backdrop of historical segregation and marginalisation, the judgment underscores the need for states to ensure that measures addressing language barriers do not result in unjustified separation or discrimination of Roma and Traveller pupils.

cases.title: ASSOCIATION OF CITIZENS RADKO AND PAUNKOVSKI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
The case of Association of Citizens Radko and Paunkovski v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia" was brought by the Association of Citizens “Radko” and its chairman, Mr. Vladimir Paunkovski, who holds both Macedonian and Bulgarian nationality. The applicants did not identify as Roma or Travellers, nor did the facts of the case indicate any connection to Roma or Traveller identity; rather, the Association was founded to promote the cultural and historical identity of Slavs from Macedonia who identify as Bulgarians.

The central issue concerned the dissolution of the Association by the Macedonian authorities, who argued that its aims and activities—particularly its reference to the Bulgarian identity of Macedonian Slavs and its association with the controversial historical figure Ivan Mihajlov—posed a threat to the constitutional order and incited national or religious hatred. The Association’s registration was annulled by the Constitutional Court in March 2001, which found that its programme and articles were incompatible with the Macedonian Constitution.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that their rights to freedom of expression (Article 10) and freedom of association (Article 11) had been violated. The Court declared the application admissible but, as of the date of the admissibility decision, had not yet ruled on the merits or awarded remedies. This case is notable for its examination of the limits of freedom of association in the context of national identity debates in Macedonia, but it does not concern Roma or Traveller rights.

cases.title: AFFAIRE SAMPANIS ET AUTRES c. GRECE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire jointe au fond et rejetée (non-épuisement de voies de recours internes);Violation de l'art. 13;Violation de l'art. 14+P1-2;Préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary: In Sampanis and Others v. Greece, the applicants were eleven Greek nationals of Roma origin, residing with their families in the Psari area near Aspropyrgos, in western Attica. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma children who faced systemic barriers to accessing mainstream education, highlighting the persistent segregation and exclusion experienced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe. In September 2004, as the new school year began, the applicants attempted to enrol their children in local primary schools. Despite encouragement from some school officials, the directors refused to register the Roma children, citing a lack of instructions from the Ministry of Education. Instead, authorities proposed placing older Roma children in separate preparatory classes, physically isolated from other pupils, and even considered constructing a distinct building for Roma students. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), as well as Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found that Greece had violated these provisions by discriminating against Roma children and failing to provide effective remedies. The applicants were awarded compensation for moral damage. This judgment is significant as it was among the first to address the segregation of Roma children in education, setting a precedent for challenging discriminatory practices against Roma and Traveller communities across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF SAMPANIS AND OTHERS v. GREECE - [English Translation] by European Roma Rights Centre "ERRC"
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 13;Violation of Art. 14+P1-2;Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In Sampanis and Others v. Greece, the applicants were families of Romani origin living in the Psari area near Aspropyrgos, a municipality in western Attica. The case focused on the vulnerability of Romani children who faced systemic barriers to accessing mainstream primary education, highlighting the persistent exclusion and segregation experienced by Roma and Travellers in Greece. In 2004, despite efforts by Romani parents to enrol their children in local primary schools, school directors refused registration, citing a lack of instructions from the Ministry of Education. Instead, authorities proposed separate preparatory classes for Romani children, effectively segregating them from their non-Romani peers. The applicants, supported by human rights organisations, repeatedly sought intervention from national authorities, but their children remained excluded from ordinary classes.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found that Greece had violated these provisions by failing to ensure equal access to education and by not providing an effective remedy for the discrimination suffered. The applicants were awarded non-pecuniary damages.

This judgment is significant as it was among the first to address the segregation of Romani children in education in Greece, reinforcing the principle that Roma and Traveller children must have equal access to mainstream schooling, in line with broader European efforts to combat educational discrimination against these communities.

cases.title: HUSOVIC ET  AUTRES c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Radiation du rôle
cases.summary: In the case of Husovic and Others v. Italy, the applicants—Ms. Rasema Husovic, Mr. Dani Halilovic, and their daughters Indiana and Brigida Halilovic—were members of the Roma community from the former Yugoslavia, living in Rome. Their case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing repeated forced evictions and the destruction of their homes without proper legal safeguards or alternative accommodation. After arriving in Rome, the family settled in the Casilino 900 nomad camp and were registered during a 1995 census. In 1999, they moved to the Via Salone 323 camp, where they lived in a wooden house. On 4 August 2004, municipal authorities demolished their home as part of camp restructuring, and after the family rebuilt, their new house was again destroyed on 8 November 2004. The applicants alleged that these actions were carried out without administrative orders, compensation, or offers of alternative housing. They brought their complaint under Articles 3, 8, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, before the Court could rule on the merits, the applicants withdrew their complaint after being provided with suitable housing, and the case was struck out. This case reflects the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller families face regarding housing rights and forced evictions in Europe, a persistent issue with deep historical roots.

cases.title: CASE OF SULEJMANOV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary: In the case of Sulejmanov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Sulejmanov, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the state concerning his treatment by police. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police brutality and the lack of effective investigations into such allegations, a persistent issue for these communities across Europe. On 13 March 1998, Mr. Sulejmanov and a friend, both of Roma origin, were stopped by police near the village of Balvan on suspicion of theft. According to Mr. Sulejmanov, they were immediately beaten by police officers, subjected to racist insults, and further assaulted at the police station, where they were denied water and left tied up overnight. After his release, Mr. Sulejmanov sought medical attention for a broken arm, but his injuries were not properly documented due to financial constraints and the use of a relative’s identity card. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found no substantive violation of Article 3, as it could not be established beyond reasonable doubt that the police had inflicted the injuries. However, it found a procedural violation, ruling that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into Mr. Sulejmanov’s credible allegations of ill-treatment. This judgment is significant as it underscores the ongoing need for robust, impartial investigations into police violence against Roma and Travellers, reflecting broader concerns about systemic discrimination in the region during the late 1990s.

cases.title: CASE OF DZELADINOV AND OTHERS v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Procedural aspect)
cases.summary:
In the case of Dzeladinov and Others v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants, all members of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the state following a violent incident involving police intervention. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective protection or redress when abuses occur, particularly in situations marked by ethnic tension and social exclusion. On the night of 2 August 1998, after a Roma circumcision celebration in Štip, a fight broke out involving a police-affiliated individual. Police officers responded by entering the restaurant and, according to the applicants, assaulted numerous Roma guests, including a pregnant woman who was denied immediate medical care. Several applicants were allegedly beaten, insulted on account of their ethnic origin, and detained for hours, with some forced to confess under duress. Despite photographic evidence of injuries, the authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation into the applicants’ complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. While the Court found no substantive violation of Article 3 regarding the alleged ill-treatment itself, it held that there had been a procedural violation due to the authorities’ failure to effectively investigate the applicants’ credible allegations. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in securing justice and accountability for police misconduct, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and impunity in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF STOICA v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 3;No violation of Art. 13;Violation of Art. 14+3;Remainder inadmissible;Non-pecuniary damage - award;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed
cases.summary:
In the case of Stoica v. Romania, the applicant, Constantin Stoica, a young boy of Roma origin living in Gulia—a village with a predominantly Roma population—brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of authorities to protect them or investigate abuses effectively. On the evening of 3 April 2001, during an enforcement operation involving police officers, public guards, and the deputy mayor, a confrontation occurred outside a local bar frequented by Roma residents. According to Stoica, then 14 years old and suffering from a serious brain condition, he was singled out, beaten, and left unconscious by a police officer after being asked about his Roma identity, while officials shouted racist insults. Medical examinations confirmed his injuries, and witnesses corroborated his account, but the authorities dismissed the allegations and failed to conduct an impartial investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding that Stoica had suffered ill-treatment at the hands of state agents and that this was aggravated by racial discrimination. The Court found violations of both Article 3 and Article 14 taken together with Article 3, and awarded non-pecuniary damages to Stoica. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent problem of racially motivated violence against Roma and Travellers in Europe and the need for states to ensure effective protection and accountability, especially given the historical context of systemic discrimination faced by these communities.

cases.title: BORISOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Borisov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants—five Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin and the Roma Church in Bulgaria, an organisation they founded—brought a case against the Bulgarian state. The applicants, identifying as Roma, alleged that they faced specific harm due to the disruption of their religious gatherings and obstacles to registering their religious organisation, reflecting the broader vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to discrimination and administrative barriers in exercising their rights. Between 1997 and 1998, police officers allegedly interrupted their prayer meetings in Lom, warning that religious activities without official registration were not permitted, and Mr Borisov was reportedly detained and questioned about his religious activities. In 1999, the applicants established the Roma Church in Bulgaria and sought official registration, but the authorities requested further information about their religious practices. The applicants did not respond to this request, and their appeal was dismissed as premature by the Supreme Administrative Court.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 9 (freedom of religion), 11 (freedom of assembly), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, as they had not pursued available legal avenues or responded to requests for clarification. This case highlights the procedural hurdles Roma and Traveller communities may face in seeking recognition and protection of their religious and associational rights, set against a historical backdrop of marginalisation and administrative exclusion in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF PETROPOULOU-TSAKIRIS v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (Article 35-1 - Exhaustion of domestic remedies);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+3 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture);Non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary: In the case of Petropoulou-Tsakiris v. Greece, the applicant, Ms. Petropoulou-Tsakiris, is a member of the Roma community living in the Nea Zoe settlement in Aspropyrgos, western Attica. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective protection and investigation when abuses occur. On 28 January 2002, during a large-scale police operation targeting alleged drug trafficking in the Roma settlement, Ms. Petropoulou-Tsakiris, who was two and a half months pregnant, was forcefully pushed and kicked in the back by police officers despite her protests that she was pregnant. She began bleeding but was not taken to hospital, and, as an unregistered stateless person, she feared seeking medical help alone. The following day, she was admitted to hospital, and on 1 February 2002, she suffered a miscarriage. Despite her criminal complaint and requests for an impartial investigation, the inquiry was conducted by officers from the same police station involved in the operation, and the authorities failed to identify or punish those responsible. The European Court of Human Rights found no substantive violation of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman treatment) but held that there was a procedural violation of Article 3 due to the ineffective investigation, and a violation of Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3, awarding non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent barriers Roma and Travellers face in accessing justice and protection from discriminatory police practices, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF D.H. AND OTHERS v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 14+P1-2;General measures refused;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award
cases.summary:
In the landmark case of D.H. and Others v. the Czech Republic, the applicants were eighteen children of Roma origin, representing the Roma community in Ostrava, who brought a complaint against the Czech Republic. The case focused on the systemic vulnerability of Roma children, who were disproportionately placed in “special schools” intended for pupils with intellectual disabilities, resulting in de facto segregation and limited educational opportunities. Between 1996 and 1999, the applicants were assigned to these special schools, where the curriculum was significantly reduced compared to mainstream schools, severely restricting their future prospects. Statistical evidence showed that Roma children in Ostrava were 27 times more likely than non-Roma children to be placed in such schools, with over half of all Roma children in the Czech Republic affected by this practice.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding that the applicants had suffered indirect discrimination. The Court held that the Czech authorities had failed to provide adequate safeguards against the placement of Roma children in special schools, violating their right to education without discrimination. The applicants were awarded non-pecuniary damages and partial costs.

This judgment is a milestone for Roma and Traveller rights, highlighting the persistence of educational segregation in Europe and affirming the obligation of states to ensure equal access to quality education for all children, regardless of ethnic origin.

cases.title: AFFAIRE D.H. ET AUTRES c. REPUBLIQUE TCHEQUE
cases.conclusion: Exception préliminaire rejetée (non-épuisement des voies de recours internes);Violation de l'art. 14+P1-2;Mesures générales rejetées;Préjudice moral - réparation pécuniaire;Remboursement partiel frais et dépens
cases.summary: In the landmark case of D.H. and Others v. the Czech Republic, the applicants were eighteen children of Roma origin living in Ostrava, Czech Republic. They challenged the practice of placing Roma children in “special schools” intended for pupils with mental disabilities, a system that disproportionately affected Roma and Traveller children. The core harm at issue was the systemic segregation of Roma children in education, which resulted in limited educational opportunities and reinforced social exclusion. Between 1996 and 1999, the applicants were assigned to these special schools based on psychological tests and decisions by school directors, with parental consent often given without full understanding of the consequences. Statistical evidence showed that Roma children in Ostrava were vastly overrepresented in special schools—making up over half of the pupils in such schools, despite being a small minority in the general population. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), finding that the Czech Republic had violated these provisions by failing to ensure that placement procedures did not have a disproportionately negative impact on Roma children. The Court awarded moral damages and partial costs to the applicants. This judgment is a milestone for Roma and Traveller rights, highlighting the persistence of educational segregation in Europe and affirming the need for equal access to quality education for all children, regardless of ethnic origin.

cases.title: K. v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of K. v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants were a family of Serbian nationals of Ashkaelia/Roma origin from Kosovo, represented by lawyers in Skopje. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Ashkaelia minorities facing ethnic violence and insecurity in post-conflict Kosovo, particularly the risk of life-threatening and degrading treatment if forcibly returned. After living in Germany with asylum status from 1993 to 2003, the family was deported to Kosovo, where they encountered severe ethnic unrest and displacement, including the occupation of their home and subsequent violence in March 2004. Fearing for their safety, they fled to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia in July 2004 and sought asylum, but their request was summarily dismissed, and they were ordered to leave the country. Despite interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights to prevent their expulsion, the family ultimately left Macedonia voluntarily and returned to Kosovo. The Court examined potential violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), and 13 (right to an effective remedy), but ultimately struck the case out after the applicants withdrew their complaint. This case underscores the precarious situation of Roma and Ashkaelia minorities in the Balkans during the early 2000s, reflecting broader patterns of displacement and insecurity faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: K.H. AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In K.H. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were eight Slovakian women of Roma origin who brought a case against Slovakia. The women, all from the Roma community, suspected they had been sterilised without their full and informed consent during caesarean deliveries at two hospitals in eastern Slovakia. Their vulnerability lay in the serious and lasting harm of possible involuntary sterilisation, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma women in Europe and raises profound concerns about bodily autonomy and discrimination.

Between 2002 and 2003, the applicants and their lawyers sought access to their complete medical records to investigate the cause of their infertility and to prepare potential legal claims. Despite granting powers of attorney to their legal representatives, the hospitals refused to allow photocopying of the records, citing restrictive interpretations of Slovak health law. The applicants initiated civil proceedings, but the Slovak courts upheld the hospitals’ refusal to permit photocopying, allowing only handwritten excerpts.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private life), Article 6 (right to a fair trial), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found a violation of Article 8, recognising that access to personal medical information is a crucial aspect of private life, and that the refusal to allow photocopying placed an excessive burden on the applicants. This judgment is significant as it affirms the right of Roma and Traveller women to access their own medical records, a key safeguard against abuses such as forced sterilisation, and comes in the context of a troubling history of reproductive rights violations against Roma women in Central and Eastern Europe.

cases.title: LIMONI AND OTHERS v. SWEDEN
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Limoni and Others v. Sweden, the applicants were Mr. Mehmed Limoni, his wife Mrs. Nizajete Limoni, and their six children, all Serbian citizens of Roma ethnicity, who sought asylum in Sweden. The case focused on the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing expulsion to countries where they risk discrimination, violence, and inadequate living conditions due to their minority status. The Limoni family fled Kosovo during the conflict in the late 1990s, citing persecution and violence against Roma, including sexual violence and the destruction of their home. After multiple asylum applications and returns between Sweden, Germany, and Serbia, the family was ultimately expelled from Sweden to Serbia in May 2005, where they reported living in harsh conditions in a camp and suffering from both physical and psychological harm.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the general situation in Serbia at the relevant time did not, in itself, amount to a violation of Article 3, and that the applicants had not demonstrated a real and personal risk of such treatment upon return. No remedies were awarded.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller families face in seeking protection from discrimination and violence in Europe, particularly in the context of forced returns following the Kosovo conflict and broader patterns of marginalisation.

cases.title: CASE OF COBZARU v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objections dismissed (six-month period, non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 3 both under its substantive and procedural aspects;Violation of Art. 13 on account of the lack of effective remedies in respect of the ill-treatment complained of;Violation of Art. 14+3 under its procedural aspect and Art. 13;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses award - domestic and Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In Cobzaru v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Belmondo Cobzaru, a Romanian national of Roma origin, brought a case against the Romanian state. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the failure of authorities to investigate such abuses effectively. On 4 July 1997, after a domestic dispute in Mangalia, Mr. Cobzaru voluntarily went to the local police station to report threats against him. While there, he was assaulted by police officers—beaten, kicked, and struck with a stick—while other officers looked on. The police referenced his father’s role as a Roma association leader, suggesting ethnic bias. Mr. Cobzaru suffered significant injuries, including head trauma and multiple bruises, and was later hospitalised. Despite his complaints, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, and the officers denied any wrongdoing.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 in conjunction with Article 3 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found that Mr. Cobzaru had been subjected to ill-treatment by police, that the investigation was inadequate, and that he had been discriminated against as a Roma. The Court awarded him compensation for non-pecuniary damages and legal costs.

This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent problem of police violence and institutional discrimination against Roma and Travellers in Europe, reaffirming the need for effective remedies and equal protection under the law.

cases.title: CASE OF ANGELOVA AND ILIEV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection joined to merits and dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 2;No separate issue under Art. 3;No separate issue under Art. 13;Violation of Art. 14 +2;No separate issue under Art. 14+3;Remainder inadmissible;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In the case of Angelova and Iliev v. Bulgaria, the applicants were the mother and brother of Angel Dimitrov Iliev, a 28-year-old man of Roma origin, who brought a case against Bulgaria following his violent death. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to racially motivated violence and the failure of state authorities to respond effectively to such hate crimes. On the evening of 18 April 1996, in the town of Shumen, Mr. Iliev was brutally attacked by a group of seven teenagers, who beat and stabbed him, resulting in his death the following morning. Statements from the assailants revealed that the attack was motivated by anti-Roma hatred, with explicit references to their animosity towards “Gypsies” and other minorities.

Despite the gravity of the crime and its clear racist motivation, the investigation and prosecution were marred by significant delays and procedural shortcomings. The authorities failed to pursue the racial motive adequately and allowed the statute of limitations to expire for several suspects, undermining justice for the victim’s family. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 (right to life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2, awarding non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. This judgment is significant as it underscores the obligation of states to protect Roma and Travellers from racially motivated violence and to ensure effective investigations, reflecting ongoing concerns about anti-Roma violence in Europe’s recent history.

cases.title: CASE OF ŠEČIĆ v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 3;No separate issue under Art. 8 or 13;Violation of Art. 14+3;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award
cases.summary:
In the case of Šečić v. Croatia, the applicant, Mr. Šečić, a Roma man living in Zagreb, brought a complaint against Croatia after suffering a violent, racially motivated attack. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face targeted violence and inadequate protection from state authorities. On the evening of 29 April 1999, while collecting scrap metal with others in Zagreb, Mr. Šečić was assaulted by two unidentified men wielding wooden planks, who shouted racist abuse during the attack. He sustained multiple rib fractures and later developed post-traumatic stress disorder. Despite repeated efforts by Mr. Šečić and his lawyer to prompt a thorough investigation—including providing witness names and evidence of a pattern of attacks against Roma—the authorities failed to identify or prosecute the perpetrators, and the investigation remained stalled for years.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. The Court found that Croatia had violated both Article 3, due to the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation, and Article 14 taken with Article 3, due to the discriminatory nature of the attack and the inadequate response. The Court awarded Mr. Šečić non-pecuniary damages and partial costs.

This judgment is significant as it underscores the obligation of states to protect Roma and Travellers from racially motivated violence and to investigate such crimes effectively, reflecting a broader historical context of systemic discrimination against these communities in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE ŠEČIĆ c. CROATIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'art. 3;Aucune question distincte au regard de l'art. 8 ou 13;Violation de l'art. 14+3;Préjudice moral - réparation pécuniaire;Remboursement partiel frais et dépens
cases.summary:
In the case of Šečić v. Croatia, the applicant, Mr. Šečić, is a Croatian national of Roma origin who brought a complaint against the Croatian state. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to racially motivated violence and the failure of authorities to provide effective protection and investigation. On the evening of 29 April 1999 in Zagreb, Mr. Šečić was collecting scrap metal with others when he was violently attacked by a group of unidentified men wielding wooden planks and shouting racist insults. He suffered multiple broken ribs and developed post-traumatic stress disorder, requiring ongoing psychiatric treatment. Despite repeated requests from his lawyer, the police investigation was slow and ineffective, with key witnesses not promptly interviewed and leads not fully pursued, particularly regarding the racial motivation behind the attack.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. The Court found that Croatia had violated Article 3 by failing to conduct an effective investigation and further violated Article 14 taken with Article 3 by not adequately addressing the racist nature of the attack. The Court awarded Mr. Šečić compensation for non-pecuniary damage and partial costs.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the obligation of states to protect Roma and Travellers from racially motivated violence and to investigate such crimes with particular diligence, reflecting a broader European context of persistent discrimination against these communities.

cases.title: MAKUC AND OTHERS v. SLOVENIA
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary: In Makuc and Others v. Slovenia, the applicants—eleven individuals, including Mr Milan Makuc and others—were former citizens of Yugoslavia, several of whom identified as Roma or belonged to other groups encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case against Slovenia centred on the vulnerability of “the erased,” a group that included many Roma, who lost their legal status and fundamental rights following Slovenia’s independence. After Slovenia declared independence in 1991, the applicants, who had been permanent residents, failed to apply for Slovenian citizenship within the required timeframe. On 26 February 1992, their names were deleted from the Register of Permanent Residents, rendering them foreigners overnight and stripping them of access to healthcare, employment, and social security. Some faced expulsion or were unable to regularise their status for years. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under several articles, including Articles 8 (private and family life), 13 (effective remedy), and 14 (non-discrimination), but ultimately declared the case partly inadmissible, finding that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. Although no violation was found, the case highlighted the precarious situation of Roma and other minorities affected by administrative erasure. This case remains significant as it drew international attention to the systemic exclusion faced by Roma and Travellers in post-socialist Europe, particularly during periods of state succession and legal transition.

cases.title: CASE OF KALANYOS AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Kalanyos and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Sandor Kalanyos, Tamas Kalanyos, and Istvan Rozsa—were members of the Roma community living in the hamlet of Plăieşii de Sus, Harghita County. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to violent attacks, forced displacement, and discriminatory treatment by both private individuals and state authorities. On 6 June 1991, a fight broke out between several Roma and a nightwatchman, which led to a retaliatory attack by non-Roma villagers. Two Roma men were beaten, one fatally. Despite warnings of further violence, local authorities failed to protect the Roma community, advising them to flee rather than intervening. On 9 June 1991, the applicants and other Roma villagers were forced to abandon their homes, which were then destroyed by arson. For over a year, they lived in dire conditions in stables, with little support from the authorities. Investigations into the attacks were inadequate, marred by discriminatory attitudes, and ultimately closed without identifying or prosecuting the perpetrators.

The European Court of Human Rights examined alleged violations of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13, and 14 of the Convention, relating to inhuman treatment, fair trial, respect for private and family life, effective remedy, and non-discrimination. The case was struck out following a unilateral declaration by the Romanian government, which acknowledged violations, offered compensation, and committed to general measures against discrimination. This case is significant as it highlights the persistent vulnerability of Roma communities in Europe to violence and systemic discrimination, reflecting a broader historical pattern of exclusion and inadequate state protection.

cases.title: CASE OF GERGELY v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Gergely v. Romania, the applicant, Ms. Irene Gergely, a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Romanian state following a violent attack on Roma residents in the hamlet of Caşinul Nou, Harghita County. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to racially motivated violence and the failure of state authorities to protect them or provide justice. On the night of 11 August 1990, after escalating tensions and accusations against local Roma, a large group of non-Roma villagers gathered and set fire to several Roma homes, including Ms. Gergely’s, leaving around 150 people homeless. Ms. Gergely and her four young children fled in fear for their lives, hiding in a nearby field as their house was destroyed. Despite immediate criminal complaints and repeated requests for investigation, Romanian authorities discontinued proceedings, citing the difficulty of identifying perpetrators and, later, the expiry of statutory time limits. The European Court of Human Rights received a unilateral declaration from the Romanian government, acknowledging violations of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13, and 14 of the Convention—prohibiting torture, ensuring fair trial, respect for private life, effective remedy, and non-discrimination—and offering compensation and commitments to systemic reforms. The case was struck out following this declaration. Gergely v. Romania is significant as it reflects both the historical pattern of anti-Roma violence in post-communist Europe and the persistent institutional failures to address such discrimination.

cases.title: CASE OF KONSTATINOV v. THE NETHERLANDS
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8
cases.summary:
In the case of Konstatinov v. the Netherlands, the applicant, Ms. Jadranka Konstatinov, is of Roma origin and was born in Serbia. She challenged the Netherlands’ decision to refuse her a residence permit and to declare her an undesirable alien, which would result in her expulsion and separation from her husband and son, both of whom held residence permits in the Netherlands. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, particularly regarding the risk of family separation and the difficulties faced in securing legal residence due to strict immigration requirements and the impact of criminal records.

Ms. Konstatinov entered the Netherlands as a young woman, married a man of Roma background who had permanent residence, and had a son there. Despite living in the Netherlands for many years, her applications for a residence permit were repeatedly denied, partly due to her husband’s insufficient income and her own criminal convictions. Administrative delays further complicated her situation, and in 1998, she was declared an undesirable alien, facing a five-year exclusion order.

The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court ultimately found no violation, concluding that the Dutch authorities had struck a reasonable balance between Ms. Konstatinov’s family life and the public interest in preventing crime and maintaining public order.

This case is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it illustrates the persistent barriers faced by Roma families in securing residence and family unity in Western Europe, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and administrative obstacles for Roma and Travellers across the continent.

cases.title: BERISHA AND HALJITI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Berisha and Haljiti v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants, Mr. Dzavit Berisha and Mrs. Baljie Haljiti, are citizens of Serbia of Egyptian ethnic origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. As Balkan Egyptians, they fall within the Council of Europe’s definition of “Roma and Travellers.” The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller minorities facing expulsion and criminal proceedings without adequate procedural safeguards, particularly when language barriers and lack of legal assistance are involved.

On 15 September 2003, after their asylum request had been dismissed, the applicants were apprehended by police near the village of Dragos, accused of attempting to cross into Greece illegally and of remaining in Macedonia without valid permits. They were detained, denied the opportunity to contact anyone—including a lawyer—and swiftly brought before the Bitola Court of First Instance. That same day, they were convicted of minor offences, fined, banned from re-entering the country for two years, and expelled to Serbia. The proceedings were conducted in a language the second applicant did not understand, and the applicants signed minutes stating they would not appeal.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and its related guarantees, but ultimately found the application partly inadmissible and did not establish a violation. Nevertheless, the case highlights the procedural vulnerabilities faced by Roma and Traveller minorities, especially Balkan Egyptians, in expulsion and criminal proceedings. It underscores the ongoing need for effective legal safeguards and interpretation services, reflecting broader historical challenges of access to justice for Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.

cases.title: DZELADINOV AND OTHERS v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Dzeladinov and Others v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants—Amdi Dzeladinov, Dudzihan Kamilov, Remzie Durmišova, Dagistan Alilov, and Mefail Asanovski—are Macedonian nationals of Roma origin, represented by the Association for the Protection of Roma Rights and the European Roma Rights Centre. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the lack of effective remedies for such abuses. On the night of 2 August 1998 in Štip, following a Romani circumcision celebration, the applicants and other Roma were allegedly subjected to violent police raids, including beatings, ethnic insults, and, in the case of the third applicant, mistreatment while seven months pregnant. Despite their complaints, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the alleged ill-treatment, and the applicants argued that their Roma identity was a factor in both the abuse and the lack of redress.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the Court ultimately found the application partly inadmissible, concluding that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies before turning to Strasbourg.

This case highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing justice and protection from police abuse. It reflects a broader historical context in which Roma and Travellers across Europe have struggled against systemic discrimination and institutional indifference to their rights.

cases.title: CASE OF JASAR v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 3 (alleged ill-treatment);Violation de l'Art. 3 (effective investigation into these allegations);Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses award - domestic proceedings;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In the case of Jasar v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Jasar, a Roma man living in Štip, brought a complaint against the state concerning his treatment by police. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective legal remedies, issues that have historically affected these communities across Europe. On the night of 16 April 1998, Mr. Jasar and a friend, both of Roma origin, were present in a bar when a violent incident occurred. Police arrived, detained them, and took them to the local station. Mr. Jasar alleged that, while in custody, he was severely beaten by police officers, resulting in visible injuries, as documented by a medical certificate and a newspaper photograph. Despite his formal complaint to the public prosecutor, no effective investigation was carried out to identify or punish those responsible.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). While the Court did not find sufficient evidence to conclude that Mr. Jasar had been subjected to ill-treatment contrary to Article 3, it found a violation of Article 3 in its procedural aspect, due to the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. The Court awarded Mr. Jasar non-pecuniary damages and partial costs. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the obligation of states to investigate allegations of police abuse, particularly where Roma and Traveller individuals are concerned, reflecting ongoing concerns about impunity and discrimination in post-communist Europe.

cases.title: WELLS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Wells v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Jesse Wells, is a British national who, together with his wife and five children, identifies as a Gypsy—a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing eviction from land they own due to planning regulations, and the difficulties in securing lawful accommodation that respects their traditional way of life. In April 2002, Mr. Wells moved his family and caravans onto Ashbrook Farm in Buckinghamshire, having previously lived on his father’s established Gypsy site. Shortly after, the local council served an enforcement notice requiring removal of the caravans, citing harm to the rural character of the area. Despite appeals and evidence of a shortage of Gypsy sites, the authorities maintained the enforcement, and Mr. Wells was ultimately convicted for non-compliance after a protracted legal process. He argued before the European Court of Human Rights that his rights under Articles 8 (private and family life), 14 (non-discrimination), and 6 (fair trial) of the Convention had been violated. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding no appearance of a violation. This case highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller families face in securing culturally appropriate accommodation in the UK, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and legal obstacles.

cases.title: CASE OF BORISOVA v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 6+6 - Right to a fair trial (Article 6 - Criminal proceedings;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing) (Article 6 - Right to a fair trial;Article 6-3 - Rights of defence;Article 6-3-a - Information on nature and cause of accusation;Prompt information;Article 6-3-b - Adequate facilities;Adequate time;Preparation of defence;Article 6-3-d - Examination of witnesses;Same conditions);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Borisova v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Ms. Borisova, a woman of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Bulgaria concerning the fairness of criminal proceedings initiated against her. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals, who often face rapid and summary justice without adequate procedural safeguards, especially in situations involving public order and minor offences. On 8 September 1999, Ms. Borisova was waiting in line at the Employment Office in Pazardzhik with other Roma women when a disturbance occurred. Although she was not involved in the initial incident, a police officer accused her of pushing others and, after a brief altercation, arrested her. She was detained, denied access to a lawyer or the opportunity to contact family, and brought before a court within hours, where she was convicted of minor hooliganism and sentenced to five days’ detention, without being able to call witnesses or properly prepare her defence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to a fair trial, including the rights to be informed of the accusation, to have adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence, and to examine witnesses. The Court found multiple violations of Article 6, noting that Ms. Borisova was not promptly or adequately informed of the charges, was denied sufficient time and facilities to prepare her defence, and was unable to call witnesses on her behalf. The Court awarded her compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the need for fair trial guarantees even in expedited proceedings, particularly for members of groups historically subjected to discrimination and summary justice in Europe.

cases.title: BALAZ AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Balaz and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were members of the Baláž family, Slovak nationals of Roma origin, residing in Leopoldov. The family, who operated a small entertainment park with movable trailers, alleged that they were subjected to discriminatory and arbitrary police interventions due to their Roma identity. The central harm concerned repeated police stops and alleged ill-treatment, including harsh language and physical mistreatment, as well as a lack of effective investigation into their complaints, which the applicants argued was rooted in anti-Roma bias.

The incidents occurred in September 2001, when Mr. Vincent Baláž Jr. and Ms. Jana Konečníková were stopped by police while transporting trailers without number plates. The applicants claimed that police officers used abusive language, entered their property without permission, and physically mistreated Mr. Baláž Jr. Despite numerous complaints to various authorities, including the police and prosecution services, all investigations concluded that the allegations were unsubstantiated and dismissed the complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and 17 (prohibition of abuse of rights). However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had either not exhausted available domestic remedies or were not considered “victims” under the Convention.

This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller families often face when seeking redress for alleged discrimination and police misconduct, reflecting broader historical challenges of access to justice for Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF WALLOVÁ AND WALLA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC - [English Translation] by European Roma Rights Centre "ERRC"
cases.conclusion: Remainder inadmissible;Violation of Art. 8;Not necessary to examine Art. 14;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award
cases.summary: In the case of Wallová and Walla v. the Czech Republic, the applicants, a married couple of Roma origin, brought a complaint against the Czech state after their five children were removed from their care. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families who, due to poverty and inadequate housing, face disproportionate state intervention in family life. In September 2000, Czech authorities placed the Wallová and Walla children under supervision, citing the family’s lack of adequate accommodation. Despite the parents’ efforts to improve their situation, including attempts to secure housing and employment, the courts ordered the children’s provisional and later permanent placement in care institutions. The authorities justified these measures by pointing to the parents’ inability to provide suitable living conditions, but the applicants argued that the state failed to offer sufficient support to help them overcome their material difficulties. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and found a violation, ruling that the removal of the children was not a proportionate response to the family’s poverty and that less intrusive measures should have been considered. The Court awarded the applicants non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it underscores the need for states to support, rather than penalise, Roma and Traveller families facing social and economic hardship—a recurring issue in Europe’s recent history.

cases.title: AFFAIRE PREZIOSI c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de P1-1;Non-lieu à examiner l'art. 6-1;Satisfaction équitable réservée
cases.summary:
In Preziosi v. Italy, the applicants—members of the Roma and Travellers community—brought a case against the Italian state concerning the loss of their property rights. The core vulnerability at issue was the deprivation of land owned by the applicants, a harm that has historically affected Roma and Travellers, who often face insecure property rights and inadequate legal protection. The applicants, born in 1930, 1909, and 1928 and residing in Rome, owned a plot of land in Avellino. In 1979, the municipality authorised the urgent occupation of their land for public housing construction, with a maximum period of five years. However, after the expiry of this period, the authorities continued to occupy the land without formal expropriation or compensation. Despite legal proceedings initiated by the applicants in 1985, the land was never formally expropriated, and compensation was delayed and contested for years, with the case still pending domestically at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and found a violation, holding that the applicants had been deprived of their property in circumstances incompatible with the Convention. The Court reserved the question of just satisfaction for a later stage. This judgment is significant for Roma and Travellers’ rights, as it highlights the persistent risks of property loss and legal uncertainty faced by these communities in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation and dispossession.

cases.title: SULEJMANOV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of Sulejmanov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Demir Sulejmanov, was a Roma man from Štip, represented posthumously by his sisters after his death. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and racially motivated abuse, highlighting the specific harm of ill-treatment and the lack of effective investigation or remedy, allegedly aggravated by anti-Roma prejudice. On 13 March 1998, Mr. Sulejmanov and a Roma friend were stopped by police near Balvan on suspicion of theft. According to his account, they were immediately beaten by police, subjected to racist insults such as “There is no water for gypsies!” and further assaulted at the police station, resulting in a broken arm. The authorities disputed the extent of the violence but confirmed some altercation involving the sheep owner. Despite medical evidence of injury, Mr. Sulejmanov’s complaints of police brutality and discrimination were not effectively investigated by national authorities. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately found parts of the application inadmissible. This case is significant as it illustrates the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in seeking justice for police abuse, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in post-communist Europe.

cases.title: ŠEČIĆ v. CROATIA
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Šečić v. Croatia, the applicants, Mr. Šemso Šečić and Mr. Ševko Šečić, are Croatian citizens of Roma origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Center. Their case against Croatia highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of authorities to provide effective protection or redress. On 29 April 1999, while collecting scrap metal in Zagreb, Mr. Šemso Šečić was violently attacked by a group of unidentified men who beat him with wooden planks while shouting racial abuse. Despite sustaining serious injuries, including multiple rib fractures and subsequent post-traumatic stress disorder, the investigation by Croatian authorities was slow and ineffective. The applicants’ lawyer repeatedly urged the police and State Attorney’s Office to take decisive action, but the perpetrators were never identified, and the investigation dragged on for years without meaningful progress.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found the application partly admissible, focusing on the authorities’ obligation to investigate racially motivated violence. While the judgment did not find all alleged violations, it underscored the need for prompt and thorough investigations in such cases.

Šečić v. Croatia is significant as it draws attention to the persistent problem of anti-Roma violence and the systemic failures of state authorities to protect Roma and Traveller communities, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination across Europe.

cases.title: GERGEL v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of Gergel v. Slovakia, the applicant, Mr. Ľubomír Gergel, is a Slovak national of Roma ethnic origin, represented by lawyers from the European Roma Rights Center and the League of Human Rights Advocates. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to racially motivated police violence and the barriers they face in seeking justice.
