On 19 March 2001, Mr. Gergel was stopped by Railway Police officers in Zvolen, Slovakia, who insulted him with racist remarks, physically assaulted him, and stole money from him. He suffered serious injuries, including a broken rib and kidney damage, requiring over a month of medical treatment. Despite his attempts to file a complaint, the police initially refused to accept it, and only after persistent efforts did a criminal investigation result in the conviction of one officer, who received a fine and was ordered to pay partial damages. Mr. Gergel challenged the limited scope of the conviction and the leniency of the sentence, but his appeals were dismissed on procedural grounds, and the Constitutional Court found his complaint inadmissible due to late filing. The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation of Articles 3, 13, or 14 of the Convention. This case highlights the procedural obstacles Roma and Traveller individuals often encounter when seeking redress for police abuse, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and limited access to justice in Europe.

cases.title: JASAR v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Jasar v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, the applicant, Mr. Pejrusan Jasar, is a national of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and a member of the Roma community, represented by lawyers from the European Roma Rights Centre. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the lack of effective remedies when such abuses occur. On the night of 16 April 1998 in Štip, Mr. Jasar and a Roma friend were present in a bar when a violent incident broke out. Police arrived and, according to Mr. Jasar, subjected him to severe physical abuse both at the scene and later in police custody, resulting in documented injuries. Despite filing a criminal complaint and providing medical evidence, Mr. Jasar’s allegations were not effectively investigated by the authorities, and no charges were brought against him or his friend.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as Article 35 regarding admissibility. The Court found the application admissible, meaning the complaints were sufficiently serious and substantiated to warrant further examination. While the judgment at this stage did not determine a violation, it paved the way for scrutiny of police conduct and state responsibility.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing justice and protection from ill-treatment, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination in Europe’s recent history.

cases.title: ATANASOV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Atanasov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Angel Nikolov Atanasov, is a Bulgarian national of Roma origin living in Plovdiv. He brought a case against Bulgaria, alleging discrimination and procedural unfairness in criminal proceedings against him. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma individuals within the justice system, particularly regarding claims of bias and lack of effective remedies when facing serious criminal charges.

The events unfolded on 19 March 1999, when Mr. Atanasov, who is disabled and uses a prosthesis, became involved in an altercation after drinking in a bar. Following a quarrel, he punctured a car’s tires and, during a subsequent scuffle, stabbed the car’s owner. He was arrested, charged with attempted murder, and remanded in custody. Throughout the proceedings, Mr. Atanasov argued that the courts were not impartial, that his Roma origin led to discrimination, and that his detention and trial did not meet Convention standards.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 5 (right to liberty and security), 6 (right to a fair trial), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found that several complaints, including those concerning the fairness of the trial and alleged discrimination under Article 14, were inadmissible. However, it declared admissible the complaints regarding the lawfulness and review of his detention under Article 5.

This case is significant as it demonstrates the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller individuals face in accessing justice and fair treatment in criminal proceedings. It reflects broader historical patterns of marginalisation and the need for vigilance against discrimination in European legal systems.

cases.title: CASE OF SEJDOVIC v. ITALY
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection rejected (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 6;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient;Costs and expenses partial award - domestic proceedings;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary: In Sejdovic v. Italy, the applicant, Mr. Cloce Sejdovic, identified as a member of the Roma and Travellers community, brought a case against Italy after being convicted in absentia for murder and illegal possession of a weapon. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face barriers to fair trial rights, especially when proceedings occur without their presence or effective participation. On 8 September 1992, a fatal shooting took place at a travellers’ encampment in Rome. Mr. Sejdovic, then untraceable, was declared a fugitive by Italian authorities and tried in his absence. He was assigned a lawyer, but was never personally notified of the charges or the trial. In 1996, he was convicted and sentenced to over twenty-one years in prison. Years later, after his arrest in Germany, Italian authorities sought his extradition, but German courts refused, citing concerns about his right to a retrial. The European Court of Human Rights examined Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and found a violation, noting that Mr. Sejdovic had not been given a genuine opportunity to defend himself or to have his case reheard. The Court awarded partial costs and expenses, finding the acknowledgment of the violation sufficient for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant as it reinforces the right to a fair trial for Roma and Travellers, who have historically faced exclusion and procedural disadvantages in European justice systems.

cases.title: CASE OF OGNYANOVA AND CHOBAN v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violations of Art. 2;Violation of Art. 3;Violation of Art. 5-1;Violation of Art. 13;No violation of Art. 14;Non-pecuniary damage - financial awards;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In the case of Ognyanova and Choban v. Bulgaria, the applicants, Ms. Zoya Kirilova Ognyanova and Ms. Giulfere Yusein Choban, both Bulgarian nationals of Roma ethnic origin, brought a complaint against Bulgaria following the death of Mr. Zahari Alexandrov Stefanov, also of Roma origin. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective state protection, particularly in situations involving deprivation of liberty.

On 4 June 1993, Mr. Stefanov, aged twenty-three, was arrested by police in Muglizh, Bulgaria, on suspicion of theft and taken to the Kazanluk police station. The following day, while handcuffed and being questioned in a third-floor office, he fell from a window and died from his injuries. The authorities concluded that he had jumped voluntarily, but the applicants—his de facto spouse and mother—contested this, alleging that he died as a result of police ill-treatment and that the investigation into his death was inadequate and ineffective.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 5 (right to liberty and security), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found Bulgaria in violation of Articles 2, 3, 5, and 13, awarding non-pecuniary damages and partial costs to the applicants, but did not find a violation of Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination).

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the persistent risks of police abuse and impunity faced by Roma communities in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation and inadequate state response to violence against Roma individuals.

cases.title: CASE OF D.H. AND OTHERS v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 14+P1-2
cases.summary: In the case of D.H. and Others v. the Czech Republic, the applicants were a group of children of Roma origin, representing the Roma and Travellers community, who brought a complaint against the Czech Republic. The heart of the case was the vulnerability of Roma children to systemic discrimination in education, specifically their disproportionate placement in special schools intended for pupils with learning disabilities. Between 1996 and 1999, the applicants were placed in such special schools in Ostrava, often following psychological assessments and with parental consent, though the applicants later argued that their parents had not been fully informed of the consequences. The applicants contended that this practice resulted in de facto segregation, as Roma children were overwhelmingly represented in these schools, which offered an inferior curriculum and limited future opportunities. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), but in its 2006 Chamber judgment, found no violation, concluding that the procedures had been followed and there was insufficient evidence of discrimination. This decision was significant as it highlighted the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in accessing equal education in Europe, reflecting a long history of segregation and marginalisation; the case would later be reconsidered by the Grand Chamber, marking a turning point in European anti-discrimination jurisprudence.

cases.title: CODONA v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Codona v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mrs. Leanne Codona, is a British national who identifies as a Gypsy, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Her case concerned the difficulties faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing accommodation that respects their cultural traditions, specifically the right to live in caravans rather than conventional housing. Mrs. Codona and her extended family had lived in caravans on a site in Bedfordshire from 1997, but faced repeated enforcement actions by the local council for breaching planning regulations. After a series of planning applications, appeals, and legal proceedings, the council ultimately obtained an injunction requiring the family to leave the site. When Mrs. Codona applied for housing as a homeless person, the only accommodation offered was in “bricks and mortar,” which she could not accept due to her cultural aversion to such housing.

The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaint under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found the application inadmissible, holding that Article 8 does not impose a positive obligation on states to provide a specific type of accommodation, such as a caravan site, especially where no such sites are available. The Court reaffirmed that while states must facilitate the Roma and Traveller way of life, this does not extend to creating new caravan sites to meet demand.

This decision is significant as it clarifies the limits of positive obligations under Article 8 regarding accommodation for Roma and Travellers, following the precedent set in Chapman v. the United Kingdom, and highlights the ongoing challenges these communities face in securing culturally appropriate housing in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF BEKOS AND KOUTROPOULOS v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Violations of Art. 3;No separate issue under Art. 13;No violation of Art. 14+3 (alleged racist treatment);Violation of Art. 14+3 (failure to investigate possible racist motives);Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award
cases.summary:
In the case of Bekos and Koutropoulos v. Greece, the applicants, Mr. Bekos and Mr. Koutroupoulos, are Greek nationals of Roma origin living in Mesolonghi, Western Greece. Their case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the failure of authorities to investigate possible racist motives behind such abuse. On 8 May 1998, following an attempted burglary, the two young men were arrested by police officers. Both applicants alleged that, during and after their arrest, they were subjected to repeated beatings, threats, and degrading treatment at the police station, including racist insults and threats of sexual violence. Medical evidence confirmed that they had suffered significant injuries consistent with their accounts.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. The Court found that both applicants had been subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment by the police, in violation of Article 3, and that the authorities had failed to investigate whether racist motives played a role, violating Article 14 taken with Article 3. However, the Court did not find a separate violation of Article 14 and Article 3 regarding the alleged racist treatment itself. The applicants were awarded compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent problem of police violence and impunity affecting Roma and Travellers in Europe, and it reinforces the obligation of states to investigate possible racist motives in cases of ill-treatment, reflecting ongoing concerns about systemic discrimination against Roma communities.

cases.title: AFFAIRE BEKOS ET KOUTROPOULOS c. GRECE [Extraits]
cases.conclusion: Violations de l'art. 3;Aucune question distincte au regard de l'art. 13;Non-violation de l'art. 14+3 (allégation de traitement raciste);Violation de l'art. 14+3 (absence d'investigations concernant de possibles motifs racistes)
cases.summary:
In the case of Bekos and Koutropoulos v. Greece, the applicants, Mr. Bekos and Mr. Koutropoulos, are Greek nationals of Roma origin residing in Missolonghi, western Greece. Their case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the failure of authorities to investigate possible racist motives behind such abuse. On the night of 8 May 1998, following an attempted burglary, the two applicants were arrested by police. Both men alleged that, during and after their arrest, they were subjected to severe physical abuse and degrading treatment by several police officers, including beatings with batons, punches, threats of sexual violence, and repeated racist insults referencing their Roma identity. Medical reports confirmed that both men sustained injuries consistent with their accounts. Despite their complaints, the Greek authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the alleged ill-treatment or to consider whether racist motives played a role.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. The Court found that Greece had violated Article 3 due to the police ill-treatment and further violated Article 14 taken with Article 3 for failing to investigate possible racist motives. However, it did not find a separate violation of Article 14 and Article 3 regarding the allegation of racially motivated treatment itself. The applicants were awarded just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage.

This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent problem of police violence against Roma and Travellers in Europe and the critical need for authorities to investigate potential racist motives, reflecting a broader historical context of discrimination and marginalisation faced by these communities in Greece and beyond.

cases.title: TODOROV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Partly admissible;Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Todorov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Tanko Zaprianov Todorov, identified himself as being of Roma ethnic origin and lived in the village of Chalakovi. He brought a case against Bulgaria, alleging ill-treatment by police and procedural violations during his detention and trial. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police abuse and the risk of coerced confessions, a recurring concern for Roma and Traveller communities across Europe. On 11 December 1997, following a murder in his village, Mr. Todorov was arrested, questioned by police, and signed a confession which he later retracted, claiming it was obtained under duress and physical abuse. Despite his allegations, the authorities did not open a thorough investigation into his claims of ill-treatment. He was charged with murder, held in pre-trial detention, and eventually convicted after a lengthy process, during which he continued to assert that his confession was not voluntary.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and 5 (right to liberty and security) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found parts of the application admissible but did not ultimately find a violation of Article 3 regarding ill-treatment or lack of investigation, nor did it find a violation of Article 5 concerning the lawfulness of his detention. No remedies were awarded.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma individuals face in securing protection from police abuse and ensuring fair treatment in criminal proceedings. It reflects the broader historical context of mistrust and marginalisation experienced by Roma and Traveller communities within European justice systems.

cases.title: BORISOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Borisov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were five Bulgarian nationals—Mr Boris Petkov Borisov, Mr Georgi Alexandrov Kirilov, Ms Iskra Borisova Mladenova, Mr Tassi Tsenov Tassev, and Mr Petko Borisov Traikov—along with the Roma Church in Bulgaria, an organisation they founded. All individual applicants identified as Roma, and their organisation aimed to serve the religious needs of the Roma community in Lom. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma individuals seeking to exercise their religious freedom, facing repeated police interference and obstacles to official recognition of their religious group.

Between 1997 and 1999, the applicants’ religious gatherings in Lom were frequently disrupted by police, who warned them that unregistered religious activities were not permitted and ordered them to disperse. In 1998, Mr Borisov was detained for a week and questioned about his religious activities, and the prayer house they used was locked by police. After founding the Roma Church in Bulgaria in 1999, the applicants sought registration as a religious denomination, but their application was met with bureaucratic delays and requests for further information, ultimately leading to the Supreme Administrative Court rejecting their appeal as premature.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 9 (freedom of religion), 11 (freedom of assembly), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court decided to adjourn examination of the complaints regarding disruption of religious meetings and registration, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

This case highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller communities face in exercising religious and associational rights, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation and the need for effective legal remedies in post-communist Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS  v. ROMANIA (No. 2)
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 8;Violation of Art. 3;No violation of Art. 6-1 (access to court);Violation of Art. 6-1 (length of proceedings);Violation of Art. 14+6;Violation of Art. 14+8;Pecuniary damage - financial award;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award
cases.summary:
In Moldovan and Others v. Romania (No. 2), the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin who had lived in the village of Hădăreni, Mureş district. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of state authorities to protect them. On 20 September 1993, following a fatal altercation in a village bar, a mob of non-Roma villagers, joined by local police officers, attacked Roma residents. Three Roma men were killed—two beaten to death and one burned alive—while the mob, with police complicity, destroyed thirteen Roma homes and property. Many Roma families, including the applicants, were left homeless, and some were forced to flee the village or live in dire conditions for years. Despite clear evidence, the authorities failed to properly investigate or prosecute those responsible, particularly among the police, and the reconstruction of homes was inadequate and marred by mismanagement.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 6 (right to a fair trial, specifically the excessive length of proceedings), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Articles 6 and 8. The Court awarded both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. This landmark judgment is significant as it exposed the systemic discrimination and violence faced by Roma and Traveller communities in post-communist Romania, setting a precedent for state accountability in protecting minority rights across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF NACHOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 2 (deaths);Violation of Art. 2 (failure to conduct an effective investigation);No separate issue under Art. 13;No violation of Art. 14+2 (alleged act of racial violence);Violation of Art. 14+2 (failure to investigate possible racist motives);Pecuniary damage - financial award;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In Nachova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin: Ms. Anelia Kunchova Nachova, her mother Ms. Aksiniya Hristova, and Mr. Todorka and Mr. Rangel Rangelov, the parents of the second victim. The case concerned the fatal shooting of two young Roma men, Mr. Angelov and Mr. Petkov, by a military police officer during an attempted arrest. The vulnerability at the heart of the case was the exposure of Roma individuals to excessive and potentially lethal force by law enforcement, compounded by the failure to investigate possible racist motives behind such actions.

On 19 July 1996, in the Roma district of Lesura, Bulgaria, military police sought to arrest Mr. Angelov and Mr. Petkov, both 21-year-old conscripts who had escaped from a work site. Neither man was armed. During the operation, after warnings and shots fired in the air, Major G. fired directly at the fleeing men, killing both. The subsequent investigation failed to consider whether racism played a role in the use of lethal force.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 (right to life) for both the deaths and the lack of an effective investigation, and a violation of Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) taken with Article 2, specifically for failing to investigate possible racist motives. The Court awarded both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages to the applicants.

This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it established the duty of states to investigate not only the facts of lethal force but also any potential racist motives, against a backdrop of longstanding discrimination against Roma communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS  v. ROMANIA (No. 1)
cases.conclusion: Partly struck out of the list (friendly settlement);Severed and adjourned as regards seven applicants
cases.summary:
In Moldovan and Others v. Romania (No. 1), the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin from the village of Hădăreni, who brought a case against the Romanian state. The case centred on the extreme vulnerability of the Roma community following a violent outbreak in September 1993, when a dispute escalated into the killing of three Roma men and the destruction of Roma homes by a local mob, with the alleged involvement and encouragement of police officers. Over the course of one night, thirteen Roma houses were completely destroyed and several more badly damaged, forcing families to live for years in deplorable conditions such as animal shelters, cellars, and overcrowded, unheated rooms. Many applicants and their families suffered serious health consequences as a result.

Despite criminal and civil proceedings in Romania, the applicants faced inadequate investigations, lenient sentences for perpetrators, and insufficient compensation for their losses. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case was partly resolved through a friendly settlement, with the Romanian government agreeing to pay €262,000 in compensation and to implement measures to combat discrimination and improve conditions for Roma in Hădăreni.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, particularly regarding violence, discrimination, and state failure to protect their rights—a pattern rooted in a long history of marginalisation.

cases.title: BERISHA AND HALJITI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary: In Berisha and Haljiti v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants, Dzavit Berisha and Baljie Haljiti, are nationals of Serbia and Montenegro of Balkan Egyptian origin—a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Balkan Egyptian minorities in Kosovo, particularly the threats, harassment, and discrimination they faced due to their ethnicity and Mr. Berisha’s involvement in Roma rights advocacy. After marrying in 1999, the couple fled escalating violence in Kosovo, including threats of rape and forced expulsion by the Kosovo Liberation Army, and sought refuge in Macedonia. Despite repeated asylum applications, Macedonian authorities rejected their claims, finding their fears insufficiently substantiated, and ultimately expelled them after a failed attempt to cross into Greece. The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 6 (right to a fair trial), citing both the risk of persecution upon return and procedural shortcomings in the asylum and expulsion process. The European Court of Human Rights declared most complaints inadmissible, finding no evidence that the Macedonian authorities had failed to consider their individual circumstances or that the expulsion amounted to inhuman treatment. This case highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Balkan Egyptian minorities in seeking protection from ethnic violence and underscores the importance of effective asylum procedures in the context of post-conflict Kosovo.

cases.title: GERGELY v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Gergely v. Romania, the applicant, Mrs. Iren Gergely, is a Romanian national of Roma origin who lived in Caşinul Nou, Harghita County. Represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, she brought a case against Romania concerning the violent expulsion and destruction of Roma homes in her community. The harm at the centre of the case was the targeted attack against Roma residents, who faced arson, threats to their lives, and the loss of their homes and belongings, leaving around 150 people homeless and exposing them to severe danger and trauma.

On the evening of 11 August 1990, following rising tensions and accusations against local Roma, a large group of non-Roma villagers gathered, tolled the church bells, and proceeded to burn and destroy Roma houses, including Mrs. Gergely’s. She and her four children fled and hid in a field, witnessing the destruction. Despite immediate complaints and identification of some perpetrators, the authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation, repeatedly discontinuing proceedings and ultimately blaming the Roma victims for provoking the violence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under several articles, including Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The case was declared admissible, but the judgment does not specify violations or remedies at this stage.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to collective violence and the failure of state authorities to provide protection or justice, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination and impunity in Europe.

cases.title: TANASE AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Tanase and Others v. Romania, the applicants were 24 Romanian nationals of Roma origin, all formerly residents of the village of Bolintin Deal in Giurgiu County. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to collective violence and state inaction, focusing on the destruction of their homes and the long-term deprivation that followed. On the night of 6–7 April 1991, after a Roma individual killed a non-Roma villager, a large mob—encouraged by local officials—attacked Roma homes, burning and destroying over twenty houses and forcing the entire Roma community to flee. Further attacks occurred in May 1991 when Roma families attempted to return, resulting in additional homes being set alight. The authorities failed to protect the applicants’ property or ensure their safe return, and the Roma community remained displaced, facing ongoing discrimination, lack of legal residence, and denial of access to essential services.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court declared the case admissible, recognising the serious issues raised, but had not yet issued a final judgment on violations or remedies at the time of this decision.

This case is significant as it exposes the persistent risks of mob violence, forced displacement, and institutional neglect faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of exclusion and discrimination that continues to demand robust legal protection.

cases.title: KALANYOS AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Kalanyos and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Sandor Kalanyos, Tamas Kalanyos, and Istvan Rozsa—are Romanian nationals of Roma origin living in the hamlet of Plăieşii de Sus, Harghita County. Their case highlights the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to violent collective reprisals and the failure of state protection. The events began on 6 June 1991, when a fight broke out between four Roma men, including the first applicant, and a nightwatchman. Following this, non-Roma villagers launched a revenge attack, fatally injuring one Roma man and seriously harming another. On 8 June, a public notice threatened the burning of Roma homes, prompting the Roma, including the applicants, to seek police protection. Instead of intervening, local authorities advised the Roma to flee. On 9 June 1991, non-Roma villagers cut off electricity and communications before setting fire to all twenty-seven Roma houses in the settlement, leaving the applicants and their families homeless and forced to live in stables under dire conditions for a year.

Despite clear evidence and witness statements, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, ultimately closing the case without identifying or prosecuting the perpetrators. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The case was declared admissible, but the judgment focused on the admissibility rather than a finding of violation at this stage.

This case is significant as it exposes the persistent pattern of anti-Roma violence and impunity in post-communist Europe, underscoring the urgent need for effective state protection and accountability for crimes targeting Roma and Traveller communities.

cases.title: BERISHA & OTHERS v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Berisha and Others v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants—Redjep and Djezide Berisha, along with Djafer, Shanie, and Jashar Berisha—were Yugoslav nationals of Romany origin, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma families fleeing ethnic violence and facing the threat of expulsion to a region where they risked persecution. In June and July 1999, both families were forced to flee Kosovo after being threatened, attacked, and, in one instance, physically assaulted by armed individuals in KLA uniforms. After entering Macedonia, they were granted temporary humanitarian status but were later arrested for attempting to cross into Bulgaria with forged passports. Following a swift trial, they received suspended sentences and were ordered expelled, raising fears of return to life-threatening conditions.

The applicants complained under Articles 2 and 3 (right to life and prohibition of ill-treatment), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 6 (fair trial rights) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the European Court of Human Rights found the application inadmissible: the expulsion orders were annulled, and the applicants remained in Macedonia, so they could no longer claim to be victims. The Court also found no arguable claim under Article 13 and noted that the criminal convictions had been quashed, rendering the Article 6 complaints moot.

This case illustrates the precarious situation of Roma and Traveller families displaced by conflict and the procedural hurdles they face in seeking protection. It reflects the broader historical context of Roma vulnerability in post-conflict Europe and the challenges in securing effective remedies through national and international legal systems.

cases.title: CASE OF SIDJIMOV v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 6-1;Violation of Art. 13;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In Sidjimov v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mr. Sidjimov, identified as a member of the Roma community and lived in Pazardjik, Bulgaria. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to protracted criminal proceedings, which can exacerbate social marginalisation and mistrust in the justice system. Mr. Sidjimov was arrested in August 1993, along with six other Roma individuals, on charges related to the rape of a minor, and was held in pre-trial detention before being released on bail in 1995. Despite the gravity of the charges, the investigation and prosecution were marked by repeated delays, referrals, and periods of inactivity, with the proceedings remaining unresolved for over eleven years as of 2004.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found violations of both articles, noting that the excessive length of the proceedings and the lack of effective remedies for such delays constituted a denial of justice. The Court awarded partial costs and expenses to the applicant.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the need for timely and effective justice, particularly for minority groups historically subjected to systemic discrimination and procedural neglect in many European countries.

cases.title: OGNYANOVA AND CHOBAN v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Ognyanova and Choban v. Bulgaria, the applicants, Ms. Zoya Kirilova Ognyanova and Ms. Giulfere Yusein Choban, are Bulgarian nationals of Roma ethnic origin from the village of Dabovo. Their complaint arose from the death of Mr. Zahari Alexandrov Stefanov, also of Roma origin, who was Ms. Ognyanova’s de facto spouse and Ms. Choban’s son. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective investigations into deaths in custody, particularly where ethnic bias may be present.

On 4 June 1993, Mr. Stefanov was arrested by police in Nikolaevo, suspected of theft, and taken to the Kazanlak police station. The following morning, while handcuffed and being questioned, he fell from a third-floor window and died from his injuries. The authorities concluded that he had jumped in an escape attempt, but the applicants contested this, alleging that his fall was either provoked by torture or was an attempt by police to cover up ill-treatment. They also argued that the investigation into his death was neither thorough nor impartial.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of torture), 5 (right to liberty and security), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court found the application admissible, signalling the seriousness of the allegations, but the final judgment on violations was not included in the admissibility decision.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in police custody and the importance of effective, unbiased investigations into deaths involving minority groups. Historically, Roma communities in Bulgaria and across Europe have faced systemic discrimination, making judicial scrutiny of such cases crucial for advancing minority rights and accountability.

cases.title: BEKOS AND KOUTROPOULOS v. GREECE
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary: In the case of Bekos and Koutroupoulos v. Greece, the applicants, Mr. Lazaros Bekos and Mr. Eleftherios Koutroupoulos, are Greek citizens belonging to the Roma community, represented by the European Roma Rights Center and the Greek Helsinki Monitor. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and discrimination, particularly in the context of criminal proceedings. On 8 May 1998, in Mesolonghi, Western Greece, the two young Roma men were arrested by police responding to an attempted burglary. Both applicants alleged that, following their arrest, they were subjected to severe physical abuse and degrading treatment by police officers, including beatings with truncheons, threats of sexual assault, and repeated racist insults referencing their Roma origin. Medical evidence documented significant injuries, and the applicants reported hearing each other’s cries during their detention. Despite their complaints, the investigation by Greek authorities was limited, and only one officer received a minor penalty. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention. The Court declared the application admissible, recognising the serious issues raised regarding police ill-treatment and possible ethnic discrimination. This case is significant as it reflects the persistent challenges Roma communities face in Europe, particularly regarding police abuse and the lack of effective remedies, against a backdrop of longstanding discrimination.

cases.title: BEKOS ET KOUTROPOULOS c. GRECE
cases.conclusion: Recevable
cases.summary:
In the case of Bekos and Koutropoulos v. Greece, the applicants, Mr. Lazaros Bekos and Mr. Eleftherios Koutropoulos, are Greek nationals of Roma origin residing in Missolonghi, western Greece. Their case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and discrimination, particularly in situations of arrest and detention. On the night of 8 May 1998, following an attempted break-in at a kiosk, the two young Roma men were apprehended by police. They alleged that, after being handcuffed, they were subjected to repeated beatings, threats, and degrading treatment by several police officers both at the scene and later at the police station. The applicants also reported being insulted about their Roma origin and suffering physical injuries, which were documented by a forensic doctor the following day. Despite their complaints, the investigation into the police conduct was, according to the applicants, ineffective and insufficient, and they claimed to have been intimidated into withdrawing their complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court declared the application admissible, finding that the allegations raised serious questions of fact and law requiring a full examination. This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in Europe regarding police abuse and the lack of effective remedies, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination and marginalisation.

cases.title: CASE OF SEJDOVIC v. ITALY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 6;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient;Costs and expenses (national proceedings) - claim dismissed;Costs and expenses award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary: In the case of Sejdovic v. Italy, the applicant, Mr. Cloce (or Kroce) Sejdovic, identified in the proceedings as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against Italy. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face barriers to justice, particularly when living in encampments and subject to negative stereotypes about evading legal processes. On 8 September 1992, following a fatal shooting at a Roma encampment in Rome, Mr. Sejdovic was identified by witnesses as the alleged perpetrator. Unable to locate him, Italian authorities declared him a fugitive and assigned him a lawyer, proceeding to try him in absentia. In July 1996, Mr. Sejdovic was convicted of manslaughter and illegal possession of a weapon, receiving a sentence of over twenty-one years, without ever having been notified of the charges or able to participate in his defence. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial), finding a violation due to the applicant’s conviction in absentia without effective notification or opportunity to defend himself. The Court considered the finding of a violation sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the importance of procedural safeguards and fair trial guarantees, especially for historically marginalised groups who are at heightened risk of exclusion from justice.

cases.title: WARD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Ward v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Martin Ward, is an Irish national and a member of the Traveller community, living with his family in a caravan on the Westway Travellers’ Site in London. Mr. Ward’s case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller groups who are often forced to reside in substandard and hazardous environments due to a lack of suitable accommodation options. Since 1972, Mr. Ward and his family lived on a site situated directly beneath motorway flyovers and adjacent to a railway, exposing them to persistent noise and air pollution. Environmental health reports in 1992 and 2002 confirmed that the site was unsuitable for residential use, citing high nitrogen dioxide levels and intrusive noise, yet the local authority did not relocate the residents, opting instead for site refurbishment.

Mr. Ward argued that these living conditions, and the authorities’ failure to relocate the site, violated his rights under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights found the application inadmissible, concluding that the harm did not reach the severity required under Article 3, and that Article 8 was not violated, as the applicant had voluntarily chosen to remain on the site and had not demonstrated a lack of alternatives.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in securing safe and adequate housing, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in Europe, even as legal protections have evolved since the late twentieth century.

cases.title: CASE OF MOLNAR v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 6-1 with regard to the length of the proceedings;Inadmissible under Art. 6-1 with regard to the fairness of the proceedings, Art. 13 and 14;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses award - domestic proceedings;Costs and expenses award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In the case of Molnar v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms. Molnar, a member of the Roma ethnic minority, brought a complaint against Hungary concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face systemic barriers in accessing justice and timely legal remedies. Ms. Molnar, born in 1943 and residing in Budapest, initiated legal action on 3 October 1996 to have a flat she had purchased vacated. However, the proceedings became entangled in a parallel dispute over the validity of the sale contract, leading to repeated suspensions and delays. Despite her efforts to resolve administrative obstacles—such as the misplacement of the original contract by the authorities—the case remained unresolved for nearly eight years, with the courts failing to deliver a timely decision.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The Court found a violation of this provision, noting that the length of the proceedings was excessive and unjustified. Ms. Molnar was awarded €6,000 for non-pecuniary damage and €392 for costs and expenses. This judgment is significant as it reaffirms the right of Roma and Traveller individuals to timely justice, addressing a persistent issue of judicial delay that has historically affected these communities across Europe.

cases.title: CARABULEA v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary: In Carabulea v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Carabulea, a Romanian national of Roma origin, brought a case against the Romanian state concerning the death of his brother, Gabriel Carabulea, while in police custody. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to ill-treatment and inadequate protection by law enforcement, particularly in situations involving deprivation of liberty. On 13 April 1996, Gabriel Carabulea was arrested in Bucharest by police officers, initially for alleged robbery and possession of counterfeit currency. After his arrest, he was detained in a police lock-up, where he reportedly appeared in good health. However, within days, Gabriel’s health deteriorated rapidly; he complained of pain and weakness, was transferred between several hospitals, and ultimately died on 16 April 1996. The applicant alleged that his brother’s death resulted from police ill-treatment and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of torture), 6 (right to a fair trial), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, declaring the application admissible. This case is significant as it underscores the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in police custody and the importance of thorough, impartial investigations into deaths in detention, reflecting broader concerns about systemic discrimination in post-communist Europe.

cases.title: OLAH v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Oláh v. Hungary, the applicant, Mrs. Józsefné Oláh, a Hungarian national of Roma origin, brought a case against Hungary following the fatal shooting of her Roma husband, Mr. Oláh, by a police officer in Budapest. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to excessive use of force by law enforcement and the challenges they face in seeking accountability for such incidents. On the night of 24 July 1997, Mr. Oláh and an accomplice were pursued by Sergeant L.T. after allegedly stealing a car radio near the French Embassy. Despite repeated orders to stop and two warning shots, Mr. Oláh continued to flee. In a dark courtyard, as Mr. Oláh made a sudden movement, Sergeant L.T. fired a shot that struck Mr. Oláh in the chest, leading to his death two days later. Administrative and criminal proceedings were initiated against the officer, but both concluded that the use of force had been lawful, and Sergeant L.T. was acquitted. Mrs. Oláh alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3, 6, 13, 14, and 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights, but the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible. This case underscores the persistent difficulties Roma and Traveller families encounter in obtaining effective remedies for deaths involving state agents, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF BALOGH v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Préliminary objection rejected (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 3;No violation of Art. 13;No violation of Art. 6-1;No violation of Art. 14;Pecuniary damage - financial award;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In the case of Balogh v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. Balogh, is a Hungarian national of Roma ethnic origin living in Miskolc. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the difficulties they face in obtaining justice for ill-treatment by state authorities. On 9 August 1995, while selling coal door-to-door in Orosháza, Mr. Balogh and his companions were taken to the local police station following a dispute over fuel vouchers. During police interrogation, Mr. Balogh was repeatedly slapped and punched by officers, resulting in a traumatic perforation of his left eardrum, which later required surgery and led to partial hearing loss. Witnesses confirmed seeing visible injuries on his face and ear immediately after his release, and a police officer reportedly warned them not to let “Miskolc gypsies” return to Orosháza. Despite medical evidence and witness testimony, the domestic investigation was discontinued for lack of conclusive proof, and the authorities failed to provide a plausible alternative explanation for his injuries.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and found a violation, awarding Mr. Balogh both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. The Court found no violation of Articles 6, 13, or 14. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent risks of police ill-treatment faced by Roma in Europe and the importance of effective investigations, reflecting a broader historical context of discrimination against Roma and Travellers.

cases.title: CASE OF CONNORS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 8;No separate issue under Art. 14+8;No separate issue under P1-1;No separate issue under Art. 6;No violation of Art. 6;No violation of Art. 13;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In Connors v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Thomas Connors, identified as a member of the Gypsy community—a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers—brought a case against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families to eviction from local authority caravan sites, often without sufficient procedural safeguards or consideration of their unique way of life. Mr. Connors and his family had lived for many years on the Cottingley Springs caravan site in Leeds, managed by the local council. After disputes with the council over site conditions and allegations of nuisance involving family members and visitors, the council served the Connors family with a notice to quit in January 2000, leading to their eviction. The family was not provided with detailed reasons for the eviction, nor were they given a meaningful opportunity to challenge the allegations in court.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found a violation of Article 8, ruling that the eviction was not “necessary in a democratic society” because the legal framework did not provide adequate procedural safeguards for the Connors family to contest the eviction or for the proportionality of the measure to be assessed. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages and partial costs to Mr. Connors.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it recognised the heightened vulnerability of these communities to arbitrary eviction and underscored the need for legal protections that respect their traditional lifestyles. Historically, Roma and Travellers in the United Kingdom and across Europe have faced systemic barriers to secure accommodation and equal treatment, making this decision a landmark in advancing their housing rights.

cases.title: AFFAIRE CONNORS c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'art. 8;Aucune question distincte au regard de l'art. 14+8;Aucune question distincte au regard de P1-1;Aucune question distincte au regard de l'art. 6;Non-violation de l'art. 6;Non-violation de l'art. 13;Préjudice moral - réparation pécuniaire;Remboursement partiel frais et dépens - procédure de la Convention
cases.summary:
In Connors v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Thomas Connors, is a member of the Gypsy community—a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers—who brought a case against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing eviction from public caravan sites, often without adequate procedural safeguards or consideration of their traditional way of life. Mr. Connors and his family had lived for many years on the Cottingley Springs municipal caravan site in Leeds, but in 2000, following disputes with the local council and allegations of antisocial behaviour by some family members and visitors, the council terminated their licence and sought their eviction. The family was ordered to leave without being given detailed reasons or a meaningful opportunity to challenge the allegations in court.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life and home. The Court found a violation of Article 8, ruling that the eviction process lacked sufficient procedural safeguards and failed to balance the needs of the Connors family as a vulnerable minority. The Court awarded Mr. Connors compensation for non-pecuniary damage and partial costs.

This judgment is significant as it was the first time the Court found the United Kingdom in breach of Article 8 in the context of Roma and Traveller accommodation, marking a turning point in the recognition of the specific rights and vulnerabilities of these communities in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF NACHOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Violation of Article 14+2 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 2-1 - Life;Effective investigation;Article 2 - Right to life);Pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage - award
cases.summary:
In Nachova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants—Ms. Anelia Kunchova Nachova, her mother Ms. Aksiniya Hristova, and Mr. and Ms. Rangelov—are Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin who brought a case against Bulgaria following the fatal shooting of their relatives, Mr. Angelov and Mr. Petkov. The case highlights the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to excessive use of force by law enforcement, particularly in situations where negative stereotypes and discriminatory attitudes may influence official conduct.

On 19 July 1996, Mr. Angelov and Mr. Petkov, both young Roma conscripts, were shot and killed by a military police officer during an attempted arrest in the Roma district of Lesura, Bulgaria. The two men, unarmed and fleeing after escaping from a work site, were pursued by armed officers who had been instructed to use all necessary means to apprehend them. Despite the absence of any threat to life or serious violence, the officer fired multiple shots, resulting in both men’s deaths.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 (right to life), both substantively and procedurally, as well as Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2. The Court held that the use of lethal force was not absolutely necessary and that the investigation failed to address possible racist motives or provide accountability. The applicants were awarded pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

This landmark judgment is significant for Roma rights, as it was among the first to recognise the intersection of lethal force and racial discrimination against Roma and Travellers in Europe, reflecting a broader historical context of systemic marginalisation and impunity.

cases.title: AFFAIRE NATCHOVA ET AUTRES c. BULGARIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'article 2 - Droit à la vie (Article 2-1 - Vie) (Volet matériel);Violation de l'article 2 - Droit à la vie (Article 2-1 - Enquête efficace) (Volet procédural);Violation de l'article 14+2 - Interdiction de la discrimination (Article 2-1 - Vie;Enquête efficace;Article 2 - Droit à la vie);Dommage matériel et préjudice moral - réparation
cases.summary:
In the case of Nachova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin, including Ms. Anelia Kuntchova Natchova, her mother Ms. Aksiniya Hristova, and the parents of Mr. Petkov, all identifying as Roma. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to lethal force and discriminatory treatment by law enforcement, particularly the risk of excessive violence and lack of accountability in police operations involving Roma individuals.

On 19 July 1996, in the village of Lesura, Bulgaria, two young Roma men, Mr. Angelov and Mr. Petkov, who had escaped from a prison worksite, were located by military police. During the attempted arrest, a police officer shot and killed both men, who were unarmed and fleeing. The subsequent investigation by Bulgarian authorities was marked by a lack of thoroughness and failed to address possible racist motives, despite references to the victims’ Roma background in official documents.

The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Article 2 (right to life), both in its substantive and procedural aspects, and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2. The Court found that Bulgaria had violated the right to life by using excessive force and by failing to conduct an effective investigation, particularly into possible racist motives. The applicants were awarded compensation for material and moral damages.

This judgment is significant as it was the first time the Court explicitly recognised the obligation to investigate potential racist motives in cases involving lethal force against Roma, reflecting a broader historical context of police violence and systemic discrimination against Roma and Travellers across Europe.

cases.title: HALITI and OTHERS v. DENMARK
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Haliti and Others v. Denmark, the applicants—Murat Haliti, Gjylperian Haliti, and their three children—are nationals of Serbia and Montenegro of Roma origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. Their case against Denmark focused on the vulnerability of Roma and related groups facing persecution and harassment in Kosovo, particularly after the 1999 conflict, and the risk of inhuman or degrading treatment if returned. The Haliti family entered Denmark in July 2001, seeking asylum due to past violence, including a beating by the Kosovo Liberation Army and ongoing harassment and threats upon their return to Kosovo. Danish authorities denied their asylum claim, finding that the incidents described did not meet the threshold for persecution and that the general security situation in Kosovo, with international protection present, did not pose a concrete risk to them. The European Court of Human Rights examined their complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but declared the application inadmissible. The Court found no evidence of a real risk of ill-treatment upon return and noted that domestic remedies were still pending. This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and related communities face in seeking international protection, especially in the context of post-conflict Kosovo and evolving European asylum standards.

cases.title: HIDA v. DENMARK
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Hida v. Denmark, the applicant, Muhammad Hida, a national of Serbia and Montenegro of Roma origin, brought a case against Denmark after his asylum application was refused. Mr. Hida, his spouse (according to Roma traditions), and their son entered Denmark in February 2001, fleeing Kosovo after suffering violence and harassment due to their Roma identity. He claimed that, as a Roma, he had faced persecution in Kosovo and Serbia since 1995, including beatings by the Kosovo Liberation Army, and argued that returning would expose him and his family to further harm.

The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and related groups, who have historically faced discrimination, violence, and exclusion in the Balkans, particularly during and after the Kosovo conflict. Mr. Hida’s asylum and humanitarian residence requests were denied by Danish authorities, who found inconsistencies in his account and concluded that the incidents described did not meet the threshold for persecution under Danish law. They also noted improvements in Kosovo’s security situation and suggested he could safely reside elsewhere in Serbia and Montenegro.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case primarily under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), but declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that, while the general situation for Roma in Kosovo remained difficult, Mr. Hida had not demonstrated a real and personal risk of ill-treatment if returned. This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Travellers face in securing international protection, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation and the high evidentiary threshold required for asylum claims in Europe.

cases.title: KALANYOS AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary: In Kalanyos and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Sandor Kalanyos, Tamas Kalanyos, and Istvan Rozsa—are Romanian nationals of Roma origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The case highlights the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of state authorities to protect them or provide justice. In June 1991, following a dispute in the hamlet of Plăieşii de Sus, Harghita County, tensions escalated after a non-Roma night-watchman insulted Roma individuals, leading to a fight and subsequent police detention of the first applicant. In retaliation, non-Roma villagers assaulted two Roma men, resulting in the death of Adam Kalanyos, the uncle of two applicants. Shortly after, a public threat was posted warning that Roma homes would be burned. Despite being informed, local authorities failed to intervene and instead advised the Roma to flee. On 9 June 1991, non-Roma villagers destroyed all twenty-eight Roma houses by arson, forcing the applicants and their families to live in stables under inhumane conditions for a year, without compensation for their losses. Investigations by Romanian authorities were inadequate, marked by ethnic bias and eventual closure due to prescription periods, with officials blaming the victims. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found the application partly inadmissible. This case remains significant as it exposes the persistent impunity for anti-Roma violence in post-communist Europe and the systemic barriers Roma and Travellers face in accessing justice.

cases.title: GERGELY v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of Gergely v. Romania, the applicant, Ms. Iren Gergely, is a Romanian national of Roma origin who lived in the hamlet of Caşinul Nou, Harghita County. Represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, Ms. Gergely brought her case against the Romanian state, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to collective violence and the failure of authorities to protect their rights. The case arose from a violent incident on 11 August 1990, when, following rising tensions and accusations against local Roma, a large group of non-Roma villagers attacked the Roma community. The attackers burned or destroyed Roma homes, including Ms. Gergely’s, leaving around 150 people homeless and forcing families, including Ms. Gergely and her four children, to flee for their lives. Despite criminal complaints and some witness statements identifying perpetrators, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, repeatedly discontinuing proceedings and neglecting to identify those responsible. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under several articles, including Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 6 (right to a fair trial), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately found the application partly inadmissible and did not establish a violation. This case remains significant as it highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in seeking justice for ethnically motivated violence, reflecting a broader historical pattern of impunity and marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Moldovan and Others v. Romania, the applicants were 25 Romanian nationals of Roma origin, all former residents of the village of Hădăreni in Mureş county. Represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, they brought their case against the Romanian state, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma and the severe harm they suffered due to racially motivated violence and the authorities’ failure to protect them. The case arose from events on 20 September 1993, when a conflict in Hădăreni escalated into a violent mob attack against the Roma community. Following the killing of a non-Roma villager, a crowd, including local police officers, set fire to the house where three Roma men were hiding, resulting in their deaths. The violence then spread, with villagers destroying Roma homes and property, while police failed to intervene. Many Roma families were left homeless, and the subsequent state response was inadequate, with only a few houses rebuilt and many families living in dire conditions for years.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court declared the case admissible, recognising the applicants’ claims as raising serious issues under the Convention. Although this 2003 decision concerned admissibility, it marked a crucial step in acknowledging the systemic discrimination and violence faced by Roma communities in Romania. The case is significant as it brought international attention to the persistent marginalisation of Roma and Travellers in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of anti-Roma violence and state inaction.

cases.title: BALOGH v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Balogh v. Hungary, the applicant, Mr. Sándor Balogh, is a Hungarian national of Roma origin living in Miskolc, Hungary. Mr. Balogh’s case highlights the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police ill-treatment and the challenges they face in seeking justice for such abuses. On 9 August 1995, while selling coal door-to-door in Orosháza, Mr. Balogh was taken to the local police station after a dispute over fuel vouchers. During police interrogation, he alleged that officers slapped him repeatedly and punched him, demanding information about the vouchers. Following his release, witnesses observed his swollen and reddened face, and medical examinations confirmed a traumatic perforation of his left eardrum, requiring surgery and resulting in lasting hearing loss.

Despite medical evidence and witness testimony, criminal proceedings against the police officers were discontinued due to inconclusive evidence, and Mr. Balogh’s subsequent attempts to seek compensation were rejected on procedural grounds. He complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), alleging police brutality, lack of effective investigation, and discrimination based on his Roma identity. The Court found the application admissible, recognising the seriousness of the allegations and the procedural barriers faced.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent obstacles Roma and Traveller communities encounter in accessing justice and protection from ill-treatment, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination in post-communist Europe during the 1990s.

cases.title: DAVIES et AUTRES contre la ROUMANIE
cases.conclusion: Irrecevable
cases.summary:
In Davies and Others v. Romania, the applicants were a British family—husband, wife, and four children—who settled in Miercurea-Ciuc, Transylvania, in 1990. While not themselves Roma or Travellers, the applicants became involved in supporting disadvantaged children from the Roma minority through charitable work. The case arose after Romanian authorities, citing concerns about illegal international adoptions, revoked the husband’s residence permit in May 1995 and barred his re-entry. This decision was based on reports and witness statements alleging his involvement in facilitating the illegal removal of newborns from Romania for adoption abroad, though no criminal charges were ultimately brought. The husband challenged the exclusion order in Romanian courts, arguing the allegations were unfounded and that he had only cared for abandoned Romanian children in Hungary. His appeals were dismissed, with courts relying on witness testimony and official reports. The rest of the family remained in Romania for another year before joining him in Hungary, and later the UK.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 6 (fair trial), 8 (private and family life), 13 (effective remedy), and Protocol No. 7 (expulsion of aliens), but found them inadmissible. The Court held that decisions on entry and residence of foreigners do not engage Article 6, and that Article 8 does not guarantee a right to choose one’s country of residence. The applicants’ claims under Articles 13 and Protocol No. 7 were also rejected, as the husband had access to judicial review and was not formally expelled. The case is notable for its clarification that Article 8 does not oblige states to accept non-nationals as residents, even where family life is affected.

cases.title: CONNORS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Connors v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr James Connors, is a United Kingdom national who, together with his family, identifies as Gypsies—a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case highlights the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families to eviction from local authority caravan sites, raising concerns about the adequacy of legal protections for their homes and family life. Mr Connors and his family had lived for many years at Cottingley Springs, a local authority-run site in Leeds, after abandoning a traditional travelling lifestyle due to frequent evictions and harassment. In 2000, following allegations of nuisance caused by his adult children and visitors, the Council served the family with a notice to quit and initiated summary possession proceedings, ultimately evicting them from the site without providing detailed reasons or an opportunity to challenge the allegations in court.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found the application admissible, signalling serious questions about whether the eviction process and the lack of procedural safeguards were compatible with the Convention. This case is significant as it addresses the historical marginalisation of Roma and Traveller communities in the UK, particularly regarding their right to adequate housing and protection from arbitrary eviction, and foreshadows later judgments strengthening procedural rights for these groups.

cases.title: LACKO AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Lacko and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants—Mr. Ján Lacko, Ms. Júlia Demeterová, and Mr. Miroslav Lacko—are Slovak nationals of Romani origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Center. Their case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing repeated displacement and exclusion from housing due to discriminatory actions by local authorities and non-Romani residents. Beginning in 1981, the applicants and other Romani families worked and lived in an agricultural cooperative in Krásny Brod, but after its closure in 1989, they lost both employment and housing. Over the next several years, they were forced to move frequently, as local officials and residents in various municipalities—including Rokytovce and Ňagov—refused to allow them to settle, sometimes threatening violence or destroying their temporary dwellings.

The applicants challenged municipal resolutions that explicitly excluded Roma from settling in these villages, arguing violations of their rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement). However, the European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that the applicants had not demonstrated that the contested resolutions were actually enforced against them or that their rights had been directly violated.

This case highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing secure housing and equal treatment in Europe. Although the Court did not find a violation, the case reflects the historical context of systemic discrimination and exclusion experienced by Roma and Travellers in Slovakia and across the continent.

cases.title: CASE OF ANGUELOVA v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 2 in respect of death of applicant's son;Violation of Art. 2 in respect of failure to provide timely medical care;Violation of Art. 2 due to lack of effective investigation;Violation of Art. 3;Violation of Art. 5;Violation of Art. 13;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary:
In Anguelova v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Mrs. Assya Anguelova, a Bulgarian national of Roma origin, brought a case against Bulgaria concerning the death of her 17-year-old son, Anguel Zabchekov, who also belonged to the Roma community. The case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and neglect, particularly in situations of police custody, where systemic discrimination and lack of accountability have historically placed Roma individuals at heightened risk.

On the night of 28–29 January 1996 in Razgrad, Bulgaria, Anguel Zabchekov was arrested by police after being suspected of attempted theft. Witnesses confirmed he was in good health before his arrest. However, after several hours in police custody, he died from a fatal skull injury. The authorities claimed the injury predated his arrest and attributed other injuries to accidental falls, but Mrs. Anguelova contested this, pointing to inconsistencies in the investigation and evidence of possible ill-treatment.
