The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 5 (right to liberty and security), and 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found Bulgaria responsible for the death, for failing to provide timely medical care, for not conducting an effective investigation, and for other violations, awarding just satisfaction to the applicant.

This judgment is significant for Roma rights as it underscores the urgent need for effective safeguards against police abuse and impunity, especially for Roma and Travellers, who have long faced disproportionate risks in police custody across Europe.

cases.title: THE GYPSY COUNCIL and OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In the case of The Gypsy Council and Others v. the United Kingdom, the applicants included two organisations—the Gypsy Council for Education, Culture, Welfare and Civil Rights and Friends, Families and Travellers—alongside Mr. Thomas O’Doherty and Mr. Terence Green, both members of the Romany Gypsy community. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller groups whose traditional cultural gatherings, such as the Horsmonden Horse Fair in Kent, faced prohibition by local authorities, threatening their cultural expression and community life. The Horsmonden Horse Fair, a significant annual event for the Romany Gypsy community, had been held for at least fifty years, with claims of a tradition spanning three centuries. In 2000, following concerns about public order and disruption, the local Parish Council sought and obtained a prohibition order under the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, effectively banning the fair within a five-mile radius. The applicants challenged this order in the High Court, arguing it disproportionately interfered with their rights under Articles 6, 11, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights found that while the prohibition order interfered with the right to freedom of assembly, the measure was lawful, pursued legitimate aims, and was proportionate, given the disruption anticipated. The Court declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation of the Convention. This case highlights the ongoing tension between the protection of Roma and Traveller cultural traditions and public order concerns, reflecting broader historical challenges faced by these communities in asserting their rights across Europe.

cases.title: SEJDOVIC et SULEJMANOVIC contre l'ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Partiellement recevable;Partiellement irrecevable (Art. 35) Conditions de recevabilité;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae
cases.summary: In the case of Sejdovic and Sulejmanovic v. Italy, the applicants, Fatima Sejdovic and Izet Sulejmanovic, are Roma from the former Yugoslavia, who brought the case on their own behalf and that of their minor children against Italy. Their Roma identity placed them in a particularly vulnerable position, as they faced both the precariousness of life as migrants and the specific marginalisation experienced by Roma and Travellers in Europe. After fleeing Bosnia-Herzegovina, the family settled in the Casilino 700 camp in Rome, a spontaneous settlement known for its dire living conditions and lack of basic sanitation. In 1999 and 2000, following a census and increased police surveillance, the Italian authorities issued expulsion orders against the applicants, citing irregular immigration status, and ultimately removed them from Italy in March 2000. The applicants argued that their expulsion exposed them and their children to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that they lacked effective remedies, raising issues under Article 13. The Court found the case partially admissible, deciding that the applicants’ complaints about expulsion and the risk of ill-treatment warranted further examination on the merits. This case highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, particularly regarding forced evictions and the lack of adequate procedural safeguards, against a backdrop of historical exclusion and discrimination.

cases.title: SULEJMANOVIC et SULTANOVIC contre l'ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Partiellement recevable;Partiellement irrecevable (Art. 35) Conditions de recevabilité;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae
cases.summary:
In the case of Sulejmanovic and Sultanovic v. Italy, the applicants were four members of an extended family of Roma origin from Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Paso and Hadzira Sulejmanovic, their son Nenad, and his wife Halida Sultanovic. The family, who identified as “Tziganes” (a term historically used for Roma), fled the war in the former Yugoslavia and settled in Italy, making their home in the Casilino 700 camp in Rome.

The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing expulsion and precarious living conditions. The applicants alleged that their forced removal from Italy exposed them, as Roma, to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment upon return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, where Roma communities faced discrimination, poverty, and social exclusion.

After arriving in Italy in the early 1990s, the family lived in the Casilino 700 camp, which was overcrowded and lacked basic sanitation. In 1999 and 2000, Italian authorities conducted police checks and issued expulsion orders against the applicants, citing irregular immigration status and lack of legal income. The applicants challenged these measures, arguing that their expulsion would violate Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the case partially admissible, finding that the applicants’ complaints under Article 3 warranted further examination due to the complex factual and legal issues involved. However, other aspects were found inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies or as being outside the Court’s jurisdiction.

This case is significant as it highlights the precarious situation of Roma and Traveller families in Europe, particularly those displaced by conflict and facing exclusion both in their countries of origin and in host states. It reflects the broader historical context of systemic discrimination and marginalisation experienced by Roma and Travellers across the continent.

cases.title: NACHOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary: In Nachova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants—Ms. Anelia Kunchova Nachova, her mother Ms. Aksiniya Hristova, and the parents of Private Petkov—are Bulgarian nationals who identify as being of Romany origin, thus falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case centres on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to excessive use of force and potential racial discrimination by state authorities. On 19 July 1996, Privates Angelov and Petkov, both young Roma conscripts, were killed by military police during an attempted arrest after escaping from a military-detention facility in Lesura, Bulgaria. Neither man was armed, and the operation involved heavily armed officers who fired multiple shots, resulting in the deaths of both privates as they tried to flee. The applicants alleged that the use of lethal force was unjustified and that the authorities failed to investigate possible racist motives behind the killings. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 2 (right to life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding the applications admissible and warranting a full examination of the facts and legal issues. This case is significant as it highlights the persistent risks Roma and Traveller communities face regarding police violence and the need for thorough investigations into possible discriminatory motives, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF ČONKA v. BELGIUM
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;No violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-1 - Lawful arrest or detention;Article 5-1-f - Expulsion);Violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-2 - Information in language understood;Information on reasons for arrest);Violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-4 - Procedural guarantees of review;Review of lawfulness of detention;Take proceedings);Violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 - Prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens-{general};No violation of Article 13+3 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 3 - Prohibition of torture);Violation of Article 13+P4-4 - Right to an effective remedy (Article 13 - Effective remedy) (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 - Prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens-{general});Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
cases.summary:
In the case of Čonka v. Belgium, the applicants were Mr. Ján Čonka, Mrs. Mária Čonková, and their two daughters, all Slovakian nationals of Roma origin. Their case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing expulsion from Western European countries, especially when fleeing violence and discrimination in their home states. The Čonka family had suffered repeated violent attacks by skinheads in Slovakia in 1998, with police refusing to intervene, prompting them to seek asylum in Belgium in November of that year.

After their asylum applications were rejected, the family received orders to leave Belgium. In September 1999, they and other Slovakian Roma families were summoned to a police station under the pretext of completing asylum paperwork, only to be detained and served with deportation orders. The family was not adequately informed of the reasons for their detention in a language they understood, nor were they given a real opportunity to challenge their expulsion before an independent authority.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 5 §2 (right to be informed of reasons for arrest), Article 5 §4 (right to review of detention), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens). The Court awarded the applicants non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it was the first time the Court found a violation of the prohibition on collective expulsion, setting a crucial precedent for the protection of Roma and Travellers against discriminatory and summary removal practices in Europe.

cases.title: LAKATOS v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Lakatos v. the Czech Republic, the applicant, Mr. Lakatos, is a Slovak national who identified himself as a member of the Roma minority. He brought a complaint against the Czech Republic, where he had lived since 1984, primarily with relatives in Prague. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing expulsion from countries where they have established deep personal, social, and family ties, raising concerns about the disproportionate impact such measures can have on Roma individuals who have long faced exclusion and marginalisation.

Mr. Lakatos, who had a history of criminal convictions in Slovakia and the Czech Republic, was sentenced in 1996 by Czech courts to two years’ imprisonment and expulsion from the Czech Republic following an assault conviction. The courts justified the expulsion by citing his repeated criminal behaviour and lack of close family ties in the Czech Republic, despite his long residence and employment there. Mr. Lakatos argued that the expulsion was disproportionate and would severely disrupt his private and family life, invoking Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 6 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding that Mr. Lakatos had not exhausted all domestic remedies, particularly regarding his fair trial complaints. The Court also reiterated that expulsion proceedings do not generally fall under Article 6 protections. This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Travellers often face in accessing justice at the European level, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and the ongoing struggle for effective protection of their rights.

cases.title: CLARK AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Clark and Others v. the United Kingdom, the applicants—Susan Clark, Fred Clark, Claudine Clark, Yvonne Clark, Irene Clark, and Clara Cartwright—were members of the Roma and Traveller community living in Braintree, Essex. Their case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing eviction and criminal penalties due to planning laws that restrict their ability to live according to their traditional way of life. In 1993, after being forced to leave a previous site, the applicants purchased land and stationed their caravans there, seeking retrospective planning permission for a residential caravan site for seven families. The local council refused permission, citing harm to the rural landscape and road safety concerns, and issued enforcement notices requiring the applicants to vacate the land. Despite appeals and efforts to find alternative sites, the applicants were ultimately convicted for failing to comply with the enforcement notices and fined.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found the application inadmissible, referencing its earlier decision in Buckley v. the United Kingdom and concluding that the planning authorities had sufficiently considered the applicants’ interests within the existing legal framework.

This case is significant as it reflects the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing lawful accommodation in Europe, at a time when planning policies often failed to accommodate their cultural needs and contributed to their marginalisation.

cases.title: GORZELIK AND OTHERS v. POLAND
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Gorzelik and Others v. Poland, the applicants—Jerzy Gorzelik, Rudolf Kołodziejczyk, and Erwin Sowa—were Polish nationals who identified themselves as “Silesians.” They sought to register an association called the “Union of People of Silesian Nationality,” aiming to promote Silesian culture, protect the ethnic rights of persons of Silesian nationality, and strengthen Silesian national consciousness. The case did not concern Roma or Traveller identity, but rather the recognition of Silesians as a distinct national minority.

The vulnerability at the heart of the case lay in the applicants’ exclusion from the right to freely associate on the basis of their claimed Silesian identity. In December 1996, the applicants applied to the Katowice Regional Court to register their association. The authorities, however, objected, arguing that “Silesian” denoted a local ethnic group rather than a national minority, and that the association’s statutes were unclear about membership criteria. The Governor of Katowice further argued that registering the association would improperly grant it privileges reserved for recognized national minorities.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 11 (freedom of association) of the European Convention on Human Rights. In this admissibility decision, the Court found the application admissible, allowing the case to proceed to a full examination of whether Poland’s refusal to register the association violated the applicants’ rights under Article 11. The judgment did not establish a violation or award remedies at this stage. The case is significant for its focus on the legal recognition of minority identities and the scope of freedom of association in the context of national minorities in Poland.

cases.summary: In the case of Cyprus v. Turkey, the Republic of Cyprus brought an inter-State application against Turkey, raising, among other issues, the treatment of the Roma and Traveller community—referred to in the judgment as the “Gypsy community”—in northern Cyprus. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who faced discrimination, restrictions on movement, and denial of access to education and property rights in the territory under Turkish control. Following the Turkish military intervention in northern Cyprus in 1974, Roma and Traveller families living in the area experienced severe hardship: they were prevented from returning to their homes, faced obstacles in accessing their property, and were subjected to social exclusion and inadequate living conditions. The European Court of Human Rights examined a wide range of Convention rights, including Articles 3 (prohibition of degrading treatment), 5 (liberty and security), 8 (respect for private and family life), 9 (freedom of religion), 10 (freedom of expression), 13 (effective remedy), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The Court found multiple violations, notably of Articles 3, 8, 9, 10, 13, and Protocol No. 1, confirming that the Roma and Traveller community had suffered from degrading treatment, denial of home and property rights, and lack of effective remedies. This landmark judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it recognised the compounded discrimination faced by these communities in conflict zones, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation across Europe.

cases.title: HARRISON v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Harrison v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Jean Harrison, a Romany Traveller, brought a case against the United Kingdom after being refused planning permission to live in her caravan on her own land in Christchurch, Dorset. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities, who often face significant barriers to securing lawful accommodation that respects their traditional way of life. Ms. Harrison, together with her elderly mother and grandchildren, had lived in caravans on the site since 1985, in an area known for its longstanding Traveller presence. Despite this, local authorities denied her planning permission, citing Green Belt policies and concerns about the visual impact on the rural landscape. Enforcement notices required her to remove her caravan, and appeals to planning authorities and the Secretary of State were unsuccessful, even though alternative sites offered were unsuitable for her family’s needs. Ms. Harrison argued that these measures interfered with her right to respect for her home and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and amounted to discrimination under Article 14. The European Court of Human Rights, however, declared the application inadmissible, finding that the national authorities had sufficiently considered her interests and that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims. This case reflects the ongoing struggle of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe to secure adequate accommodation and recognition of their cultural needs, against a backdrop of restrictive planning policies and historical marginalisation.

cases.title: SMITH v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Beatrice and John Smith, are Romany Gypsies—members of the Roma and Travellers communities—who brought a case against the United Kingdom. Their complaint centred on the difficulties and harm they faced as Roma in securing a lawful place to live in accordance with their traditional way of life, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to eviction and lack of suitable accommodation. Between 1993 and 1997, after moving their caravans onto their own land in Headcorn, Kent, the Smiths repeatedly sought planning permission to reside there but were consistently refused by local authorities, who cited harm to the rural landscape. The Smiths faced enforcement actions, fines, and eventual eviction, leading them to move from site to site, including public spaces and relatives’ gardens, while their children’s schooling and family life were disrupted. The European Court of Human Rights examined their complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately declared the application inadmissible, finding that the authorities had offered alternative accommodation and had not acted disproportionately. This case is significant as it illustrates the persistent barriers Roma and Travellers face in securing culturally appropriate housing in the UK, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and marginalisation across Europe.

cases.title: MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
cases.conclusion: Partly inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Moldovan and Others v. Romania, the applicants were 25 Romanian nationals of Roma origin, all agricultural workers from the village of Hădăreni, Mureş county. The case arose from a violent episode of anti-Roma collective punishment and destruction, highlighting the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of state protection. On the evening of 20 September 1993, following a fatal altercation between three Roma men and a non-Roma villager, a large mob of villagers, joined by local police, attacked the Roma community. The mob set fire to the house where the Roma men were hiding, resulting in the deaths of Rapa Lupian Lăcătuş, Aurel Pardalian Lăcătuş, and Mircea Zoltan. The violence escalated as villagers, with police present, destroyed thirteen Roma homes and other property, forcing many Roma families to flee.

Despite the gravity of the events, the Romanian authorities failed to protect the Roma residents or to conduct an effective investigation. The applicants alleged that the police not only failed to intervene but also enabled the violence and destruction. The European Court of Human Rights examined the admissibility of the case under Article 35 of the Convention, ultimately declaring parts of the application inadmissible at this stage, with no finding of a violation or remedies awarded.

This case is significant as it brought international attention to the systemic discrimination and violence faced by Roma communities in post-communist Romania, reflecting a broader pattern of anti-Roma pogroms and state inaction across Europe in the 1990s.

cases.title: SMITH v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Smith, a British national of Romany Gypsy origin, brought a case against the United Kingdom concerning her right to live in a caravan on her own land. As a member of the Gypsy community—a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers—Ms. Smith’s case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing repeated evictions and planning restrictions that threaten their traditional way of life. After decades of being moved on by police and experiencing hostility on official sites, Ms. Smith and her husband, who suffered from serious health issues, purchased land in Bedfordshire in 1996 and applied for planning permission to station caravans there. The local council refused permission, citing Green Belt policies and environmental concerns, and issued an enforcement notice requiring them to leave. Ms. Smith argued that these measures interfered with her right to respect for private and family life and home under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights acknowledged that the planning decisions interfered with Ms. Smith’s Article 8 rights, given the centrality of caravan living to her ethnic identity. However, the Court found the interference was justified as “necessary in a democratic society” for environmental protection and thus declared the application inadmissible. This case is significant as it reflects the ongoing tension between environmental planning policies and the rights of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, echoing longstanding challenges faced by these minorities in securing secure and culturally appropriate accommodation.

cases.title: EATSON v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary: In Eatson v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Eatson, a British national born into a Gypsy family and living a traditional nomadic lifestyle, brought a case against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities—specifically, the harm caused by planning laws that restrict their ability to live according to their cultural traditions. For over a decade, Ms. Eatson and her family faced repeated evictions and harassment by authorities as they travelled in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire. After purchasing land in Tilsworth to establish a nursery business, they were denied permanent planning permission to live in a caravan on their own land, despite their clear Gypsy identity and lack of suitable alternative accommodation. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), acknowledging that the planning decisions interfered with Ms. Eatson’s ability to maintain her identity and way of life. However, the Court found the application inadmissible, holding that the interference pursued a legitimate aim—environmental protection—and that national authorities had a wide margin of appreciation in balancing these interests. This case is significant as it reflects the ongoing tension between environmental policies and the rights of Roma and Traveller communities, at a time when European states were only beginning to grapple with the need for culturally sensitive planning laws.

cases.title: PORTER v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Porter v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Porter, a British national of Gypsy origin, brought a case against the United Kingdom after she and her husband, both identifying as Gypsies within the broader Roma and Traveller communities, faced eviction from their own land in Buckinghamshire. The core issue was the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families to planning laws that restrict their ability to live according to their traditional way of life, particularly when local authorities refuse permission for caravan sites. In 1984, Ms. Porter and her husband purchased land and settled there in their caravans, but repeated applications for planning permission were denied by the local council, citing the land’s location within the Green Belt and environmental concerns. After years of legal challenges, the High Court ordered the removal of their caravans in 2000, with the matter later adjourned pending the entry into force of the Human Rights Act 1998.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). While the Court acknowledged that the applicant’s occupation of caravans was integral to her ethnic identity as a Gypsy and that the planning measures interfered with her rights, it ultimately found the application inadmissible. The Court held that the interference pursued a legitimate aim—environmental protection—and that national authorities had a wide margin of appreciation in balancing these interests.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent tension between environmental planning policies and the rights of Roma and Traveller communities to maintain their traditional lifestyles. It reflects the historical challenges faced by these minorities in securing accommodation that respects both their cultural identity and legal requirements.

cases.title: CASE OF CHAPMAN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of P1-1;No violation of Art. 6-1;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary:
In Chapman v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Chapman, identified as a Gypsy by birth—a term encompassed within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers—brought a case against the United Kingdom. The heart of the case lay in the persistent vulnerability faced by Roma and Traveller families who, due to a lack of authorised sites, are forced into a cycle of eviction, instability, and disrupted access to education and healthcare. Ms. Chapman and her family, lifelong travellers in Hertfordshire, purchased land in 1985 to settle in a mobile home after years of being moved on by authorities and facing harassment detrimental to their children’s education and family health. Despite applying for planning permission to live on their own land, the local council repeatedly refused, citing Green Belt restrictions, and issued enforcement notices. The family faced fines and, after exhausting appeals, were compelled to return to a nomadic life, again suffering instability and educational disruption for their children.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), 6 (right to a fair hearing), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found no violation of these rights, concluding that the planning controls pursued a legitimate aim and that sufficient consideration had been given to Ms. Chapman’s circumstances. While no remedies were awarded, the case is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing stable accommodation in Europe. Set against a backdrop of historical marginalisation and legislative changes in the UK, Chapman v. the United Kingdom remains a landmark in the struggle for equal treatment and recognition of the rights of Roma and Travellers.

cases.title: CASE OF BEARD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary:
In the case of Beard v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Beard, identified as Gypsies by birth and long-standing members of the Roma and Traveller community, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. Their case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families who, due to their traditional nomadic lifestyle, face significant barriers in securing lawful sites for their caravans, often resulting in forced evictions and instability. In 1986, the Beards purchased a plot of land in Lancashire with the intention of establishing a small family caravan site. After cleaning up the land, they moved onto it in August 1991 and applied for planning permission, which was refused on grounds of highway safety and visual impact. Despite appeals, the authorities issued an enforcement notice requiring them to vacate the land, and the Beards were ultimately forced to leave, becoming homeless and unable to find suitable alternative accommodation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found no violation of either article, concluding that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and that the authorities had sufficiently considered the applicants’ circumstances. No remedies were awarded. This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in accessing secure accommodation, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and the ongoing tension between planning law and minority rights in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF COSTER v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of P1-1;No violation of P1-2;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary:
In Coster v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Coster, identified as Gypsies by birth—a group encompassed within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers—brought a case against the United Kingdom. Their complaint centred on the acute vulnerability faced by Gypsy families in securing lawful, culturally appropriate accommodation, and the risk of forced eviction due to planning restrictions. After marrying in 1982 and struggling to find a legal place to park their caravan in Kent, the Costers were repeatedly refused pitches on official sites and ultimately accepted council housing, which proved unsuitable for their traditional way of life. In 1988, they purchased land and stationed their caravan there, but local authorities denied planning permission, issued enforcement notices, and prosecuted them for non-compliance. Despite appeals highlighting their cultural needs and lack of alternatives, the authorities prioritised environmental concerns and the prevention of site “overconcentration.”

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found no violation of these provisions, concluding that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and that the authorities had sufficiently considered the applicants’ circumstances. This judgment is significant as it illustrates the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in accessing lawful accommodation in the UK, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and restrictive land-use policies affecting these communities across Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF LEE v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of P1-1;No violation of P1-2;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary:
In the case of Lee v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Lee, and his wife, both Gypsies by birth and part of the broader Roma and Traveller communities, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Gypsy families who, due to their nomadic lifestyle and lack of authorised sites, faced repeated evictions and legal obstacles to securing a permanent home. Over a four-year period, Mr. Lee and his family were evicted from more than 40 sites in Kent, England, prompting him to purchase a small plot of land in 1991 to provide a settled base for his family, including his children and grandchildren.

Despite their efforts to establish a lawful residence and contribute to the local economy through agricultural work, the local council issued an enforcement notice in 1992 requiring the removal of their caravans, citing planning policies protecting the landscape. Mr. Lee’s appeal was dismissed, and the authorities maintained that the site’s location in a Special Landscape Area outweighed the family’s needs, despite a recognised shortfall in authorised Gypsy pitches.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), but found no violation. The Court concluded that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and were proportionate in the circumstances. This case is significant as it reflects the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing lawful accommodation in the UK, against a backdrop of historical marginalisation and restrictive planning regimes.

cases.title: CASE OF JANE SMITH v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of P1-1;No violation of P1-2;No violation of Art. 6-1;No violation of Art. 14
cases.summary:
In the case of Jane Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Smith, identified herself as a Gypsy by birth—a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of “Roma and Travellers.” She and her family had lived a nomadic life in Surrey, England, facing persistent difficulties in securing lawful and stable accommodation due to their identity and way of life. The core harm in this case was the repeated exclusion of Ms. Smith and her family from official and private caravan sites, forcing them to move constantly and live in precarious conditions, which affected their health, education, and well-being.

Over many years, Ms. Smith and her husband, both illiterate due to lack of formal education, unsuccessfully applied for places on local sites. In 1993, after purchasing a plot of land in a Green Belt area, they moved their mobile home there, only to face planning refusals and enforcement actions from the local council, citing environmental and planning policies. Despite government guidance encouraging flexibility for Gypsy site applications, the family was denied permission to remain, and their appeals were dismissed.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found no violation of these rights, concluding that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and were proportionate in the circumstances.

This case is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Traveller families in accessing secure accommodation in the United Kingdom, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and the tension between planning law and minority rights.

cases.title: AFFAIRE CHAPMAN c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'art. 8;Non-violation de P1-1;Non-violation de l'art. 6-1;Non-violation de l'art. 14
cases.summary:
In Chapman v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Chapman, identified as a member of the Roma and Traveller community—specifically as a Gypsy by birth—brought a case against the United Kingdom. The heart of the case was the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families who, due to their traditional nomadic lifestyle, face significant barriers in securing lawful and stable accommodation, often resulting in repeated evictions and disruption to family life and education. Ms. Chapman and her family, long accustomed to travelling for work in Hertfordshire, purchased land in 1985 to settle in a mobile home, hoping to provide stability for their children’s schooling. However, local authorities repeatedly refused her planning permission to station caravans or build a bungalow on her land, citing environmental and planning regulations, and issued enforcement notices that led to fines and forced the family to resume a nomadic existence, disrupting the children’s education and family life.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court acknowledged the special vulnerability of Roma and Travellers and the integral role of caravan living in their identity, but ultimately found no violation of the Convention, holding that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and were proportionate in the circumstances.

This case is significant as it was among the first to explicitly recognise the unique cultural identity and vulnerability of Roma and Travellers under the European Convention, even as it highlighted the ongoing tension between minority rights and state planning policies in late 20th-century Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE JANE SMITH c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'art. 8;Non-violation de P1-1;Non-violation de P1-2;Non-violation de l'art. 6-1;Non-violation de l'art. 14
cases.summary:
In the case of Jane Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Smith, identified as a member of the Gypsy community—a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Together with her family, she had lived a traditional nomadic life in Surrey, England, facing significant barriers due to her ethnicity and way of life. The core vulnerability in this case was the persistent lack of authorised caravan sites for Gypsies, which forced Ms. Smith and her family into a cycle of instability, frequent evictions, and exclusion from both public and private sites, despite repeated applications for legal accommodation.

Chronologically, after years of unsuccessful attempts to secure a lawful place to live, Ms. Smith purchased a plot of land in Runnymede in 1993 and stationed her mobile home there. However, her application for planning permission was refused on the grounds that it contravened local and national policies protecting the green belt. Despite her family’s health issues and the lack of alternatives, enforcement action was taken to remove her from the land.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), 6 (right to a fair hearing), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found no violation of these provisions, concluding that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and that the authorities had sufficiently considered Ms. Smith’s circumstances.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in accessing secure accommodation, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and the tension between minority rights and land-use policies in Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE COSTER c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'art. 8;Non-violation de P1-1;Non-violation de P1-2;Non-violation de l'art. 14
cases.summary:
In the case of Coster v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Coster, identified as Gypsies (a term included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers), brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. Their case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families who, due to planning restrictions and a shortage of authorised caravan sites, face persistent threats of eviction and are often forced to abandon their traditional way of life. The Costers, having travelled with their families in Kent, England, sought a permanent site for their caravan to provide stability for their children’s education. After being unable to secure a place on authorised sites and facing repeated refusals from local authorities, they purchased land in Headcorn in 1988 and settled there in a caravan. However, their requests for planning permission were denied, enforcement actions were taken against them, and they were ultimately compelled to leave their land.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found no violation of these articles, concluding that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims and that the authorities had struck a fair balance between the applicants’ rights and the general interest. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it reflects the ongoing tension between traditional lifestyles and planning regulations in Europe. Historically, such cases illustrate the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller communities face in securing culturally appropriate accommodation.

cases.title: AFFAIRE LEE c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'art. 8;Non-violation de P1-1;Non-violation de P1-2;Non-violation de l'art. 14
cases.summary:
In Lee v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Lee, is a member of the Gypsy community—part of the broader Roma and Travellers group as defined by the Council of Europe—who, along with his family, led a nomadic life in Kent, England. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing repeated evictions and the struggle to maintain their traditional way of life in the face of restrictive planning laws. Over four years, Mr. Lee and his family were evicted from more than forty sites, prompting him to purchase a small plot of land in 1991 to establish a stable home for his family and grandchildren, who had begun attending school regularly. However, the local council refused planning permission for their caravans, citing landscape protection policies, and issued an enforcement notice requiring their removal.

Mr. Lee argued that these actions interfered with his right to respect for private and family life and home under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) and freedom from discrimination (Article 14). The European Court of Human Rights acknowledged the impact of the measures on Mr. Lee’s ability to maintain his Gypsy identity and traditional lifestyle but ultimately found no violation of the Convention. The Court held that the interference was justified by the legitimate aim of protecting the environment and was proportionate in the circumstances.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent tension between the rights of Roma and Traveller communities to preserve their way of life and the enforcement of planning regulations in Europe. It reflects the historical challenges faced by these minorities in securing stable accommodation and recognition of their cultural identity.

cases.title: AFFAIRE BEARD c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'art. 8;Non-violation de l'art. 14
cases.summary:
In Beard v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Beard, identified as Gypsies (a term included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers), brought a case against the United Kingdom. The heart of the case was the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families who, due to planning restrictions, face obstacles in maintaining their traditional way of life—specifically, living in caravans on land they own. The Beards, after years of moving between official and unofficial sites in Lancashire, purchased a plot of land in 1986 to establish a permanent family base. In 1991, they settled on this land and applied for planning permission to station six caravans. Their application was refused on grounds of landscape protection and road safety, and they were fined for illegal occupation, ordered to remove their caravans, and required to restore the land.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Court acknowledged that living in caravans is integral to the applicants’ identity as Gypsies and that the planning decisions interfered with their rights. However, it found no violation of either Article 8 or Article 14, concluding that the interference was justified by legitimate planning considerations and was proportionate.

This case is significant as it highlights the ongoing tension between the rights of Roma and Traveller communities to preserve their traditional lifestyles and the enforcement of planning laws in Europe. It reflects the historical challenges faced by Roma and Travellers in securing legal recognition and accommodation for their way of life.

cases.title: CASE OF VAREY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list (friendly settlement)
cases.summary: In the case of Varey v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, who identified as Gypsies by birth and were part of the broader Roma and Traveller communities, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. Their vulnerability stemmed from the persistent difficulties faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing lawful places to live, particularly due to restrictive planning policies and the lack of authorised caravan sites. The applicants, having lived nomadically in the Stafford area, purchased land that had historically been used by Gypsies and sought planning permission to establish a residential caravan site. Despite repeated applications and appeals between 1988 and 1997, the local council and the Secretary of State consistently refused permission, citing Green Belt development policies. The applicants faced enforcement notices, criminal convictions, fines, and ultimately, the threat of imprisonment and forced eviction, leaving them with no lawful alternative accommodation. The case raised issues under Articles 6 (right to a fair hearing), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, before a final judgment, the parties reached a friendly settlement, and the European Court of Human Rights struck the case out of its list. This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing secure housing in the United Kingdom, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation and legal obstacles across Europe.

cases.title: AFFAIRE ROMA c. ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Violation de l'art. 6-1;Dommage matériel - demande rejetée;Préjudice moral - réparation pécuniaire;Frais et dépens - demande rejetée
cases.summary:
In the case of Roma v. Italy, the applicant, Mr. Nicola Roma, brought proceedings against the Italian State. While the applicant’s surname is “Roma,” the judgment does not indicate that he belongs to any Roma or Traveller group as defined by the Council of Europe; rather, he is an individual creditor involved in a civil dispute. The case focused on the harm caused by excessive delays in civil proceedings, a problem that has affected many litigants in Italy. Mr. Roma initiated proceedings in 1989 to recover a debt from the municipality of Controne, Salerno. Despite an initial payment order, the municipality contested the claim, leading to a protracted trial before the Salerno tribunal. Over the next decade, the case was repeatedly postponed due to procedural delays, expert appointments, and administrative issues, with the final settlement only reached in April 2000—almost eleven years after the proceedings began.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. The Court found a violation of this provision, noting that the length of the proceedings reflected a broader pattern of systemic delays in Italy. Mr. Roma was awarded 12,600,000 Italian lire for non-pecuniary damage, but his claims for material damages and legal costs were rejected. The judgment specifically highlights the aggravating circumstance of repeated failures by Italian courts to ensure timely justice.

cases.title: ANGUELOVA v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Anguelova v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Ms. Anguelova, a Bulgarian national of Roma origin, brought a case against Bulgaria following the death of her 17-year-old son, Anguel Zabchekov, who was also Roma. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police mistreatment and inadequate investigations, particularly when ethnic bias is alleged to play a role in state responses to deaths in custody. On 29 January 1996, Anguel Zabchekov died after several hours in police custody in Razgrad, Bulgaria, following his arrest for attempted theft. Witnesses confirmed that he was in good health before his arrest, but he died soon after being apprehended by an off-duty police officer. The authorities concluded that his death was due to an accidental injury predating his arrest, a finding contested by his mother, who also pointed to the use of ethnic slurs by police and alleged that her son’s Roma identity influenced the officers’ actions and the subsequent investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights examined alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 5 (right to liberty and security), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case was declared admissible, allowing the Court to proceed to a full examination of the merits. This case is significant as it addresses the persistent issue of police violence and impunity affecting Roma and Travellers in Europe, reflecting a broader historical context of systemic discrimination and the urgent need for effective protection of minority rights.

cases.title: CASE OF VELIKOVA v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Violation of Art. 2 with regard to the applicant's death;Violation of Art. 2 with regard to the lack of effective investigation;Violation of Art. 13;No violation of Art. 14;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses partial award
cases.summary:
In Velikova v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Ms. Velikova, a Bulgarian national residing in the village of Bukovlak, brought a case to the European Court of Human Rights following the death of her long-term partner, Mr. Slavtcho Tsonchev, who belonged to the Roma community. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective state protection, particularly in situations involving police custody. On 24 September 1994, Mr. Tsonchev was arrested by police in connection with cattle theft and was held in custody in Pleven. He died after approximately twelve hours in detention, during which time there were allegations of ill-treatment and neglect by the authorities. Despite the suspicious circumstances of his death, the investigation by Bulgarian authorities was inadequate and failed to clarify the cause or assign responsibility.

The Court examined violations of Article 2 (right to life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), among others. It found that Bulgaria had violated Article 2 both in relation to Mr. Tsonchev’s death and the lack of an effective investigation, as well as Article 13 due to the absence of an effective remedy. However, it did not find a violation of Article 14. The Court awarded Ms. Velikova both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

This judgment is significant for Roma rights as it underscores the duty of states to protect the lives of Roma and Travellers in custody and to conduct thorough investigations into deaths, reflecting longstanding concerns about police violence and impunity affecting these communities in Europe.

cases.title: ROMA contre l'ITALIE
cases.conclusion: Recevable
cases.summary:
In the case of Roma v. Italy, the applicant, Mr. Roma, an Italian national residing in Salerno, brought a complaint against the Italian state. The applicant’s surname is “Roma,” but the judgment does not indicate that he belongs to the Roma or Traveller communities as defined by the Council of Europe; rather, he is described simply as an Italian citizen. The case does not concern Roma-related vulnerability or exclusion, but instead focuses on the excessive length of civil proceedings in Italy.

The facts of the case began on 15 May 1989, when Mr. Roma obtained a payment order against the municipality of Controne. The municipality opposed the order, and litigation commenced before the Salerno tribunal on 13 June 1989. Over the next decade, the proceedings were marked by repeated delays: hearings were postponed for various reasons, including judicial strikes, the absence of an expert, and administrative issues. By 20 September 1999, more than ten years after the case began, the proceedings were still pending.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. The Court declared the application admissible, finding that the length of the proceedings warranted further examination. No violation or remedy was determined at this stage, as the decision was limited to admissibility. This case is notable for its focus on procedural delay rather than minority rights.

cases.title: VELIKOVA v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary: In Velikova v. Bulgaria, the applicant, Ms. Velikova, a Bulgarian national, brought a case concerning the death of her long-term partner, Mr. T., who belonged to the Roma community, against the Bulgarian state. The case highlights the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to ill-treatment and neglect while in police custody, as well as the risk of bias and inadequate investigation into their deaths. On 24 September 1994, Mr. T. was arrested in the village of B., Pleven district, on suspicion of cattle theft. He was reportedly healthy at the time of arrest but was described as intoxicated by police and witnesses. Over the next twelve hours in police custody, Mr. T. exhibited signs of severe illness, including vomiting and difficulty walking, yet received no meaningful medical care despite the arrival of emergency medical staff. He died in the early hours of 25 September 1994 at the police station. The applicant alleged violations of Article 2 (right to life) due to the authorities’ failure to protect Mr. T.’s life and to conduct an effective investigation, as well as Article 6 (right to a fair trial) regarding the excessive length and inadequacy of the criminal proceedings. The case was declared admissible, allowing the Court to examine whether Bulgaria fulfilled its obligations under the Convention. Velikova v. Bulgaria is significant as it exposes systemic failings in the protection of Roma individuals in police custody and the persistent lack of accountability for deaths in detention, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination against Roma and Travellers in Europe.

cases.title: CASE OF ASSENOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
cases.conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (abuse of process);Preliminary objection dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);No violation of Art. 3 (ill-treatment);Violation of Art. 3 (effective investigation);No violation of Art. 6-1;Violation of Art. 13;No violation of Art. 3 (detention);No violation of Art. 5-1;Violation of Art. 5-3 (judge or other officer);Violation of Art. 5-3 (trial within a reasonable time);Violation of Art. 5-4;Violation of Art. 25-1;Non-pecuniary damage - financial award;Costs and expenses award - Convention proceedings
cases.summary:
In the case of Assenov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were a Roma family from Shoumen, Bulgaria: Anton Assenov, a minor at the time, and his parents, Fidanka Ivanova and Stefan Ivanov. Their Roma identity was central to the case, as it highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police abuse and inadequate legal protection in Bulgaria. The harm at the heart of the case involved allegations of police violence against Anton, then 14 years old, and his mother, as well as the authorities’ failure to properly investigate these claims—an issue that disproportionately affects Roma and Traveller communities across Europe.

On 19 September 1992, Anton was arrested by an off-duty policeman while gambling in a market square. His parents, both working nearby, intervened, leading to a confrontation with police. Anton and his father were handcuffed and detained at the police station, where Anton alleged further physical abuse. Medical examinations shortly after the incident documented multiple bruises on both Anton and his mother, consistent with their account of police violence. Despite a formal complaint, the ensuing investigation by the authorities was superficial and failed to address the applicants’ allegations adequately.

The European Court of Human Rights examined several articles of the Convention, notably Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 5 (right to liberty and security), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). While the Court did not find a substantive violation of Article 3 regarding ill-treatment, it held that Bulgaria had violated Article 3 procedurally by failing to conduct an effective investigation. The Court also found violations of Article 5 (regarding judicial oversight and promptness of proceedings), Article 13, and Article 25, awarding non-pecuniary damages and costs to the applicants.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it established the obligation of states to investigate allegations of police abuse thoroughly and impartially, especially where vulnerable minorities are concerned. The case came at a time when Roma communities in post-communist Europe were increasingly drawing attention to systemic discrimination and police misconduct.

cases.title: AFFAIRE ASSENOV ET AUTRES c. BULGARIE
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'Art. 3 (mauvais traitements);Violation de l'Art. 3 (enquête effective);Non-violation de l'Art. 6-1;Violation de l'Art. 13;Non-violation de l'Art. 3 (détention);Non-violation de l'Art. 5-1;Violation de l'Art. 5-3 (juge ou autre magistrat);Violation de l'Art. 5-3 (jugé dans un délai raisonnable);Violation de l'Art. 5-4;Violation de l'Art. 25-1;Préjudice moral - réparation pécuniaire;Remboursement frais et dépens - procédure de la Convention
cases.summary:
In the case of Assenov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were a Bulgarian Roma family—Anton Assenov, then a 14-year-old boy, and his parents, Fidanka Ivanova and Stefan Ivanov—residing in Shumen, Bulgaria. Their Roma identity was central to the case, as it highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to police abuse and lack of effective legal protection.

The harm at the heart of the case concerned allegations of police violence against a Roma child and his mother, and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. On 19 September 1992, Anton Assenov was apprehended by an off-duty police officer for playing dice at a market. His parents intervened, but both Anton and his father were handcuffed and taken to the police station, where Anton alleged he was beaten by police officers. Medical evidence documented bruises and injuries consistent with his account. Despite a formal complaint, the authorities failed to carry out a thorough and impartial investigation into the alleged ill-treatment.

The European Court of Human Rights examined several articles of the European Convention on Human Rights. While it found no substantive violation of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) regarding the alleged ill-treatment itself, it held that Bulgaria had violated Article 3 by failing to conduct an effective investigation. The Court also found violations of Article 5 (right to liberty and security), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 25 (right of individual petition), awarding moral damages and costs to the applicants.

This judgment is significant for Roma rights as it established the obligation of states to investigate allegations of police abuse, particularly where vulnerable minorities such as Roma and Travellers are concerned. The case came at a time when Roma communities across Europe were increasingly drawing attention to systemic police violence and impunity.

cases.title: SINKO v. THE SLOVAK REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Sinko v. the Slovak Republic, the applicant, Mr. Sinko, a Slovak national and fireman residing in Trnava, brought a case against Slovakia after receiving a death threat. The threat, signed "Gypsies from Trnava," followed his public opposition at a local meeting to the accommodation of persons of Roma origin in his neighborhood. Although the applicant himself is not described as Roma or Traveller, the case arose from tensions surrounding Roma settlement in Trnava.

The harm at the center of the case was the applicant’s exposure to threats and distress after his photograph was published in a weekly newspaper, linking him to anti-Roma sentiment. Mr. Sinko sought compensation from the publisher, claiming the publication endangered his safety and disrupted his family life. However, his civil claim was discontinued because he could not pay the required court fees, and his requests for exemption were denied by the Slovak courts, which found his income insufficiently low to justify exemption.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 § 1 (right of access to a court) and Article 8 (right to respect for private life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Commission found the application inadmissible, concluding that the court fees were not excessive or disproportionate and that the Slovak courts had not acted arbitrarily. The Commission also found no unreasonable delay in the proceedings. The case is notable for illustrating the procedural barriers individuals may face in seeking remedies for threats linked to Roma-related community tensions, even when the applicant is not a member of the Roma or Traveller communities.

cases.title: COSTER v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Coster v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, a married couple of Gypsy origin—falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of “Roma and Travellers”—brought a case against the United Kingdom. Their complaint centred on the vulnerability of Gypsy families who, due to a shortage of authorised caravan sites, face repeated evictions and are prevented from living according to their traditional way of life. After marrying in 1982 and struggling to find a lawful place to park their caravan in Kent, the Costers were refused pitches on official sites and ultimately forced to accept unsuitable council accommodation. Finding this incompatible with their culture, they purchased land in Headcorn in 1988 and moved their caravan there, but local authorities refused planning permission, issued enforcement notices, and prosecuted them for non-compliance, citing harm to the rural landscape.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), among others. The case was declared admissible, meaning the applicants’ complaints raised serious questions under the Convention, but no violation was ultimately found at this stage.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing culturally appropriate accommodation in the UK, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and legal obstacles for these communities across Europe.

cases.title: BEARD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Beard v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Beard, are British citizens who identify as Gypsies by birth, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case against the United Kingdom centred on their struggle to maintain their traditional way of life—living in caravans—on land they owned in Lancashire. The harm at the heart of the case was the applicants’ inability to lawfully reside in their caravans on their own land, facing repeated refusals of planning permission, enforcement notices, and criminal prosecution, despite their efforts to comply with regulations and their lack of viable alternatives due to safety concerns on official sites.

Chronologically, the Beards purchased a plot of land in 1986, cleaned it up, and applied for planning permission in 1991 to establish a small family caravan site. Their application was refused on grounds of visual amenity and highway safety, and subsequent appeals were dismissed. Enforcement notices required them to vacate the land, and they faced prosecution for unlawful occupation. Attempts to find alternative sites failed, as the only available official site was unsafe due to previous violent attacks against them.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights, declaring the application admissible but not finding a violation at this stage. No remedies were awarded.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing lawful accommodation that respects their traditional lifestyle, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and the ongoing tension between planning regulations and minority rights in Europe.

cases.title: SMITH v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Smith, is a British citizen who identifies as a Gypsy by birth, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Her case highlights the acute vulnerability faced by Gypsy families in the United Kingdom, particularly regarding access to lawful and stable accommodation that respects their cultural traditions. For decades, Ms. Smith and her family led a nomadic life in Surrey, moving frequently due to the lack of available official or private sites for Gypsies. Despite repeated applications for authorised sites and attempts to secure stable housing, they were consistently turned away due to full waiting lists and restrictive local policies. In 1993, Ms. Smith purchased a plot of land in Runnymede and moved her family’s caravan there, only to be denied planning permission on the grounds that the land was in a protected Green Belt area. Her appeals were dismissed, and she faced enforcement action, leaving her family at risk of eviction and further instability.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), among others. The case was declared admissible, but no violation was ultimately found. Smith v. the United Kingdom is significant as it underscores the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing lawful accommodation, reflecting broader patterns of exclusion and the tension between planning laws and minority rights in late 20th-century Britain.

cases.title: LEE v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Lee v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Lee, a British citizen of Gypsy origin, brought a case against the United Kingdom, asserting his rights as a member of the Roma and Traveller communities. Mr. Lee and his family, who have a traditional nomadic lifestyle, faced persistent difficulties in securing lawful accommodation due to their identity as Gypsies. Over four years, Mr. Lee was evicted from more than 40 sites and repeatedly prosecuted for illegal encampment, prompting him in 1991 to purchase a plot of land in Chartham, Kent, to provide a settled home for his family. Despite this, local authorities issued an enforcement notice in 1992 requiring the removal of their caravans, citing planning restrictions in a designated Special Landscape Area. Mr. Lee’s appeals were dismissed, and he continued to live under threat of eviction and criminal prosecution, while the official sites offered to him were, in his view, unfit for habitation.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 10 (freedom of expression), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The case was declared admissible, but no violation was ultimately found. Lee v. the United Kingdom is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in securing adequate accommodation and recognition of their traditional lifestyles, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in the UK and Europe during the late twentieth century.

cases.title: VAREY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Varey v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, British citizens of Gypsy origin, challenged the United Kingdom’s planning laws as they affected their traditional way of life as part of the Roma and Traveller communities. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers who, due to a shortage of authorised sites and restrictive planning policies, face criminalisation and forced eviction when seeking to live in accordance with their nomadic traditions. The Varey family, having lived in the Stafford area for most of their lives, purchased land to establish a caravan site after finding it increasingly difficult to secure legal stopping places. Despite repeated applications and appeals for planning permission, all were refused by the local council and the Secretary of State, citing Green Belt protections. The applicants faced multiple prosecutions and fines for remaining on their land, with no alternative legal sites available.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The application was declared admissible, recognising the serious questions raised about the proportionality of planning controls and their impact on Roma and Traveller families. While the case did not proceed to a final judgment on the merits, its admissibility underscored the need for states to balance environmental policies with the rights and needs of Roma and Travellers. This case is significant as it reflects the persistent barriers faced by Roma and Traveller communities in securing lawful accommodation, a longstanding issue in the United Kingdom and across Europe.

cases.title: SMITH  v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Smith, a British citizen of Gypsy origin, brought a case against the United Kingdom concerning his right to live according to his traditional Traveller lifestyle. Mr. Smith, who was born into a Gypsy family and spent much of his life travelling and living in caravans, faced persistent difficulties securing a lawful place to live. After moving onto a council-provided Gypsy site and later into a house at his wife’s request, Mr. Smith struggled to adapt and eventually purchased land in Iver, Buckinghamshire, intending to live there in a caravan. However, he encountered repeated refusals of planning permission, enforcement notices, and threats of eviction, all of which made it nearly impossible for him to maintain his traditional way of life.

The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities, who often face legal and practical barriers to living in accordance with their culture. Mr. Smith’s attempts to secure a lawful home for his family were met with planning restrictions and enforcement actions, despite government guidance encouraging local authorities to accommodate Gypsies’ needs.

Mr. Smith alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, 13, 14, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing that he was denied respect for his home and family life, discriminated against, and deprived of effective remedies. However, the European Commission of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation of the Convention.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in securing lawful accommodation and recognition of their cultural practices, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation in the United Kingdom and across Europe.

cases.title: CHAPMAN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Admissible
cases.summary:
In Chapman v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Chapman, is a British citizen who identifies as a Gypsy by birth, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities who, due to a shortage of authorised sites and restrictive planning laws, are often unable to pursue their traditional way of life without facing legal penalties. Ms. Chapman and her family, lifelong travellers in Hertfordshire, purchased land in 1985 to settle in a caravan after years of being moved on by authorities and experiencing harassment that disrupted their children’s education and family health. Despite repeated applications, local authorities consistently refused her planning permission to live on her own land, citing Green Belt restrictions, and issued enforcement notices that led to fines and forced the family back into a precarious nomadic existence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 6 (right to a fair hearing), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The case was declared admissible, meaning the Court found the complaints raised serious questions under the Convention, but at this stage, no violation was found or remedies awarded.

Chapman v. the United Kingdom is significant as it addresses the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing stable accommodation and exercising their cultural rights, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and exclusion from mainstream housing policies in Europe.

cases.title: WEBB v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Webb v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, a married couple of Romany Gypsy heritage, brought a case against the United Kingdom after facing repeated obstacles to living in their caravans on land they owned in Wiltshire. As members of the Roma and Travellers community, the applicants’ vulnerability lay in the persistent difficulties they encountered in maintaining their traditional nomadic lifestyle, particularly the lack of lawful sites for encampment and the refusal of planning permission by local authorities. Beginning in 1990, the couple purchased land and sought permission to station their caravan, but their applications were consistently refused on planning grounds, and enforcement notices were issued to remove their caravans. Despite appeals, offers to relocate to distant and expensive alternative sites, and attempts to challenge decisions in court, the applicants were ultimately unable to secure a lawful place to live in accordance with their cultural traditions.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), as well as Articles 3, 13, 14, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Commission found that while there was interference with the applicants’ rights, the measures were lawful, pursued legitimate aims such as environmental protection, and were not disproportionate. The application was declared inadmissible.
