This case highlights the ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Travellers in securing accommodation that respects their way of life, reflecting broader patterns of exclusion and the tension between planning controls and minority rights in late 20th-century Europe.

cases.title: ZENTRALRAT DEUTSCHER SINTI UND ROMA AND ROSE v. GERMANY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Zentralrat Deutscher Sinti und Roma and Rose v. Germany, the applicants were the Central Council of German Sinti and Roma—a registered association representing local and regional Sinti and Roma groups—and its president, Mr. Rose, both identifying with the Sinti and Roma communities. The case arose from a judgment by the Bochum District Court in 1996, which justified a landlord’s refusal to accept a Roma individual as a tenant, citing discriminatory stereotypes about Roma and Sinti as “traditionally unsettled” and unsuitable tenants. This judicial statement reflected a broader vulnerability faced by Roma and Sinti in Germany, namely, the persistence of prejudicial attitudes that can affect access to housing and reinforce social exclusion.

The applicants, though not parties to the original court proceedings, learned of the judgment through the media and raised their concerns with the Minister of Justice, seeking public condemnation and disciplinary action against the judge. They argued before the European Commission of Human Rights that the judgment discriminated against Sinti and Roma, violating Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

However, the Commission declared the application inadmissible, finding that neither the association nor Mr. Rose could claim to be a “victim” under the Convention, as they were not directly affected by the judgment. This case highlights the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller organisations face in challenging systemic discrimination at the European level, at a time when recognition of Roma and Sinti as national minorities was gaining ground in Europe.

cases.title: COOPER v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary:
In the case of Cooper v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, a British citizen of Gypsy origin, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom regarding his right to live in accordance with his traditional way of life. Mr. Cooper, who identified as a Gypsy and is included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers, faced persistent difficulties in securing a lawful place to station his caravans with his family in Hampshire. The core issue was the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families to planning restrictions that disrupt their nomadic lifestyle and family life, often resulting in repeated evictions and instability.

From the 1980s through the mid-1990s, Mr. Cooper and his family were repeatedly refused planning permission to reside in caravans on land they owned, despite support from the local county council and evidence that agricultural workers’ mobile homes had been permitted nearby. The planning authorities cited harm to the rural character of the area and maintained that alternative council-run sites were available, leading to enforcement actions, fines, and an injunction against the family.

Mr. Cooper alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), arguing that planning policies discriminated against Gypsies and failed to accommodate their traditional lifestyle. However, before the European Commission of Human Rights could examine the merits, Mr. Cooper withdrew his application, and the case was struck out.

Although no substantive judgment was issued, the case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller families face in securing accommodation that respects their cultural identity—a recurring issue in the UK and across Europe, especially during the late twentieth century when planning laws often conflicted with nomadic traditions.

cases.title: WOOLHEAD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Woolhead v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Woolhead, is a British citizen of Romany Gypsy origin, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. He brought a case against the United Kingdom after being refused planning permission to live in a caravan with his family on his own land in North Weald, Essex. The harm at the centre of the case concerned the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals who, due to planning restrictions and a shortage of authorised sites, face obstacles in maintaining their traditional way of life and risk being forced into illegality or homelessness.

Mr. Woolhead, who had lived a nomadic lifestyle since childhood, purchased land in 1984 and settled there with his family. Despite the site’s previous use for vehicle repairs, local authorities issued enforcement notices and repeatedly refused planning permission for his caravan, citing green belt policies. Although a planning inspector recognised special circumstances and recommended approval, the Secretary of State ultimately dismissed the appeal in 1992, arguing that no exceptional justification existed for development in the green belt and that alternative sites might be available.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for home and private life), Article 6 (fair trial), Article 14 (non-discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property). However, it declared the application inadmissible, finding that the authorities’ actions fell within their margin of appreciation and that procedural safeguards had been respected.

This case highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing lawful accommodation and recognition of their cultural identity, reflecting broader patterns of exclusion in the late twentieth century.

cases.title: TURNER v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Turner v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Turner, is a British citizen who identifies as a Gypsy, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Her case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities facing barriers to living according to their traditional lifestyle, particularly through restrictive planning policies that disproportionately affect their ability to reside in caravans on private land. Ms. Turner had lived in her own caravan on a former British Telecom depot in Ibsley since 1993. In 1994, she applied for planning permission to remain on the site, but the local council refused, citing policies aimed at protecting the countryside and the New Forest Heritage Area. Her appeals, including to the High Court, were unsuccessful, with the courts upholding the planning policy and finding no discrimination or violation of her rights under domestic law.

Ms. Turner brought her case to the European Commission of Human Rights, alleging violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 6 (right to a fair hearing). The Commission examined whether the planning and judicial procedures provided sufficient safeguards and found the application inadmissible, concluding that the review available in the High Court met the requirements of the Convention.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller individuals face in securing legal recognition and protection for their traditional way of life, particularly in the context of restrictive land use policies—a recurring issue in the United Kingdom and across Europe during the late twentieth century.

cases.title: WITNEY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Witney v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Witney, a British citizen identifying as a Gypsy by birth and thus falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities facing barriers to maintaining their traditional lifestyle due to planning regulations and a shortage of authorised sites. Mr. Witney and his wife, after years of travelling and experiencing harassment both from other Travellers and the police, sought to settle on their own land in Buckinghamshire for health and family reasons. Despite purchasing land and applying for planning permission to live in a mobile home there, his application was refused on environmental and planning grounds, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. Mr. Witney argued that these decisions interfered with his rights under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (respect for private and family life), as well as Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). However, following the European Court’s judgment in Buckley v. the United Kingdom, which found no violation in a similar context, Mr. Witney withdrew his application, and the case was struck out. This case reflects the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing lawful residence and recognition of their cultural needs, particularly in the context of restrictive planning policies in the United Kingdom during the 1990s.

cases.title: BUCKLAND AND FAMILY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Struck out of the list
cases.summary: In the case of Buckland and Family v. the United Kingdom, the applicants were Ms. Buckland, her immediate and extended family, all of whom identified as Romany Gypsies—a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The core issue concerned the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing obstacles to maintaining their traditional nomadic lifestyle and securing stable accommodation, particularly when local planning laws restrict their ability to settle on their own land. In October 1993, Ms. Buckland and her sister purchased a plot known as the Paddock in Tanworth in Arden, Warwickshire, aiming to provide a permanent base for their families, especially to support the education and health needs of their children, including a terminally ill daughter. After moving onto the land in April 1994, the local authority served an enforcement notice requiring the removal of their caravans due to lack of planning permission. Despite appeals highlighting their cultural, medical, and educational needs, the planning inspector rejected their case in March 1996, citing environmental and safety concerns. The applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). However, following the European Court’s judgment in the related Buckley v. the United Kingdom case, which found no violation, the applicants withdrew their complaint, and the Commission struck the case out. This case illustrates the persistent legal and practical barriers faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing accommodation, a challenge rooted in longstanding patterns of exclusion across Europe.

cases.title: RÉKÁSI v. HUNGARY
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of RÉKÁSI v. Hungary, the applicant, a Hungarian pensioner residing in Budapest, challenged the outcome of regulatory offence proceedings against her. The case arose after a street quarrel on 9 June 1994, during which the applicant addressed Mrs. H. with highly offensive language, including the phrase "you shitty leprotic gypsy whore, you stupid goose." While the judgment does not explicitly confirm Mrs. H.'s identity, the applicant’s insult invoked anti-Roma slurs, suggesting the incident involved a person perceived as belonging to the Roma community. The applicant was fined for libel under Hungarian law, with the penalty confirmed after several rounds of administrative appeals. She also unsuccessfully sought criminal proceedings against Mrs. H. for alleged false accusations.

The applicant complained under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing that the proceedings were unfair and that her freedom of expression was violated. However, the European Commission of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible. The Commission found that Hungary’s reservation to Article 6, which excluded access to courts in regulatory offence cases, was sufficiently precise and valid under the Convention. As a result, the applicant’s lack of access to a court did not breach the Convention, and no violation was found.

cases.title: CASE OF BUCKLEY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of Art. 14+8
cases.summary:
In the case of Buckley v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mrs. Jane Buckley, a British citizen identifying as a Gypsy and thus part of the broader Roma and Traveller communities, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals facing difficulties in securing lawful accommodation for their traditional way of life, particularly due to restrictive planning laws and enforcement actions that disproportionately affect their ability to live in caravans.

Mrs. Buckley and her children had lived in caravans on land she owned in Willingham, Cambridgeshire, a practice consistent with her family’s longstanding Gypsy heritage. In 1989, she applied retrospectively for planning permission to station her caravans on her land but was refused by the local council, which cited overprovision of Gypsy sites, landscape protection, and road safety concerns. An enforcement notice was issued, requiring her to remove the caravans. Despite appeals, the authorities maintained their position, leaving Mrs. Buckley at risk of eviction and unable to lawfully continue her traditional lifestyle.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately found no violation. The Court concluded that the interference with Mrs. Buckley’s home was justified in the interests of environmental protection and planning control, and that the procedures had been fair. This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe regarding accommodation rights, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and legal obstacles to their traditional ways of life.

cases.title: AFFAIRE BUCKLEY c. ROYAUME-UNI
cases.conclusion: Non-violation de l'Art. 8;Non-violation de l'Art. 14+8
cases.summary:
In the case of Buckley v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mrs. Jane Buckley, is a British national of Roma (Gypsy) origin whose family has lived as Travellers in the Cambridge-South district for generations. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers facing restrictions on their traditional way of life, particularly the right to live in caravans on their own land. In 1988, Mrs. Buckley, seeking stability for her young children, settled her caravans on a plot she owned in Willingham, England. Despite her deep roots in the area and her desire to pass on her Traveller traditions, local authorities refused her planning permission, citing landscape protection and the availability of other sites, and ordered her to leave the land.

Mrs. Buckley argued that these actions interfered with her right to respect for her home and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and amounted to discrimination under Article 14. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the refusal of planning permission and the enforcement measures constituted a violation of these rights. Ultimately, the Court found no violation of Article 8 or Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, concluding that the interference was justified and proportionate in the circumstances.

This case is significant as it highlights the ongoing tension between planning laws and the rights of Roma and Traveller communities to maintain their traditional lifestyles. At a time when many Roma and Travellers across Europe faced increasing legal and social barriers, the judgment underscored the need for states to balance individual rights with broader public interests.

cases.title: BURTON v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In Burton v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Burton, is a British citizen of Romany Gypsy origin residing in Carmarthen, Wales. Her case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities, particularly regarding the right to maintain their traditional way of life in the face of restrictive local authority policies and planning laws. After years of living in settled accommodation due to repeated evictions and the absence of permanent caravan sites, Ms. Burton, diagnosed with terminal cancer, wished to spend her final days in a caravan according to Romany Gypsy tradition. Despite her family's efforts to secure a lawful site for their caravan, the local council was unable to provide suitable accommodation, and requests to live in a council-owned mobile home were refused.

Ms. Burton alleged that the council’s failure to accommodate her wishes amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment (Article 3), an unjustified interference with her private and family life (Article 8), and discrimination (Article 14) under the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Commission of Human Rights found her complaints inadmissible, concluding that the treatment did not reach the severity required for Article 3, and that Article 8 did not impose a positive obligation on authorities to provide accommodation of her choosing. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

This case is significant as it illustrates the legal and practical barriers Roma and Traveller individuals face in preserving their cultural traditions, especially in the context of end-of-life dignity, at a time when the rights of these communities were only beginning to receive wider recognition in European human rights law.

cases.title: SLEPCIK v. THE NETHERLANDS AND THE CZECH REPUBLIC
cases.conclusion: Inadmissible
cases.summary:
In the case of Slepčík v. the Netherlands and the Czech Republic, the applicants were a Roma family from Pardubice, Czech Republic, consisting of a husband, wife, and their four children. As members of the Roma and Travellers community, they alleged that they faced persecution by skinheads in the Czech Republic and that the authorities there failed to protect them, prompting their repeated asylum applications in the Netherlands. The core vulnerability at issue was the risk of racially motivated violence and the lack of effective state protection for Roma, compounded by difficulties in acquiring citizenship following the dissolution of Czechoslovakia.

The family first sought asylum in the Netherlands in August 1992, citing attacks and threats in their hometown. After their initial request was rejected and subsequently withdrawn, they returned to the Netherlands in May 1993 to reapply, but were again refused. Their legal efforts included appeals and interim measures, but Dutch courts ultimately found their claims insufficiently substantiated, noting some police action in response to the attacks in Pardubice and ongoing citizenship proceedings in the Czech Republic.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but found the application inadmissible. The Commission held that asylum and residence proceedings did not fall within the scope of Article 6, and that the applicants had not shown a real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment if returned. No remedies were awarded.

This case highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Travellers face in securing protection from racial violence and statelessness in Europe, reflecting the broader historical context of exclusion and legal uncertainty following the breakup of Czechoslovakia in the 1990s.
